Introduction
Taiwan, which also calls itself the Republic of China (ROC) and was once known as Formosa, is a self-governing East Asian democracy located across the Taiwan Strait from mainland China. Taiwan’s popularly elected leaders govern 23.2 million people on the main island of Taiwan; the archipelagoes of Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu; and other outlying islands. Taiwan is a semiconductor manufacturing powerhouse and, in 2025, was a top-five United States merchandise trading partner.
Since 1979, when the United States broke diplomatic relations with the ROC in order to establish diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China (PRC), the United States and Taiwan have maintained close unofficial relations. The 1979 Taiwan Relations Act (P.L. 96-8; 22 U.S.C. §§3301 et seq.) provides the legal basis for the unofficial relationship. PRC leaders have long expressed a determination to take control of Taiwan, whether peacefully or by force. U.S. policymakers have debated whether—and, if so, how and how much—to support the people of Taiwan in the face of PRC threats and coercion. A steady growth in PRC military capabilities since the 1990s and the increased intensity of PRC operations around Taiwan since 2022 have lent urgency to congressional debates.
Figure 1. Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu
/
Source: Graphic by CRS. Map generated using data from NGA, DoS, Esri, and DeLorme.
Note: Taiwan authorities also administer Tungsha Island (Pratas) and Taiping Island (Itu Aba) in the South China Sea (not pictured).
Taiwan’s Modern History
The Qing Empire—the predecessor polity to modern China—gained control of Taiwan in 1683, made Taiwan a province in 1885, and then ceded it to Japan in 1895 after losing a war to Japan. Taiwan’s subsequent half century as a Japanese colony ended in 1945, with Japan’s defeat in World War II. The ROC, founded on mainland China in 1912, assumed control of Taiwan and its outlying islands from the Japanese. ROC forces and the forces of the Communist Party of China (CPC) then fought for control of mainland China. In 1949, the victorious CPC established the PRC on mainland China, while the defeated ROC government retreated to Taiwan. 
On Taiwan, the ROC’s ruling party, the Kuomintang (KMT), imposed martial law and for decades systematically privileged “mainlanders”—those whose families had arrived on Taiwan from mainland China with the KMT—over the larger local “Taiwanese” population. In 1987, then-ROC President Chiang Ching-kuo lifted martial law, paving the way for political liberalization. His successor legalized opposition parties in 1989. Taiwan held its first direct election for the Legislative Yuan, Taiwan’s unicameral parliament, in 1992, and its first direct presidential election in 1996. Since 2000, the presidency has three times passed peacefully between Taiwan’s two leading parties, the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the KMT. 
U.S. Policy Toward Taiwan
For three decades after the ROC’s 1949 retreat to Taiwan, the United States continued to recognize the ROC as the legal government of China, even as the ROC no longer controlled territory on mainland China. The United States switched diplomatic recognition to the PRC on January 1, 1979. In a U.S.-PRC joint communiqué issued on the eve of derecognition of the ROC, the U.S. government stated it “acknowledges the Chinese position that there is but one China and Taiwan is part of China.” In an accompanying U.S. statement, the U.S. government said it would withdraw U.S. military personnel from Taiwan and terminate a U.S.-ROC Mutual Defense Treaty in effect since 1955. Per the statement, “In the future, the American people and the people of Taiwan will maintain commercial, cultural, and other relations without official government representation and without diplomatic relations.” 
The policy of maintaining official relations with the PRC and unofficial relations with Taiwan is at the core of the long-standing U.S. “one-China” policy. (See CRS In Focus IF12503, The U.S. “One-China” Policy and Taiwan.) A U.S. Department of State spokesperson publicly confirmed the second Trump Administration’s commitment to the U.S. one-China policy in July 2025. Echoing statements made in the previous two Administrations, the spokesperson referred to U.S. policy as being guided by the Taiwan Relations Act, three U.S.-China joint communiqués—concluded in 1972, 1978, and 1982—and the “Six Assurances,” statements that President Ronald Reagan authorized to be conveyed to Taiwan’s government in 1982. They include assurances that in negotiations with the PRC over the 1982 U.S.-PRC joint communiqué, the United States did not agree to prior consultation with the PRC on arms sales to Taiwan and did not agree to take any position on Taiwan’s sovereignty. (See CRS In Focus IF11665, President Reagan’s Six Assurances to Taiwan.) 
Pursuant to the Taiwan Relations Act, the United States conducts relations with Taiwan through the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT), a nonprofit corporation that operates under a contract with the U.S. Department of State. AIT’s Taipei Main Office performs many of the same functions as an embassy and is staffed by U.S. government personnel. Among the Taiwan Relations Act’s provisions is a directive that the United States “will make available to Taiwan such defense articles and defense services in such quantity as may be necessary to enable Taiwan to maintain a sufficient self-defense capability.” The act states, too, that it is U.S. policy “to maintain the capacity of the United States to resist any resort to force or other forms of coercion” against Taiwan. The act creates so-called “strategic ambiguity” by not specifying whether the United States would defend Taiwan in the case of a PRC attack.
In a January 2026 statement on PRC military exercises near Taiwan, the Department of State reaffirmed other long-standing elements of U.S. policy: “We urge Beijing to exercise restraint, cease its military pressure against Taiwan, and instead engage in meaningful dialogue. The United States supports peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait and opposes unilateral changes to the status quo, including by force or coercion.” 
Some of President Donald Trump’s statements and actions related to Taiwan have fed anxieties in Taiwan about the durability of U.S. support. While in Beijing for a May 2026 summit with PRC leader Xi Jinping, the President alleged in a Fox News interview that Taiwan President Lai Ching-te “wants to go independent.” The President stated, “I’m not looking to have somebody go independent, and you know, we are supposed to travel 9,500 miles to fight a war. I'm not looking for that. I want them to cool down.” (He added, “I want China to cool down.”) In the same interview, the President stated that he was holding “in abeyance” a $14 billion arms sales package for Taiwan—a follow-on to the largest-ever package of U.S. arms sales to Taiwan by value, an $11 billion package that his Administration announced in December 2025. The President stated that the second arms package was “a very good negotiating chip for us.” Returning to the United States from Beijing on Air Force One, the President told reporters that he and Xi had discussed Taiwan arms sales “in great detail.” 
After hosting Xi at the White House in September 2026, President Trump stated that he and Xi, “didn't spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan,” adding that Xi “understands very much how I feel.” According to a readout of Xi’s visit from China’s top diplomat, Xi “urged the U.S. side to adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence.’” The Trump Administration has not commented on the PRC statement. Longstanding U.S. policy has been to state that the United States “does not support” independence for Taiwan, rather than to state that it opposes it.
The President has repeatedly alleged that Taiwan “stole” its semiconductor industry from the United States. The second Trump Administration also imposed tariffs on Taiwan and most other U.S. trading partners starting in April 2025. (See CRS In Focus IF10256, U.S.-Taiwan Trade and Economic Relations.)
In June 2026 congressional budget hearings, Secretary of State and National Security Advisor Marco Rubio stated that “we don’t consult with the Chinese” on arms sales to Taiwan and that “our policy on Taiwan is not changing and did not change” during the May 2026 Trump-Xi summit. In September 2026, Rubio stated of the proposed $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, “anytime we do any sales—not to Taiwan, to anybody, it is always balanced against what are our own needs in different parts of the world and whether we can afford to sell something, because we may need it for ourselves.” (See CRS In Focus IF12481, Taiwan: Defense and Military Issues.)
Domestic Taiwan Politics 
President Lai (also known as William Lai) of the DPP took office in May 2024. The KMT and the smaller Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) together control the 113-seat Legislative Yuan. President Lai, who serves concurrently as DPP chairman, has highlighted “the threat of annexation from China” and asserted that Taiwan is a sovereign country. He has prioritized cooperation with the United States. The KMT broadly supports lowering tensions with the PRC through engagement and maintains openness to eventual unification with a democratic mainland China. The TPP presents itself as a centrist alternative to the DPP and KMT. Since 2024, the KMT and TPP have often worked together against the DPP executive.
Taiwan is to hold local elections—known as the Nine-in-One elections—on November 28, 2026. Voters are to elect mayors and city councilors in six special municipalities that report directly to Taiwan’s central government, plus county magistrates and other positions in 16 counties and county-level cities. In 2022 elections, KMT candidates won the top positions in 14 of the 22 jurisdictions. Presidential and Legislative Yuan elections are to be held in January 2028. 
Cross-Strait Relations
PRC leader Xi has declared the PRC will “strive for peaceful reunification,” but “will never promise to renounce the use of force” to secure control of Taiwan. To persuade Taiwan and the world to acquiesce to unification, the PRC has stepped up its military and maritime “law enforcement” activities around Taiwan, sought to coopt elements of Taiwan society, and sought to isolate Taiwan internationally. (See CRS In Focus IF12646, Taiwan and the International Community). In an October 10, 2026, speech marking the anniversary of the founding of the ROC, President Lai stated, “Taiwan cherishes peace, but we will not give up our freedom. We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination.”
Taiwan Legislation in the 119th Congress
The 119th Congress has supported security assistance for Taiwan, including Foreign Military Financing and the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative (P.L. 119-60 and P.L. 119-75). The Taiwan Non-Discrimination Act (P.L. 119-60) directs the U.S. governor of the International Monetary Fund to support Taiwan’s admission to the Fund. The Taiwan Assurance Implementation Act (P.L. 119-45) directs the State Department to review and reissue its guidance on contacts with Taiwan every five years.

Overview
Congress oversees the Farm Credit Administration (FCA), which is the federal financial regulator responsible for ensuring the safety and soundness of Farm Credit System (FCS) institutions and the Federal Agricultural Mortgage Corporation (Farmer Mac). FCA is directed by a three-member board of directors nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate (12 U.S.C. §2242). Currently, two positions are vacant, and one board member is serving beyond the end of his term.
Congressional oversight is provided by the House Committee on Agriculture and the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. The most recent oversight hearings with board members as witnesses were in the Senate on May 19, 2016, and in the House on November 19, 2019. The Senate committee most recently held a nomination hearing for an FCA board member in 2022.
Farm Credit Administration
FCA sets the policies, regulations, charters, and examinations of FCS and Farmer Mac entities. This includes compliance with laws concerning eligibility and regulations protecting the rights of borrowers. FCA is an independent agency with about 300 employees. It is located in McLean, VA, and conducts examinations from several field offices. FCA reports to Congress on the financial condition of FCS. Statutory authority for FCA is in the Farm Credit Act of 1971 (12 U.S.C. §§2241 et seq.), as amended, notably by the Agricultural Credit Act of 1987. Regulations are at 12 C.F.R. Part 600.
FCA’s operating expenses are paid through assessments on FCS banks and associations, not by congressional appropriations. However, annual Agriculture Appropriations Acts place limits on FCA’s expenses ($106.5 million in FY2026).
Farm Credit System 
FCS is a privately owned, federally chartered, nationwide financial cooperative that lends to full- and part-time farmers, farming-related businesses, rural homeowners, farmer-owned cooperatives, and certain rural utilities. Borrowers must meet creditworthiness requirements. FCS is not a lender of last resort.
Established in 1916 as a government-sponsored enterprise (GSE), FCS has a statutory mandate—and limitation—to serve agriculture. FCS is the only direct lender among the GSEs. It receives tax benefits, but FCS operates without any direct federal appropriations. Statutory authority for FCS is in the Farm Credit Act of 1971 (12 U.S.C. §§2001 et seq.), as amended.
FCS is composed of 4 regional banks that provide funds and support services to 55 smaller credit associations that in turn provide loans to eligible borrowers. FCS associations are owned by their borrowers, who are required to purchase stock as part of their loans. FCS banks and associations do not take deposits like commercial banks. It obtains funds by selling bonds on capital markets through the Federal Farm Credit Banks Funding Corporation. FCS banks are jointly and severally liable for the debt, meaning they stand collectively behind the obligations to repay bonds. The Farm Credit System Insurance Corporation ensures timely payment of principal and interest on bonds. 
As of December 31, 2025, FCS had $457 billion in total loans outstanding to agriculture, agribusiness, rural utility, and other borrowers. Agricultural loans are the largest portion ($289 billion). FCS provided 46% of loans on the sector-wide farm balance sheet at the end of 2024, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).
Farmer Mac
Farmer Mac is a secondary market for agricultural mortgages. It purchases loans from originating lenders and provides other risk management tools. Farmer Mac was created by Congress in 1987 as a privately funded GSE. It is an investor-owned corporation that is financially and corporately separate from FCS. Statutory authority for Farmer Mac is in the Farm Credit Act of 1971 (12 U.S.C. §§2279aa et seq.). 
As of December 31, 2025, Farmer Mac’s total business volume (a measure similar to assets) was $33 billion.
Board Members
As a regulator, FCA is directed by a three-member board of directors nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate (12 U.S.C. §2242). 
Terms for board members are six years in length, fixed when they begin, and staggered so that one term begins every two years regardless of whether a new member has been confirmed. Board members may not be reappointed after serving a full term or more than three years of an unexpired term. A board member may continue to serve beyond the end of his/her term until a replacement has been confirmed. This helps maintain continuity on the board if confirmation of successors is delayed. Not more than two members of the board may be from the same political party. Board member qualifications are to include some background in agricultural economics, financial reporting, finance, law, or financial regulation.
The President designates one member as chairman—not subject to further confirmation—who has often held that role until the end of his/her term. The chairman is also the chief executive officer (CEO) of FCA (12 U.S.C. §2244).
Current Board Member
The current FCA board has one member serving in an expired term. Two seats are vacant (Table 1). This leaves the board without the necessary quorum to conduct business (12 U.S.C. §2242(c)).
On January 20, 2025, President Trump designated Jeffery S. Hall, board member since 2015, as chairman and CEO of FCA. 
Hall replaced Vincent Logan, board member and chairman from 2022 to 2025, as chairman. Logan resigned from the FCA board on March 31, 2025, creating a vacancy. Subsequently, Glen R. Smith, board member since 2017 and chairman from 2019 to 2022, left the board after he was confirmed as USDA Under Secretary for Rural Development on August 7, 2026 (Figure 1). 
Table 1. Farm Credit Administration Board Members

Nominations
On September 28, 2026, President Trump nominated three individuals for the FCA board: Carl Bednarski (PN1365-1, for a vacancy set to expire in 2034), John Grunewald II (PN1365-2, for the vacancy set to expire in 2032), and James Russell Middleton (PN1365-3, for the seat held by Hall set to expire in 2030). The nomination for Bednarski includes a prospective term that would begin in 2028. Their nominations have been referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition and Forestry.
President Trump may nominate people for all three positions, given that there are two vacancies and the incumbent is serving beyond his original term. Bednarski and Grunewald are Republicans and Middleton is a Democrat, consistent with the requirement that not more than two members are from the same political party. The most recent time a President nominated someone outside his party was in 2015, when President Obama nominated Hall (PN40/114th Congress). President Obama also made a prospective reappointment; Kenneth A. Spearman was confirmed in 2009 to complete a term ending in 2010 with a simultaneous reappointment for a term ending in 2016 (PN817 and PN818/111th Congress).
History of Board Members 
Figure 1 is a timeline showing the service by board members since 2015. The timeline shows that terms are fixed, six years in length, and staggered (gray lines). A board member’s service depends on Senate confirmation and may extend beyond the end of a term (blue lines) until a successor is confirmed. Service as chairman is by presidential appointment (gold lines).
Historically, a full board occurred when board members typically served until their successors were confirmed. FCA last had a single board member for about 11 months in 1989. Since 2015, FCA has operated three times with a two-member board: twice following deaths and once following a resignation. Hall’s 10 years of service, with continuation after the end of his term in 2018, makes him the longest-serving board member in FCA history.

Appointments as chairman (in gold) are named by the President. Years are graphed from January 20 to coincide with inauguration years. The member serving the in the term before Jeffery S. Hall was Leland A. Strom. The member serving before Dallas P. Tonsager was Jill Long Thompson. Kenneth A. Spearman and Tonsager died while in office. Vincent G. Logan resigned. Glen R. Smith resigned after being confirmed as USDA Under Secretary for Rural Development.

The Significance of the Multi-Domain Task Force (MDTF)
Congress has expressed concern about the military threat posed by Russia and China. The Army believes to address this threat, it must be able to operate in a multi-domain (air, land, water, space, cyber, information) environment, requiring new operational concepts, technologies, weapons, and units. The MDTF is the Army’s self-described organization centerpiece of this effort. The Army’s Chief of Staff Paper #1: Army Multi-Domain Transformation Ready to Win in Competition and Conflict  describes the MDTF as “theater-level maneuver elements designed to synchronize precision effects and precision fires in all domains against adversary anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) networks in all domains, enabling joint forces to execute their operational plan (OPLAN)-directed roles.” 
MDTF Organization
Figure 1 depicts a generic MDTF.
Figure 1. Generic MDTF
/
Source: Army Information Paper provided to CRS, April 10, 2025.
Notes: MDEB = Multi-Domain Effects Battalion; HHC = Headquarters and Headquarters Company; MI = Military Intelligence; ERSE = Extended Range Sensing Element; ID = Information Dominance; LRFB = Long-Range Fires Battalion; HHB = Headquarters and Headquarters Battery; LRHW = Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon; MRC =Mid-Range Capability (also referred to  as Strategic Mid-Range Fires [SMRF]); HIMARS = High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems; FSC = Forward Sustainment Company; IFPC = Integrated Fire Protection Capability; BSB = Brigade Support Battalion.
MDTFs are to be tailored to Combatant Commander requirements, so it is possible the generic MDTF in Figure 1 may contain more, fewer, or other types of units depending on the requirements of its assigned theater of operations. 
Army Plans for MDTF Development 
The Army originally planned to build five MDTFs: two aligned to the Indo-Pacific region; one aligned to Europe; one stationed in the Arctic region and oriented on multiple threats; and a fifth MDTF aligned for global response. 
1st MDTF
The 1st MDTF was activated on September 16, 2020, and is headquartered at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, WA, and aligned to the U.S. Army Pacific.
2nd MDTF 
On April 13, 2021, the Army announced it would station its 2nd MDTF in Germany. The Germany-based MDTF is to support U.S. Army Europe and Africa. On September 16, 2021, the Army activated the 2nd MDTF at Clay Kaserne in Wiesbaden.
Split Stationing of the 2nd MDTF at Fort Drum, NY
On December 13, 2023, Senator Charles Schumer and Representative Elise Stefanik announced in 2025 Fort Drum, NY, would become the home of 1,495 soldiers and personnel from the 2nd MDTF’s Long-Range Fires Battalion (LRFB), Brigade Support Battalion (BSB), and Air Defense (IFPC) Battalion. The 2nd MDTF’s Headquarters and Effects Battalions, activated in 2021, would remain in Germany.
3rd MDTF
The Army activated the 3rd MDTF at Schofield Barracks, HI, in September 2022. The 3rd MDTF is to support the U.S. Army Pacific as a component of U.S. Pacific Command (USPACOM). 
2024 Army Force Structure Transformation Initiative and MDTFs
On February 27, 2024, the Army released a white paper, Army Force Structure Transformation, outlining plans to transform the force. The white paper noted the Army intended to “complete the build out of the Army’s five MDTFSs” and that
Three task forces will be assigned to U.S. Army Pacific (USARPAC); one will be assigned to U.S. Army Europe-Africa (USAREUR-AF); and another will be service-retained with a likely focus on the CENTCOM area of responsibility.  
April 2024 Update on MDTF Alignment and Stationing
According to an April 2024 Defense News article, the Army updated MDTF pre-decisional plans. The Army reportedly plans to consolidate Mid-Range Capability and Long-Range Hypersonic batteries under an LRFB and complete programming of the remaining Indirect Fire Protection Capability (IFPC) battalions over the next five years. The Army also plans to convert all brigade support companies to battalions. In terms of specific MDTFs
The 1st MDTF is to be fully established in FY2024 with a Multi-Domain Effects Battalion (MDEB), an IFPC battalion, a BSB, and an LRFB.
The 2nd MDTF is to be headquartered in Germany with an MDEB and other elements stationed at Fort Drum, NY, with an IFPC battalion, a BSB, and an LRFB. The 2nd MDTF is to be fully operational in FY2025 with the addition of the LRFB in FY2026. The 2nd MDTF is to focus on supporting the European theater.
The 3rd MDTF, headquartered in Hawaii with an MDEB, is to consist of an IFPC battalion, a BSB, and an LRFB stationed at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, WA, and is to be fully operational by FY2026.
The 4th MDTF is planned to be stationed at Fort Carson, CO, but is to focus on the Indo-Pacific theater and is to be fully operational by FY2027.
The 5th MDTF is planned to be stationed at Fort Bragg, NC, and is to concentrate on regions as determined. The 5th MDTF is to be fully operational by FY2028.
Potential Change to 2nd MDTF LRFB Deployment Plans
Reportedly, based on a May 1, 2026, Administration decision to remove 5,000 U.S. troops from Germany:
one full brigade will leave Germany and a long-range fires battalion that was due to be deployed later this year will be cancelled. 
While specific units were not identified, the 2nd MDTF’s LRFB had previously been designated by the Army as European-aligned.
Possible 2nd MDTF Troop Deployment to Korea
Reportedly, the Army plans to move “hundreds of multidomain troops from Germany to South Korea within the year,” although this was not confirmed by the Pentagon. The report suggests that the 2nd MDTF’s MDEB “would join U.S. Forces Korea to strengthen capabilities against North Korea while bolstering deterrence against China.”
Multi Domain Command Europe
In January 2026, the Army created Multi Domain Command Europe (MDC-E) by merging the 56th Artillery Command with the 2nd MDTF. According to the Army, MDC-E “plans, integrates, executes, and assesses long-range precision fires and multi-domain effects for U.S. Army Europe and Africa to destroy enemy A2/AD capabilities and disrupt ground forces.”
Multi Domain Command Pacific
According to U.S. Army Pacific, the 1st MDTF is to merge with the 7th Infantry Division (ID) to form Multi Domain Command Pacific (MDC-PAC). U.S. Army Pacific further noted the following: “The new command merges the 7th Infantry Division’s two Stryker infantry brigades with the multidomain fires, cyber, space, electronic warfare and intelligence capabilities developed by the 1st MDTF.”
4th MDTF Activated
On October 8, 2026, the Army activated the 4th MDTF at Fort Carson, CO. The 4th MDTF, consisting of almost 2,100 soldiers, along with the 1st MDTF “reports to the 7th Infantry Division, designated as the multi-domain operational headquarters.”
MDTFs and How the Army Fights
On October 7, 2026, the Vice Chief of Staff of the Army published How the Army Fights. This new operational warfighting guidance
builds on the Army’s multidomain operations doctrine by explaining how the force employs land power at the operational level of war. The guidance aligns how the Army organizes, trains, equips and sustains its formations for contested, high-intensity conflict.
Neither the MDTF’s nor MDC’s operational or doctrinal roles are specifically discussed in How the Army Fights, except in a hypothetical vignette on pages 32 and 33.
Possible Oversight Issues for Congress
Possible oversight issues for Congress could include
Did MDCs, MDTFs, or subordinate units play an operational role in Operation Epic Fury and ongoing operations in the Middle East? If so, what are some of the emerging lessons and how might they influence future MDC and MDTF development and alignment?
If the 2nd MDTF’s LRFB is not to be forward stationed in Germany as originally planned, how might this impact the 2nd MDTF’s concept of operational support of U.S. European Command (USEUCOM) and NATO? Also, if elements on the 2nd MDTF are deployed to Korea as reported, how might this impact operations in Europe and Africa?
In view of the release of How the Army Fights, has the Army’s thinking about MDTFs and newly established MDCs changed or evolved since the Army’s 2024 white paper Army Force Structure Transformation? If so, what are the associated changes and how might they affect MDC and MDTF force structure, basing, regional alignment, and operational role?

api_metadata.summary:
The Internal Revenue Service’s (IRS’s) Free File Program (FFP) is a public-private partnership between the IRS and Free File, Inc. (FFI), a group of tax software companies. The FFP allows certain taxpayers to electronically file (e-file) their federal income tax return free of charge using guided software provided by participating tax preparation companies. According to a 2023 FFP memorandum of understanding (MOU), the objective of the program is to increase e-filing of tax returns, especially for economically disadvantaged populations, through collaboration between the IRS and member companies. 
In general, expanding e-filing options was originally intended to save taxpayers and the government time and money. According to a 2002 press release from the Department of the Treasury (Treasury), e-filing benefits include quicker refunds, lower taxpayer filing errors, and lower government processing costs. 
This In Focus summarizes the FFP’s origin and evolution, taxpayer participation and experience, and policy issues. 
Origin of the FFP
The IRS developed the FFP to comply with provisions in law. The IRS Restructuring and Reform Act of 1998 (RRA; P.L. 105-206) directed the IRS to increase the share of e-filed individual returns from 23% in 1998 to 80% by 2007, with input from the private sector. This goal was prioritized by President George W. Bush’s E-Government Initiative. A 2001 directive from the Office of Management and Budget’s Quicksilver Task Force identified the EZ Tax Filing Initiative as one of 24 projects to achieve the E-Government Initiative’s main objectives. The EZ Tax Filing Initiative was intended to help the IRS reach the individual e-filing goal established in the RRA. The IRS first achieved the 2007 e-filing goal in 2012, when 83% of federal individual income tax returns were e-filed. In FY2025, e-filing was the most predominant filing method, with over 93% of federal individual income tax returns filed online.  
Initially, the IRS tried to accomplish the aims of the EZ Tax Filing Initiative by developing free digitized versions of Form 1040 and related instructions; however, in January 2002, the Treasury asked the IRS to establish a partnership with tax software companies to develop a free online filing system that would be managed by the IRS for low-income taxpayers, who were most likely to file paper returns. The Treasury asserted that a public-private partnership was the best way to encourage growth in e-filing because it allowed the IRS to leverage the expertise of established companies in the field rather than requiring the IRS to develop its own software. 
The FFP originated later that year, in October 2002, when the IRS signed an agreement with the 17 original FFI member companies.
Evolution and Structure of the FFP
The October 2002 agreement provided a division of authority and responsibility between the IRS and the member companies. It required the companies to provide their tax preparation and filing services through IRS.gov at no cost to the bottom 60% of individual taxpayers, ranked by adjusted gross income (AGI).
The companies, not the IRS, set the eligibility requirements for free filing based on a taxpayer’s age, income, and state of residence. To participate in the FFP, a company had to prove that it could serve at least 10% of individual filers. 
A controversial element of the agreement was a commitment by the IRS to not compete in the market for tax filing and preparation. Preventing the IRS from becoming a competitor was a major incentive for tax software companies to participate in the FFP. Other incentives for member companies included marketing benefits or the potential for retaining FFP participants as paid customers if they later became ineligible for the FFP.
The IRS and FFI have extended and revised the original agreement several times. The second (2005) agreement reduced the free services a member company could offer to eligible taxpayers, barred member companies from providing free filing to more than 50% of eligible taxpayers, and increased the share of taxpayers eligible for the FFP to the bottom 70% of individuals ranked by AGI. The third (2009) agreement expanded the FFP—by making free fillable individual income tax forms available to any taxpayer, regardless of income—and required FFI companies to embed a link to IRS.gov in their FFP online pages. 
These subsequent agreements are linked to various MOUs intended to implement the revised agreements. The first MOU was signed in 2006. The current MOU was signed in 2023 and has been extended to October 31, 2029. It includes provisions intended to raise taxpayer awareness of the FFP, encourage eligible taxpayers to regularly use it, and prevent participating companies from excluding their Free File pages from internet searches. In a departure from previous rules, the MOU contains no commitment from the IRS to not develop its own free direct e-filing system.
The number of companies participating in the FFP has decreased from the 17 original members in 2002 to 8 members in 2026. According to the Government Accountability Office (GAO), two of the largest companies—H&R Block and Intuit—left the program at the end of the 2020 and 2021 tax filing seasons, respectively. These two companies combined had served approximately 70% of FFP participants. 
Taxpayer Participation and Experience
The FFP provides eligible taxpayers with access to member companies’ free online guided tax preparation and filing software tools. These tools use a self-directed tax preparation method, in which taxpayers input information about their tax situations that member companies use to complete and e-file the tax returns. The FFP is focused on covering taxpayers that are least able to afford e-filing, and it is currently available to taxpayers with an AGI of $89,000 or less. 
Since the FFP’s inception, participation among eligible taxpayers has averaged 3% each year. Participation peaked at roughly 6% (5.1 million taxpayers) in 2004, while the lowest participation rates were 2% each year from 2016 through 2018 (2.5 million to 2.6 million taxpayers). In FY2025, roughly 3% of taxpayers eligible for the FFP (3.2 million taxpayers) used the FFP, including both free fillable forms and guided tax preparation software. In tax year 2019, 44% of taxpayers who used the FFP had an AGI of $17,000 or less. Most users were single filers, under the age of 35, and did not claim dependents. 
Most FFP-eligible taxpayers used other options for filing their tax return that likely would have required a fee. While a lack of awareness of the FFP may explain some of the low take-up for the program, there is also evidence that many first-time FFP users do not maintain usage in future years, even if they are still eligible for the program. A 2020 Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) evaluation found that reasons contributing to low program participation were “complexity, confusion, and lack of taxpayer awareness about the operation and requirements of the [FFP].” GAO estimated that roughly 40% of FFP users opted to use other filing options for the following year’s tax return. 
GAO reported that despite efforts to improve the taxpayer experience, opportunities remained to better align taxpayer experiences with existing guidelines for federal digital services. These opportunities could include optimizing the FFP for mobile devices, increasing access for taxpayers with disabilities, and providing the software in more languages. 
Policy Considerations
Some concerns about the FFP’s performance surfaced in 2019 during congressional consideration of a bill to reform certain aspects of IRS’s taxpayer service. In April of that year, the House passed a bill (the Taxpayer First Act) that supporters intended to strengthen and codify taxpayer rights and further transform the IRS into a customer-friendly agency. One provision would have codified the existing FFP and permanently banned the IRS from providing its own direct e-file service.
The prospect of a statutory ban on an IRS direct-file tool triggered debate over the potential advantages and disadvantages of the FFP. The enacted bill (P.L. 116-25) did not include a provision to codify the FFP. The amended Free File MOU adopted in 2019 removed the provision banning the IRS from developing its own direct-file tool. 
Direct File
The IRS developed its own free tax preparation tool in a pilot program called Direct File (DF). The law commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (P.L. 117-169) provided the IRS with $15 million to create a DF task force to explore the feasibility of an IRS-run DF program; the IRS launched DF for use by eligible taxpayers in 2024.
Similar to software provided in the FFP, DF provided taxpayers with a free guided tax preparation and filing tool. Although DF was available to taxpayers regardless of income, the tool was only able to support taxpayers with relatively simple tax returns in a limited number of participating states.
DF was offered in the 2024 and 2025 filing seasons but was suspended for the 2026 filing season. In October 2025, the Treasury announced that it was suspending the DF program “due to the program’s high costs, limited participation, and the [IRS’s] need to focus resources on other priorities.” 
Potential Advantages and Disadvantages of the FFP 
FFP proponents, including FFI companies, argue that the program should be retained because of its significant cost savings. According to one estimate, FFP filing saved taxpayers $1.5 billion in tax preparation and filing fees and saved the IRS millions of dollars in processing costs from 2003 to 2018. 
Another potential advantage of the FFP cited by proponents is that it has the current technology to support a broad population.  Although most tax returns filed through the FFP were simple returns, the tax preparation software available to taxpayers can support complex tax returns. Some participating members also offer free state tax returns for certain taxpayers, even though the FFP MOU does not require free state tax filing.  
FFP critics say the FFP should be replaced by an IRS DF tool open to all taxpayers, regardless of income. Among the problems cited by critics are the following: (1) member company web pages for FFP filing are confusing and, in some cases, misleading; (2) the participation rate remains low; and (3) there are concerns relating to taxpayer privacy and security.  
Critics also say that the program allows FFI companies to divert FFP-eligible taxpayers to using their paid filing services. In its 2020 report, TIGTA found that over 34.5 million FFP-eligible taxpayers e-filed their returns using member company paid services in FY2019. Other reporting found that FFI companies consistently discouraged interest in FFP alternatives.
Another potential policy option could include retaining the FFP, with additional investments in promoting the FFP among eligible taxpayers and in monitoring MOU compliance. 
Recent Developments
There is continued congressional interest in assessing free e-file options available to taxpayers, particularly the DF program and its potential impact on the FFP. In the 119th Congress, bills have been introduced to restore the DF program (S. 3948/H.R. 7806), while other bills have been introduced to prohibit the IRS from preparing tax returns through the DF program (S. 96/H.R. 451). 
In a 2025 report, the Treasury highlighted various planned efforts to improve the FFP including enhancing awareness of the program, evaluating user experience, and strengthening program oversight. Additional evaluations of the FFP by GAO are also planned and may be helpful in assessing FFP performance.

Congress has established programs to assist constituents—including individuals, organizations, and local governments—with drinking water and wastewater infrastructure projects. This In Focus includes a list of selected federal grant, loan, and other programs that support such projects. The following programs vary in scope and funding level and are not a comprehensive list of all potentially relevant programs for a given project. 
Most federal grant funds go to state and local governments, which in turn may issue sub-awards to other entities. Interested applicants can contact federal agencies, state agencies, or both, for information on eligibility, the application process, award cycles, and funding availability. Each program’s funding availability generally depends on annual appropriations. Where applicable, program websites and Assistance Listing IDs are provided herein to assist interested applicants with accessing more information about each program. Assistance Listing IDs can be used to search for potential funding opportunities at https://grants.gov.
Selected U.S. EPA Programs
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) receives annual appropriations for several drinking water and wastewater infrastructure programs. Additional information can be found at https://www.epa.gov/water-infrastructure.
State Revolving Funds Programs
The State Revolving Funds (SRFs) programs are federal-state partnerships wherein EPA provides grants to all 50 states (and Puerto Rico) to capitalize revolving funds. States then administer these funds as loans (or as additional subsidization, such as principal forgiveness, in certain cases) to drinking water and wastewater systems and to other entities for infrastructure projects and related activities necessary to comply with the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) or the Clean Water Act (CWA). From EPA’s SRF appropriations, the agency provides funding directly to the U.S. territories, the District of Columbia, and federally recognized tribes for eligible water infrastructure projects, because these entities do not administer SRF programs. Assistance Listing ID 66.468 (Drinking Water SRF); and Assistance Listing ID 66.458 (Clean Water SRF)
Sewer Overflow and Stormwater Reuse Municipal Grants Program
This program provides grant funding to states for projects that help communities address combined sewer overflows, sanitary sewer overflows, or stormwater infrastructure, among other activities. Assistance Listing ID 66.447
Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act 
The Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (WIFIA) program provides long-term, low-cost loans for eligible drinking water and wastewater infrastructure projects, including those eligible under the SRFs. EPA awards loans directly to recipients. The minimum project cost is $20 million for large communities and $5 million for small communities (populations of 25,000 or less). Assistance Listing ID 66.958
Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation (WIIN) Act Programs
The Assistance for Small and Disadvantaged Communities Grant Program, which the Trump Administration has renamed as the Small, Rural, and Tribal Drinking Water Grant Program, generally provides grants to states, territories, and tribes to assist water systems with meeting the requirements of SDWA, among other eligibilities. Assistance Listing ID 66.442
The Reducing Lead in Drinking Water Program awards funding on a competitive basis to assist disadvantaged communities with lead reduction projects such as replacing lead service lines and removing potential sources of lead in drinking water. Assistance Listing ID 66.443
The Voluntary School and Child Care Lead Testing and Reduction Grant Program provides funding to states, territories, and tribes to remediate lead in drinking water at schools and childcare facilities. Assistance Listing ID 66.444
Training and Technical Assistance for Small Systems Funding
This program funds technical assistance efforts for small drinking water and wastewater systems, including training, site visits, and other support. Assistance Listing IDs 66.436 and 66.424
U.S.-Mexico Border Water Infrastructure Grant Program
This program funds drinking water and wastewater infrastructure projects in the United States and projects in Mexico that are within 62 miles of the southern border and have a U.S.-benefit. Project sponsors apply to the program through the North American Development Bank, which screens for initial eligibility and prioritizes projects using EPA’s ranking methodologies.
Selected USDA Programs
Through the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA’s) Rural Utilities Service’s Water and Environmental Programs, rural communities may be able to obtain grants, loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance to construct or improve their drinking water and wastewater disposal systems. Additional information can be found at https://www.rd.usda.gov/programs-services/water-environmental-programs.   
Water & Waste Disposal Loan & Grant Program
This program provides loans and grants to eligible rural communities to acquire, construct, or improve their water and waste disposal systems. Funds can also be used to help rural communities improve stormwater collection and disposal. Assistance Listing ID 10.760 
Water & Waste Disposal Loan Guarantees 
This program provides loan guarantees for projects that build or enhance clean and reliable drinking water systems, sanitary sewage disposal systems, and stormwater drainage to households and businesses in eligible rural areas. CDFA Number 10.760
Circuit Rider Program 
This program provides technical assistance to rural water systems that are experiencing day-to-day operational, financial, or management issues. Public bodies with legal authority to own and operate the water facility in question are eligible to receive technical assistance.
Emergency Community Water Assistance Grants 
This program provides grants to eligible rural communities to prepare for, or recover from, emergencies that threaten the availability of safe, reliable drinking water. Emergencies include natural disasters such as droughts or hurricanes and man-made disasters such as chemical spills. A federal disaster declaration is not required. Assistance Listing ID 10.763
Revolving Funds for Financing Water and Wastewater Projects
This program provides grants to qualified nonprofits for establishing revolving loan funds, which are to be used for issuing loans to eligible entities to extend and improve water and waste disposal systems in rural areas. Assistance Listing ID 10.864
Rural Decentralized Water Systems Grant Program
This program provides grants to qualified nonprofits and tribes to establish a revolving loan fund to provide loans to eligible rural households to construct, refurbish, or service their individually owned household water well and septic systems. Assistance Listing ID 10.862
Water & Waste Disposal Technical Assistance & Training Grants
This program provides grants to qualified nonprofits for providing technical assistance and training on identifying and evaluating solutions to water and waste problems for eligible rural communities. Nonprofits can also use the grants to help eligible rural communities prepare applications for USDA water and waste disposal programs. CDFA Number 10.761
Selected Other Federal Programs
U.S. Department of Commerce, Economic Development Administration, Public Works and Economic Adjustment Assistance (EAA) Programs
Public Works and EAA provide competitive grants to distressed communities for various types of economic development projects, including public works projects, such as water and sewer system improvements. On an occasional basis, supplemental EAA funding may be available for similar projects in areas impacted by certain disasters. Assistance Listing IDs 11.300 (Public Works) and 11.307 (EAA)
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Community Development Block Grants 
This program provides flexible federal funding to states and localities to support economic development, community development, and infrastructure, including drinking water and wastewater projects. Assistance Listing IDs 14.228 and 14.218
U.S. Small Business Administration, Office of Disaster Assistance
This program provides low-interest, long-term loans following a federally certified disaster. Loans are available to private for-profit and private nonprofit drinking water and wastewater utilities. Assistance Listing ID 59.008
U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Reclamation, WaterSMART Grants
WaterSMART grants provide cost-shared financial assistance on a competitive basis for water management improvements and conservation, including water efficiency, water marketing, and projects that save water or mitigate the risk of conflict over water. Projects must be located in the 17 Western States or United States Territories. Assistance Listing ID 15.507   
Federal Regional Commissions and Authorities (FRCAs)
FRCAs are congressionally chartered, federal-state partnerships that were developed to address economic distress in targeted geographic regions. Active FRCAs receive congressional appropriations for regional economic development, which may be used for drinking water and wastewater projects, among other purposes. Active commissions include the Appalachian Regional Commission, the Delta Regional Authority, the Denali Commission, the Northern Border Regional Commission, the Southeast Crescent Regional Commission, and the Southwest Border Regional Commission.

Background
The Army’s XM-30, previously known as the Optionally Manned Fighting Vehicle (OMFV), is being designed to replace the M-2 Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle (see Figure 1 for an XM-30 conceptual example). Optionally manned means the OMFV is to have the capability to conduct remotely controlled operations while a crew is not in the vehicle. The M-2 Bradley, in service since 1981, transports infantry on the battlefield, provides fire support to dismounted troops, and can destroy enemy fighting vehicles. Updated numerous times since its introduction, the M-2 Bradley is widely considered to have reached the technological limits of its capacity to accommodate new electronics, armor, and defensive systems.  
Acknowledging the M-2’s limitations, the Army is interested in adopting a fuel-efficient hybrid-electric drive to accommodate silent running and watch and to power new electronic warfare systems, counter uncrewed aerial systems defenses, and active protection and mission command systems. The Army also seeks to upgrade the M-2 Bradley’s 25mm main gun to 50mm and to incorporate loitering munitions launchers to enhance lethality.
Two past efforts to replace the M-2 Bradley—the Future Combat System (FCS) Program and the Ground Combat Vehicle (GCV) Program—were cancelled for programmatic and cost-associated reasons. On June 26, 2023, on the completion of the initial digital design phase, the Army redesignated the OMFV as the XM-30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle.
Figure 1. Conceptual XM-30 
/
Source: U.S. Army Acquisition Support Center, “Digital Engineering Learning Curve,” accessed September 1, 2026, https://asc.army.mil/web/news-digital-engineering-learning-curve/.
Note: This is a conceptual example; the Army’s XM-30 selected for production may differ from this example.
Role of the XM-30
According to the 2024 Department of Defense (DOD) FY2025 Program Acquisition Cost by Weapon System (DOD is “using a secondary Department of War designation,” under Executive Order 14347 of September 5, 2025),
[t]he XM-30 Combat Vehicle (previously OMFV), as part of an Armored Brigade Combat Team (ABCT), will replace the Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle to provide the capabilities required to defeat a future near-peer competitor’s force. The XM-30 is an optionally manned platform that maneuvers Soldiers to a point of positional advantage to engage in close combat and deliver decisive lethality during the execution of combined arms maneuver. It is designed to operate with and may operate without a crew and Soldiers under armor based on the commander’s decision. 
XM-30 Acquisition Approach
The XM-30 began as a Middle Tier of Acquisition (MTA) rapid prototyping program. The XM-30 is to be designed from the onset as a Modular Open Systems Architected (MOSA) platform based on an Army-defined and -owned open standard. As technology and software evolve, MOSA could facilitate rapid XM-30 modernization at a reduced cost. XM-30 open architecture could also offer more opportunities for industry competition and innovation for future XM-30 upgrades. The Army is conducting a five-phase XM-30 acquisition approach: 
Phase 1 consists of Market Research and Requirement Development.
Phase 2, Concept Design, includes modeling, simulation, and analysis (MS&A) to inform requirements and support initial design activities. 
Phase 3, Detailed Design, includes detailed design activities to mature XM-30 designs and concludes with a Critical Design Review (CDR), a technical review to ensure the initial product baseline is established. Successful completion of CDR provides the technical basis for proceeding into fabrication, integration, development, test, and evaluation of a system.
Phase 4, Prototype Build and Test, verifies prototype performance against performance specifications. Later in this phase, a limited user test (LUT) is to be conducted. 
Phase 5, Production and Fielding, is to result in a single Low-Rate Initial Production (LRIP) contract for production, testing, and initial fielding.  
Program Activities
Phase 2 Contracts Awarded
The Army announced the award of five firm-fixed price contracts for XM-30 Phase 2 Concept Design using full and open competitive procedures on July 23, 2021. The contracts were awarded to Point Blank Enterprises, Inc. (Miami Lakes, FL); Oshkosh Defense, LLC (Oshkosh, WI); BAE Systems Land and Armaments L.P. (Sterling Heights, MI); General Dynamics Land Systems (GDLS), Inc. (Sterling Heights, MI); and American Rheinmetall Vehicles, LLC (Sterling Heights, MI). The total award value for all five contracts was approximately $299.4 million. In this phase, competing firms were asked to develop digital designs. 
Phase 3 and 4 Contracts Awarded
On June 26, 2023, the Army announced
the award of two firm-fixed price contracts for the Optionally Manned Fighting Vehicle [XM-30] Phase III and IV Detailed Design and Prototype Build and Testing phases, using full and open competitive procedures. The contracts were awarded to General Dynamics Land Systems Inc. [GDLS] (Sterling Heights, Michigan) and American Rheinmetall Vehicles LLC (Sterling Heights, Michigan). The total award value for both contracts is approximately $1.6 billion.
XM-30 Preliminary Design Review (PDR)
Reportedly, GDLS and American Rheinmetall completed their PDR in August 2024, and development of physical prototypes was planned to begin after a CDR. According to Defense News,
[p]rototypes will take 18 to 20 months to construct after the critical design reviews wrap up. Once prototypes are delivered, the Army will move into a test and evaluation phase with both competitors before deciding on a winner in [FY]2027. The first vehicles are expected to be fielded in [FY]2029.
Milestone B Decision 
In June 2025, the U.S. Army reportedly approved Milestone B for the XM-30 program, advancing it to the engineering manufacturing development phase after both competitors completed CDRs. In February 2026, Army leadership reportedly opted not to sign documentation finalizing the Milestone B decision and transition to a Major Capability Acquisition (MCA) pathway to avoid locking the service into a specific design or a slow acquisition path, effectively pausing formal program transition and prompting a reevaluation of the program’s approach.
XM-30 Milestone B Pause and a New Request for Information (RFI)
According to the February 2026 report, the then Chief of Staff of the Army General Randy George and then Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll decided not to sign off on the Milestone B decision “to leave the door open to a major reworking of the XM-30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle program.” Reportedly, regarding the pause, an Army spokesman stated the following:
“We are actively assessing multiple, competing designs for the XM-30 to foster a truly competitive environment.... We continue to look for partners who can deliver cutting-edge solutions now, not decades from now.” 
FY2027 XM-30 Budget Request
According to Army Budget documents, the Army is requesting $547 million in procurement funding for 19 prototype vehicles for evaluation. The Army notes that prime contractors have yet to be identified, but award decisions for the 19 vehicles will be based on contractor performance during testing and operational evaluations.
Fall 2026 XM-30 Testing
Reportedly, the 1st Cavalry Division at Fort Hood in Texas is to be the first unit to receive new prototypes of the XM-30 this fall. Reportedly,
[t]he Army’s largest division will take on two platoons of the XM30, designed to replace the Bradley Fighting Vehicle, and one platoon of M1E3 Abrams tanks by the end of the year. From there, soldiers will be “shooting, moving and communicating” at the National Training Center [NTC] at Fort Irwin, CA, through March [2027]. 
The Army Test and Evaluation Command (ATEC) reportedly is to “work in conjunction with the division to monitor the assessments from 1st Cavalry soldiers, who will provide feedback to engineers for minor adjustments.’”
First XM-30 Prototypes Delivered
Reportedly, GDLS delivered its first prototype, the Wolf, at the end of August 2026, and American Rheinmetall delivered its first prototype, known as the Lynx, on September 1, 2026, to support Fort Hood operational testing scheduled for fall 2026.
Change in XM-30 Acquisition Pathway
Reportedly, “because the Milestone B didn’t happen the way it had been anticipated previously,” the XM-30 program will now adopt an MTA rapid prototyping pathway. According to Army officials, “MTA’s help cut costs and timelines for new programs, allowing acquisition organizations develop and deliver high need capabilities to the Army faster than an MCA.” Under the XM-30 MTA pathway, down selection to a single vendor is expected in late spring or June 2027.
Potential Oversight Issues for Congress
Potential oversight issues could include the following:
New Army Leadership and the XM-30
With General George’s retirement in April 2026 and Secretary Driscoll’s reported resignation on August 31, 2026, the Army is presently without Senate-confirmed senior leadership. At some point in the future, a new Secretary of the Army and Chief of Staff of the Army are likely to be nominated for confirmation. Once confirmed, a new Secretary of the Army and Chief of Staff could have differing views on the requirements for a Bradley replacement, the current XM-30 program, and Army modernization priorities altogether. Once new Army leadership is confirmed, Congress might decide to seek clarification from the Army on its views on the future of the XM-30 program.
XM-30 Organic Counter Uncrewed Aerial Systems (C-UAS) Capability
While the Army has stated that the XM-30 is to have an organic active protection system (APS) that can detect, track, and neutralize anti-tank threats by means of kinetic and passive countermeasures, it is not clear if the XM-30 also will have an organic C-UAS capability. Some have suggested that UAS, loitering munitions, and one-way attack drones could make armored fighting vehicles (AFVs) obsolete; others contend new technologies are needed to improve AFV survivability against UAS and other aerial systems. Congress might decide to examine the Army’s approach to providing organic protection to the XM-30 against aerial threats.

The Marketing Assistance Loan (MAL) program has been a significant feature of U.S. farm commodity support policy and farm bills since the 1930s. The MAL program provides low-interest loans to eligible farmers collateralized by eligible stored commodities. MALs help farmers meet cash flow needs while allowing them to delay sales of harvested commodities until later in the marketing year when market conditions may improve. The MAL program also provides price support to borrowers when market prices drop below levels specified in statute. Congress has authorized the Loan Deficiency Payment (LDP) program in farm bills since the 1980s. The LDP program provides payments equivalent to the price support benefits available under the MAL program to eligible farmers who have not taken out MALs for their stored commodities. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Farm Service Agency administers both programs. The FY2025 budget reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21) extended the MAL and LDP programs through crop year 2031 and made changes to increase the support provided to participating farmers.  
Marketing Assistance Loan Program
The MAL program offers producers or processors—depending on the commodity—nine-month-term nonrecourse and recourse loans for qualifying stored commodities. Under nonrecourse loans, USDA must accept the forfeited crop pledged as collateral as full payment of an outstanding loan. Under recourse loans, the borrower is liable for repaying the loan in full. Borrowers cannot sell or otherwise market their stored commodities until they repay their MALs. Borrowers may repay loans at any time before maturity without penalty. Interest rates are fixed at 1% above U.S. Treasury rates. Commodities may be stored in an approved warehouse or on the farm.
MALs are valued at commodity-specific, statutory loan rates (Table 1). For example, consider a hypothetical farmer who has 10,000 bushels of corn in storage on a day in 2026 when the local market price is $5.00 per bushel. The farmer could sell the corn in the market for $5.00 per bushel that day and receive $50,000. If the farmer takes out a MAL that day, the loan amount would be $24,200—not $50,000—because the 2026 statutory loan rate for corn is $2.42 per bushel. At loan maturity, the farmer would be responsible for repaying $24,200 plus interest charges.      
Nonrecourse MALs offer price support benefits at any point in time while a commodity’s price is below the loan rate. If local market prices fall below the MAL rates, farmers may repay nonrecourse loans at the market price or surrender the commodity used as collateral in lieu of repayment, and USDA waives any accrued interest charges. Farmers receive the difference between the lower market price and the higher MAL rate as a marketing loan gain.

The 2019-2025 upland cotton MAL rate was the average price over two years, limited to a range of $0.45- $0.52/lb.
Other oilseeds include canola, crambe, flaxseed, mustard seed, rapeseed, safflower, sesame seed, and sunflower seed.
Assume the hypothetical farmer with 10,000 bushels of corn took out a MAL worth $24,200. If one day the local market price drops to $2.30 per bushel, the farmer could surrender his corn to USDA or pay off the MAL in cash at the local market price of $2.30 per bushel, $23,000 total. In both cases, the farmer would retain the difference between the original loan amount ($24,200) and the repaid amount (either $23,000 in cash or $23,000 worth of forfeited corn) as a marketing loan gain ($1,200).  
USDA announces local market prices for all commodities eligible for MALs. For most commodities, the local price is posted daily and based on U.S. prices. In accordance with statute, USDA announces weekly prices for cotton and rice based on international prices. 
Loan Deficiency Payment Program
Eligible farmers who do not sign up for MALs may elect to participate in the LDP program. When market prices fall below the MAL rates, the LDP program provides payments to eligible producers equal to the amount of the MAL gains, in lieu of executing a MAL. LDPs are available for the same commodities eligible for MALs, with two exceptions. Extra-long staple cotton is eligible for MALs but not LDPs. Unshorn pelts are eligible for LDPs but not MALs. 
Funding and Program Outlays
The MAL and LDP programs receive mandatory appropriations of “such sums as necessary” through USDA’s Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC). Program outlays vary from year to year on the basis of enrollments and market conditions (Figure 1). Between 2021 and 2024, commodity prices were relatively high. During that time, farmers took out fewer MALs, total lending decreased, and fewer price support payments were triggered compared with prior years. 
Figure 1. Marketing Assistance Loans Made and Loan Gains Plus Loan Deficiency Payments, Crop Years 2016-2025
/
Source: CRS calculations using U.S. Department of Agriculture program data, downloaded September 28, 2026. 
Notes: Values adjusted for inflation to 2026 dollars using the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis Implicit Price Deflators for Gross Domestic Product, updated October 2026.
Between 2018 and 2025, farmers took out MALs totaling approximately $6.5 billion per year on average (not adjusted for inflation) for all eligible commodities with the exception of crambe and sesame seeds. Over that period, price support benefits were triggered at times for chickpeas, cotton, honey, lentils, mohair, peanuts, soybeans, wheat, wool, and unshorn pelts. Farmers received approximately $334.1 million in MAL gains and LDPs and forfeited commodities to USDA worth approximately $71.5 million (not adjusted for inflation). 
FY2025 Budget Reconciliation Law
The FY2025 budget reconciliation law made changes to increase the support provided to farmers from the MAL and LDP programs. The law increased the statutory loan rates for all eligible commodities (Table 1) for crop years 2026-2031. The law increased the minimum storage payment for forfeited cotton and made changes to how cotton world prices are calculated for the purpose of repaying MALs.
2026 Farm Bill
The House-passed and Senate committee-reported versions of the 2026 farm bill (H.R. 7567 and S. 5526) would make no changes to the MAL or LDP programs. However, both bills would allow farmers to repay nonrecourse MALs when USDA employees are furloughed because of a lapse in USDA appropriations.
Issues for Congress
MALs are intended to incentivize farmers to store more of their production after harvest, potentially allowing for more consistent supplies and market prices throughout the year. During the 1950s, 1960s, and 1980s, market prices remained below loan rates for extended periods. This led to frequent loan forfeitures and large government stock holdings at relatively high costs to taxpayers. Farmers also planted crops on the basis of loan rates rather than market prices. Congress created the LDP program and additional MAL program features in the 1980s. These changes reduced commodity forfeitures and USDA’s expenditures for storing and selling commodities. Congress has expanded the list of eligible loan crops over the decades, most recently adding dry peas, lentils, and small and large chickpeas in 2002.
The Agriculture Improvement Act (2018 farm bill; P.L. 115-334) removed limitations on the maximum benefits that an individual or legal entity can receive per year from the MAL and LDP programs. Some policymakers advocate for tighter limits to lower program costs and respond to concerns about payments to large farms. Others contend that large farms should not be penalized for the economies of size and efficiencies they have achieved.
Congress and USDA provided supplemental commodity support for some of the commodities eligible for MALs and LDPs in 2024 and 2025; this was timed to help farmers manage cash flow needs after harvest. Congress could consider whether to further modify the MAL and LDP programs to reduce the need for future supplemental commodity support, taking into account that any expansion in these programs under the existing farm bill baseline may require funding reductions for other farm bill priorities. Higher MAL rates allow farmers to receive higher valued loans for their stored commodities. Higher MAL rates also increase the likelihood of triggering MAL gains and LDP payments. Interest payments from repaid MALs partially offset the program’s cost to taxpayers.

api_metadata.summary:
The federal crop insurance program (FCIP) offers insurance coverage for crops and livestock to help mitigate potential financial consequences of adverse growing and market conditions. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) regulates the policies offered and subsidizes the premiums that farmers pay in order to encourage farmer participation in the program. Premium subsidies were approximately $15 billion in 2026, which accounted for about 66% of the total premium on average for all policies sold in 2026. Since its inception in 1938, the FCIP has grown from an ancillary program with low participation to a central pillar of federal farm support. In the 10-year period from 2017 to 2026, the program grew from insuring more than 311 million acres to more than 572 million acres (84% increase) and from insuring more than $106 billion to more than $209 billion in crop and livestock value (96% increase in nominal terms, 48% in inflation-adjusted terms) (Figure 1). 
Figure 1. Acres and Value Insured by the Federal Crop Insurance Program, 2000-2026
/
Source: CRS calculations using data from U.S. Department of Agriculture Risk Management Agency Summary of Business database, downloaded September 25, 2026. 
Notes: Years are crop years. Values adjusted for inflation using the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis Implicit Price Deflators for Gross Domestic Product where 2026=100, updated October 2026. 
By law, the FCIP operates as a public-private partnership. Farmers purchase FCIP policies from private sector companies—Approved Insurance Providers (AIPs)—who sell and service FCIP policies under contracts with USDA. USDA provides administrative and operating (A&O) subsidies to compensate AIPs for the cost of selling and servicing FCIP policies. USDA also provides insurance for the AIPs (i.e., reinsurance) for most policies sold and shares the gains and losses from reinsurance with the AIPs as per the terms of the contracts.
The FCIP is permanently authorized under the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938 (P.L. 75-430, 52 Stat. 72) and the Federal Crop Insurance Act of 1980 (P.L. 96-365, 7 U.S.C. §§1501 et seq.), as amended. The FY2025 budget reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21) made changes to increase premium subsidies, expand certain coverage offerings, allow farmers to purchase certain FCIP policies when enrolled in the Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) commodity support program, and increase compensation for AIPs in years of relatively large losses, among other changes. Title XI of the House-passed and Senate committee-reported drafts of the 2026 farm bill (H.R. 7567 and S. 5526, respectively) would make further changes with implications for policyholders and how the program is administered.
Program Funding
The Federal Crop Insurance Corporation—the agency that finances FCIP operations—receives mandatory appropriations of “such sums as necessary.” Annual federal program outlays averaged $12.1 billion for FY2016-FY2025, in inflation-adjusted 2026 dollars (Figure 2). Outlays tend to increase with the number of policies sold, increases in commodity prices, and increases in natural disasters and adverse weather events. Between 2016 and 2025, premium subsidies for corn, soybeans, wheat, and cotton—the top four crops in terms of acreage planted in the United States each year—averaged 74% of all premium subsidies paid. 
Figure 2. Federal Crop Insurance Program Outlays, FY2000-FY2025
/
Source: CRS using data from U.S. Department of Agriculture, Federal Crop Insurance Corporation/Risk Management Agency’s Financial Statements, audit reports, various fiscal years.
Notes: Adjusted for inflation using the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis Implicit Price Deflators for Gross Domestic Product where 2026=100, updated October 2026. 
Policies Offered
The FCIP offers insurance for most field crops, a wide variety of specialty crops, certain types of livestock and animal products, and grazing lands. FCIP coverage is available for purchase in all U.S. counties, although coverage for some crops may be limited in certain areas. To receive coverage, farmers must purchase policies by specific deadlines that vary by commodity but are before planting usually begins. Farmers can choose among many types of policies and policy options to customize coverage to their farm businesses’ specific needs. Farmers receive premium subsidies based on the coverage purchased. USDA fully subsidizes premiums for catastrophic-only (CAT) coverage; farmers pay only an administrative fee. Farmers pay an increasing share of premiums for higher levels of coverage, up to a maximum of 59% of the total premium for farm-level coverage. For certain county-level coverages, farmers pay 20% of the total premium.  
FCIP policies insure against losses of expected yield or revenue due to unavoidable natural events. Covered perils or “causes of loss” include adverse weather conditions (e.g., hail, frost, drought, flooding); failure of irrigation water supply; fire; plant diseases; and insect and wildlife damage. Certain policies also insure against losses from seasonal market price declines. Farmers are required to follow USDA’s guidance on good farm management practices in order to maintain coverage eligibility.
FY2025 Budget Reconciliation Law
The FY2025 budget reconciliation law made changes to the FCIP. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that these changes would increase the program cost by about $6 billion for FY2025-FY2034. 
The FY2025 budget reconciliation law increased premium subsidies for farm-level coverage, the first increase since 2002. For farm-level coverage levels of 55%-75% of expected yield or revenue, the law increased premium subsidies by 5%. For 80% and 85% coverage levels, the law increased premium subsidies by 3%. The law made no changes to premium subsidies for other farm-level coverage levels. The law also increased the additional premium subsidies available for beginning farmers and ranchers.   
The FY2025 budget reconciliation law expanded the maximum coverage levels for Whole Farm Revenue Protection policies, a type of farm-level coverage, from 85% to 90% of expected revenue and for Supplemental Coverage Option (SCO) policies, a type of county-level coverage, from 86% to 90%. The law also increased premium subsidies for SCO policies and removed the prohibition on purchasing SCO for acres enrolled in the ARC commodity support program. 
The FY2025 budget reconciliation law required USDA to modify the terms of the contracts with AIPs to increase A&O subsidies paid to AIPs in years of relatively large losses. The law also increased A&O subsidies for specialty crop policies in certain years, required USDA to annually adjust caps on A&O subsidies for certain policies, and increased funds available for program compliance and integrity, among other changes. 
2026 Farm Bill Proposals
The House-passed and Senate committee-reported versions of the farm bill would make other changes to the FCIP, with differences between some provisions. Both bills address subsidies for veteran farmers and ranchers, address compliance procedures for AIPs, freeze A&O subsidy rates for existing policies, establish a specialty crop advisory committee, modify the rules for private sector submissions for new FCIP policies, and require USDA to conduct certain research and development and pilot activities, among other changes proposed.    
Issues for Congress
The FCIP is a central component of the federal farm safety net, a collection of programs that provide risk protection and financial support to farmers in times of low farm prices and natural disasters. In the last three farm bills and in the FY2025 budget reconciliation law, Congress expanded the FCIP to cover more commodities and more types of risks. Farmers tend to purchase FCIP coverage for all planted acres every year for many commodity crops. Some stakeholders favor further expanding the program, noting that opportunities exist to increase coverage, especially for specialty crops, livestock, and animal products.
Other stakeholders have proposed reducing the cost of the FCIP by capping AIPs’ underwriting gains, reducing and/or capping premium subsidies for producers, and introducing a means test for premium subsidies, among other proposals. Congress could consider whether existing authorities and contracts between USDA and the AIPs are sufficient to achieve desired cost control aims for the program.
All FCIP policies include a deductible—losses that a policyholder absorbs before indemnities are triggered—to incentivize policyholders to guard against crop production risks. SCO indemnities and ARC payments may defray a portion of the deductible for farm-level coverage. SCO and ARC are both triggered by declines in county revenue compared with recent historical averages and thus may compensate for some of the same loss events. Farmers pay 20% of the cost of SCO premiums; enrollment in ARC is free. Congress could consider if a different combination of SCO coverage and ARC support would more adequately incentivize farmers to avoid risk, support farm incomes, and address concerns about government spending.   
Some environmental stakeholders assert that improved soil health reduces crop production risk and propose to enhance the FCIP’s role in promoting conservation and improving soil health. Congress may consider the potential environmental benefits of these proposals and what their effects might be on program performance. Statute requires USDA to operate the program such that, on average for the program as a whole, the sum of farmer-paid premiums and premium subsides should equal or exceed indemnities paid. 
The number of private-sector insurers participating in the FCIP has decreased over time, largely due to consolidation in the insurance industry. Congress may choose to examine the drivers of this consolidation, as well as any implications of consolidation on outreach to producers in underserved areas, insurers’ willingness to market new and existing policies, program efficiency, the number of AIPs in the industry, and the profitability of the remaining AIPs.
