api_metadata.summary:
The rural development title of the farm bill reauthorizes, amends, and creates programs administered by agencies within the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Rural Development (RD) mission area. These programs focus on rural broadband, rural utilities, business development, and community facilities. The rural development title also addresses issues affecting rural communities, such as substance abuse across rural areas.
The Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (2018 farm bill; P.L. 115-334) amended, reauthorized, and codified many RD programs through FY2023. Congress enacted three one-year extensions of the 2018 farm bill, most recently through FY2026 in P.L. 119-37, Division E, Section 5002. The House-passed Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026 (H.R. 7567) and the Senate committee-reported Agricultural Act of 2026 (S. 5526) would amend and reauthorize some of the RD programs in the 2018 farm bill and create new programs. 
Congress typically provides discretionary funding for RD programs through annual appropriations acts. For instance, while the 2018 farm bill provided authorizations of appropriations for many RD programs, funding for RD programs has been provided in annual appropriations acts for FY2018-FY2026. Appropriated levels may be different from levels of appropriation authorizations.
Background
Since 1973, each omnibus farm bill has included a rural development title. The rural development title impacts programs administered by RD through its agencies: the Rural Business-Cooperative Service, the Rural Housing Service, and the Rural Utilities Service. In one case, it impacts the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA) under the Research, Education, and Economics mission area. 
Most RD programs fall within the rural development title of farm bills. However, some RD housing programs fall under the jurisdiction of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs and the House Committee on Financial Services, and most RD energy programs fall within the energy title (Title IX in the 2018 farm bill). 
Selected 2018 Farm Bill Provisions
The rural development title of the 2018 farm bill included provisions focused on rural health care, rural utilities, and rural business development. It also included provisions focused on rural broadband (for more, see CRS In Focus IF12041, Farm Bill Primer: Rural Broadband Provisions). 
Substance Abuse and Rural Health Care
Congress prioritized funding for three RD programs to address substance abuse, including opioid abuse, in rural communities through FY2025. Congress required USDA to set aside at least 20% of the funding for the Distance Learning and Telemedicine Program for telemedicine projects that provide substance abuse treatment services. The program provides grants to help rural communities gain the technology and training necessary to engage in telemedicine and distance learning (7 U.S.C. §950aaa-2). Congress authorized appropriations for the program of $82 million annually through FY2026. In FY2026, Congress appropriated $41 million for the program. 
Congress directed USDA to prioritize funding for the Community Facilities Direct Loan and Grant Program for projects that develop facilities for substance abuse prevention, treatment, and recovery services. The program provides grants and loans to help rural communities build and renovate essential community facilities (7 U.S.C. §1926(a)). Congress also required that applicants receiving prioritized funding employ staff who have the expertise and training to identify and treat people dealing with substance abuse. FY2026 appropriations for the program were $659 million for congressionally directed projects and $5 million for competitive grants.
Congress also required USDA to prioritize funding for projects that address substance abuse for the Rural Health and Safety Education Competitive Grants Program, which is administered by NIFA. The program provides grants for community-based outreach education projects focused on health and safety (7 U.S.C. §2662(i)). FY2026 appropriations for the program were $3 million.
Congress provided authority to the Secretary of Agriculture to temporarily reprioritize RD program loan and grant applications that assist rural communities in responding to public health disruptions (7 U.S.C. §2204b-2). Congress required that the Secretary consult with the appropriate public health officials as needed. Congress also restricted reprioritization to a maximum of 20% of an RD program’s annual funding. 
Congress included a provision that allows rural hospitals to use RD loans and loan guarantees to refinance existing debt if it would (1) help retain access to health services in a rural community, (2) improve the financial position of a hospital, and (3) meet the fiscal feasibility and security requirements established by RD (7 U.S.C. §1990a).
Rural Water and Waste Disposal
Congress increased the maximum grant amount from $500,000 to $1 million per project for the Emergency Community Water Assistance Program, which provides grants to help communities prepare for or recover from emergencies that threaten the availability of safe, reliable drinking water (7 U.S.C. §1926a). Congress authorized appropriations of $50 million annually through FY2026 for the program. FY2026 appropriations for the program were $7 million. 
Congress reauthorized the Household Water Well Systems Program under a new name: the Rural Decentralized Water Systems Grant Program. The program provides grants to intermediaries to create funds that issue sub-loans to rural households to carry out well and septic system projects (7 U.S.C. §1926e). Congress expanded the authority for the program to allow intermediaries to offer sub-grants, in addition to sub-loans, to eligible homeowners in rural areas. Congress increased the authorization of appropriations for the program from $5 million to $20 million annually through FY2026. FY2026 appropriations for the program were $5 million. 
Rural Business Development
Congress restricted the amount of loans issued through the Intermediary Relending Program. Congress limited the maximum amount of a loan made by an intermediary to the lesser of $400,000 or 50% of the amount that USDA loaned to the intermediary. The program provides 1% interest rate loans to intermediaries that provide loans to eligible entities for business facilities and community development projects in rural areas (7 U.S.C. §1936b). FY2026 appropriations for the program were $2.5 million for a loan subsidy to support $9 million in loan authority. 
Analyses of Selected Proposed Farm Bill Provisions
Below, selected 2026 proposals within H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 are compared with current law. For a comprehensive overview of rural development title provisions in the bills, see CRS Report R48918, The 2026 Farm Bill: Comparison of the House and Senate Bills with Current Law. 
Rural Health Care
H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would expand the prioritization of funding for rural health care in selected RD programs such as the Community Facilities Direct Loan and Grant Program and the Distance Learning and Telemedicine Program. H.R. 7567 sets priorities through FY2027 and includes projects that address behavioral, maternal, and mental health services in addition to projects that address substance abuse. S. 5526 sets priorities through FY2031 and includes projects that address substance use disorder, mental health, and behavioral health. These provisions could expand access to certain specialized health care services in rural areas. Prioritization could also reduce funding for other types of rural projects that could be funded through the RD programs.
H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would also expand the types of health care institutions eligible to refinance debt using RD loans under certain circumstances. The bills would expand eligibility from rural hospitals to also include rural health care facilities, which would include psychiatric hospitals, critical care hospitals, religious nonmedical health care institutions, and community health centers. This provision could help maintain health services provided to rural communities through a wide range of health-related facilities. It could also reduce the amount of RD loan and loan guarantees available for other projects.
Meat Processing and Supply Chain
Congress directed USDA to address food-supply-chain disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic in the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (ARPA; P.L. 117-2, Title 1, §1001). Congress provided USDA $4 billion through ARPA to carry out the provision. USDA used the ARPA funding to create programs in RD that supported the development of food supply chains, such as the Meat and Poultry Processing Expansion Program (MPPEP) and the Food Supply Chain Guaranteed Loan Program (FSCGLP). MPPEP provides grants to expand meat and poultry processing. Grants range from $50,000 to $2 million. Grants can fund renovating processing facilities, purchasing equipment, and certifying processing facilities. Congress has also provided some additional funding to this program through annual appropriations from FY2024 to FY2026. FSCGLP provided loan guarantees to eligible entities for projects that increased capacity of certain parts of the supply chain, including aggregation, processing, transportation, and distribution. 
H.R. 7567 and S. 5526 would establish a new meat processing and rendering capacity grant program at USDA similar to MPPEP. The new program would award grants for new processing facilities, including mobile processing facilities, of up to $500,000 for a term of three years. It would prioritize grants for small establishments (i.e., 10-500 employees) or very small establishments (i.e., fewer than 10 employees or annual sales of less than $2.5 million). H.R. 7567 would authorize appropriations of $3 million annually through FY2031, while S. 5526 would authorize appropriations of $25 million annually through FY2031. S. 5526 would also set some additional requirements, such as that grant recipients would need to be in operation less than two years and have the financial viability and managerial capacity to carry out the project. H.R. 7567 would also codify FSCGLP. The program would offer guarantees for individual loans of up to $40 million. The bill would require USDA to submit quarterly reports to Congress evaluating the outcomes of the assistance, a description of any debt recovery made with respect to the loan guarantees issued through the program, and recommendations regarding program implementation.
These programs could help bring meat and other food processing to more remote, rural locations. These remote areas are less likely to be near a processing facility. In some cases, the programs may be duplicative of existing RD business programs that could fund the development of processing facilities, such as the Business and Industry Guaranteed Loan Program and the Value-Added Producer Grant Program.

api_metadata.summary:
Introduction
The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA, codified in Title 8 of the U.S. Code) sets forth rules governing the selection of the country to which an alien ordered removed may be transferred. Aliens found in the interior of the United States who have been ordered removed generally must be removed to the countries they designate (typically their home countries) or, if that is not possible, other countries to which they have connections. The INA also provides that the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) may potentially remove aliens to other countries willing to accept them—referred to as third countries—when removal to the designated country or a country to which the alien has a connection would be “impracticable, inadvisable, or impossible.”
These country-selection rules operate alongside separate, humanitarian-based protections against removal to specific countries. The INA provides for withholding of removal to countries where an alien’s life or freedom would be threatened on account of a statutorily protected ground, and the Convention Against Torture (CAT) and its implementing rules bar the transfer of aliens to countries where they would more likely than not face torture. These considerations may inform and constrain removal options.
President Trump’s January 2025 Executive Order “Securing Our Borders” states that it is the policy of the United States to “promptly” remove “all aliens who enter or remain in violation of the law” and directs the Secretary of State to coordinate with the Attorney General and DHS Secretary to “take all appropriate action to facilitate additional international cooperation and agreements ... including [by entering into safe third-country agreements] or other agreements under any other applicable provision of law.”
DHS has not made data publicly available on the total number of third-country agreements or the number of aliens transferred to third countries. Based on information requests and public reporting, two advocacy groups—Refugees International and Human Rights First—are jointly tracking third-country agreements and removals. They estimate that, as of September 2026, more than 25,000 individuals have been removed during the second Trump Administration by formal or informal agreements reached with more than 30 countries, including Cameroon, Costa Rica, the Democratic Republic of Congo, El Salvador, Eswatini, Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, Poland, Uzbekistan, and Mexico, with Mexico receiving the most individuals.
The U.S. government has used the third-country removal process in the past, but reportedly its current utilization substantially outpaces past practices. Many such individuals lack citizenship, legal status, social ties, a common language, or cultural familiarity in these third countries. 
Standard Removal Process
Aliens in the interior of the United States who are identified for removal by DHS are typically placed in standard removal proceedings in immigration court within the U.S. Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR). Standard removal proceedings begin when DHS files a charging document (a Notice to Appear) with an immigration court. During removal proceedings, an alien has the right to apply for relief or protection from removal and present evidence and testimony before an immigration judge (IJ), who ultimately decides whether to grant relief or protection (such as asylum) or order removal. If relief or protection is denied, the IJ generally issues an order of removal, which becomes final in specified circumstances—for example, after any administrative appeal is dismissed or when the time to appeal has expired and the alien does not file an appeal within that time period. 
Within DHS, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is generally responsible for the detention of aliens, including those ordered removed. The U.S. Supreme Court has generally limited the period of detention after a final removal order is issued to six months, after which the individual may be released.
Selection of Removal Country
Most aliens ordered removed in standard removal proceedings may select the country of removal. If the individual cannot be returned to that country, he or she generally must be removed to an alternative country “of which the alien is a subject, national, or citizen.” If removal to that alternative country is not possible, additional removal countries may be considered, including—as a last option—“a country whose government will accept the alien into that country” if removal to certain other countries to which the alien has some connection is “impracticable, inadvisable, or impossible.” 
DHS may remove foreign nationals to third countries willing to accept them and to which they have few or no ties for several reasons. Some countries may simply refuse to accept the return of their nationals or refuse to issue travel documents permitting their repatriation. Some countries will not accept their own nationals if they have engaged in criminal activity or may limit the total number of persons they are willing to accept. Other countries may have poor or nonexistent relations with the U.S. government. Additionally, removal to a particular country may not be an option if an alien has been granted withholding of removal or CAT protection with respect to that country.
Expanding Third-Country Removal
In February 2025, DHS issued internal policy guidance identifying several categories of foreign nationals with final removal orders that should be considered for third-country removals. They include, for example, aliens who cannot be removed to their home countries because the IJs determined that they qualified for withholding of removal or CAT. The guidance also applies to aliens who were previously released from ICE custody due to “no significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future” to the originally designated country.
Legal Challenge
Following issuance of the DHS guidance, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem issued a March 2025 memorandum clarifying DHS’s third-country removal policy. A class action lawsuit challenging the policy ensued. A federal district court judge issued a preliminary injunction requiring, among other things, that aliens be provided written notice and a “meaningful opportunity” to raise CAT claims before removal to third countries. In June 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court stayed the injunction while the case continued in the lower courts, enabling DHS to resume third-country removals. In July 2025, then-ICE Acting Director Todd Lyons issued a memorandum to ICE employees clarifying the agency’s implementation of earlier guidance and outlining revised third-country removal procedures. In February 2026, the district court dissolved its injunction and vacated DHS’s third-country removal policy. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit granted the government’s motion to stay that decision pending appeal and largely affirmed the district court’s judgment. The Supreme Court granted the government’s petition seeking review of the lower court decisions and stayed the district court’s ruling pending disposition of the case, allowing the third-country policy to remain in effect for the time being. The Supreme Court scheduled oral arguments for December 9, 2026.  
Procedures for Third-Country Removals
The July 2025 ICE memorandum specifies that the United States must determine prior to a third-country removal whether the intended country has provided diplomatic assurances that the alien will not be persecuted or tortured. If the U.S. Department of State finds the assurances credible, the ICE memorandum states that “the alien may be removed without the need for further procedures.” 
If the State Department does not find such assurances credible, or they are not provided, ICE then issues a Notice of Removal that states the intended third country to which the alien will be removed, conveyed in a language the individual comprehends. ICE does not ask whether the alien fears being removed to that country; rather, the individual must proactively express fear. ICE must wait 24 hours after issuing the Notice of Removal before carrying out the removal. However, in undefined “exigent circumstances,” ICE can effectuate removal six hours after serving the notice, provided the individual is afforded “reasonable means and opportunity to speak with an attorney.” Exigent removals must be approved by senior DHS attorneys.
If the alien affirmatively expresses to ICE a fear of removal to the intended third country, ICE is to refer the alien to DHS’s U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) for an eligibility screening for withholding of removal and CAT protection. USCIS must determine if it is more likely than not that the alien would face persecution based on a statutorily protected ground or be tortured in the third country. If the alien does not meet either standard, he or she is to be removed to the third country. If USCIS determines that the alien meets either standard, ICE follows different procedures depending on whether the alien has previously been in removal proceedings. If not, USCIS refers the case to an immigration court. Otherwise, USCIS notifies ICE, which moves to reopen the case before the immigration court or EOIR’s Board of Immigration Appeals for further proceedings to determine the alien’s eligibility for withholding of removal and CAT protection with respect to the third country. A grant of withholding of removal or CAT protection tied to a specific country does not bar DHS from designating another country for removal. 
Issues for Congress
The Trump Administration has prioritized the enforcement of final orders of removal. It has justified third-country removals as a vital national security and enforcement tool necessary for removing aliens—particularly those with criminal records—who cannot be removed to their home countries. It also contends that third-country removals deter unlawful migration and encourage self-deportation of unlawfully present aliens. 
Conversely, some contend that ICE undertakes these removals without providing foreign nationals “meaningful notice and an opportunity to seek protection.” Some removed aliens have reportedly confronted human rights abuses and the absence of due process (e.g., at the CECOT maximum security prison in El Salvador), faced life-threatening civil conflict (e.g., in South Sudan), or been subsequently repatriated to the same home countries they fled. Some criticize the lack of transparency and congressional oversight of the agreements or the political pressure and financial assistance facilitating them. 
Congress may consider options to address DHS’s authority over third-country removals. For example, Congress could clarify that DHS may remove individuals with final removal orders to any designated third countries, or it may authorize removals to countries through which aliens transited to the United States. Congress could also codify into statute the July 2025 ICE memorandum or create a statutory third-country removal program for aliens with final removal orders, similar to existing safe third-country agreements.
To constrain third-country removals, Congress could require additional procedures for transfer decisions, clarify the meaning of diplomatic assurances, grant aliens the ability to contest removal to third countries before an IJ, limit authorization of third-country removals to EOIR IJs, require congressional reporting for third-country agreements, or require third-country agreements to prohibit subsequent repatriation to countries where U.S. law would have prohibited it.

api_metadata.summary:
States and localities have primary responsibility for administering elections in the United States, including for setting elections policy. Congress has sometimes used what the Supreme Court has described as its “override” authority to specify national standards for federal elections.
In the 2026 election cycle, the executive branch has also issued policy documents with implications for state and local elections policy. President Donald Trump signed executive orders (EOs) in March 2025 and March 2026 that include provisions related to state and local administration of elections. Federal agencies have taken steps toward implementing many of those provisions, including in agency regulations and notices of funding opportunities (NOFOs) for federal grants.
This In Focus provides an overview of provisions of recent EOs and related federal regulations and NOFOs that would require states and localities to conduct particular elections activities, either in general or in order to access federal funding. Several of the cited provisions are the subject of litigation as of this writing and have been blocked by the courts. The In Focus does not generally address litigation or offer analysis of legal questions, such as questions about underlying executive branch authorities. Congressional clients may contact CRS for information about the current status of individual provisions. 
Voter Registration and Citizenship
Noncitizens are prohibited by federal law from voting in federal elections. Two federal voter registration forms that states are generally required to accept—the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA) available to voters covered by the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act of 1986 and the broader-purpose federal mail voter registration form—require applicants to attest to their citizenship and eligibility to vote under penalty of perjury. States and localities have other safeguards against noncitizen voting in federal elections. They also choose whether to allow noncitizens to participate in their state and local elections or in the electoral process more broadly.
The 2025 EO, EO 14248, directs the entities charged with administering the federal voter registration forms to add proof-of-citizenship requirements to their forms. One provision of the EO directs the Department of Defense (now using a secondary Department of War designation) to supplement the FPCA’s attestations with requirements to provide documentary proof of citizenship and proof of eligibility. Other provisions direct the Election Assistance Commission (EAC) to (1) add requirements to the more general form for applicants to provide documentary proof of citizenship and election officials to record the types of documents they present and (2) condition access to its grants on acceptance of versions of the form with any such requirements.
EO 14248 also directs the Departments of Justice (DOJ) and Homeland Security (DHS) to take steps to prevent noncitizens from participating in the administration of federal elections. A provision of the 2026 EO, EO 14399, directs DHS, through its U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and in coordination with the Social Security Administration, to compile state lists of confirmed citizens who will be over 18 by an upcoming federal election and establish procedures for states to supplement and suggest changes to the lists.
In April 2025, the EAC reported initiating consultations with chief state election officials about potential changes to its voter registration form in response to EO 14248. The consultations were reportedly paused later that month in response to a court order, and resignations and removals left the agency without commissioners as of July 2026. The EAC’s staff has indicated that it does not believe it has the authority to issue regulations related to the federal mail voter registration form, develop the form, or make certain changes to accompanying state-specific instructions in the absence of commissioners. The version of the FPCA available as of this writing also does not reference requirements to document citizenship or eligibility.
DHS approved a memorandum regarding implementation of EO 14399’s state citizenship lists in June 2026 and created a page for a related portal. Its Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) also included elections-policy-related conditions in the NOFO for its FY2026 homeland security grant programs. According to the NOFO, to access their full funding allocations under the grant programs, states and localities would have to use USCIS’s SAVE system to verify the citizenship of individuals who are on their voter rolls, work at polling places, or operate election systems. States’ chief election officials would also have to take timely action to remove verified noncitizens from their voter rolls, consistent with applicable law, and bar noncitizens from working at the polls or operating election systems. FEMA announced in an October 2026 bulletin that it was rescinding these and other funding conditions in response to a court order.
Absentee and Mail Voting
Federal law requires states to allow certain military and overseas voters to vote by absentee ballot in federal elections and accept the FPCA as an absentee ballot application. All states also permit at least some other eligible voters to use absentee or mail voting, with some sending ballots to all active registered voters and others requiring absentee or mail voters to request a ballot or to request a ballot and have one of a specified list of excuses.
Deadlines for requesting and returning absentee and mail ballots vary by state. For example, some states count only ballots returned by the close of polls on Election Day, while others accept ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrive within a set number of days later. States and localities also specify other aspects of absentee and mail voting like the design of mail ballot envelopes, although the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) has long offered review of and recommendations for ballot mail designs.
President Trump’s 2026 EO addresses the design and transmission of absentee and mail ballots, directing USPS to initiate rulemaking to make some of its long-standing ballot mail design recommendations mandatory, specify that it will carry ballots only from voters who have been enrolled with USPS on a state list, and establish procedures for states to supplement and suggest changes to their lists.
The 2025 EO addresses absentee and mail ballot return deadlines. It says that the EAC is to condition states’ access to its grants on setting Election Day as the deadline for ballot receipt and that DOJ is to take “all necessary action to enforce 2 U.S.C. 7 and 3 U.S.C. 1 against States that violate these provisions by” counting ballots received after Election Day.
In its June 2026 decision in Watson v. Republican National Committee, the Supreme Court held that 2 U.S.C. §§1 and 7 and 3 U.S.C. §1 do not require ballots to be received by Election Day. The instructions the EAC provided states for accessing its FY2026 Election Security Grants also do not reference an Election Day deadline for receipt of absentee or mail ballots.
USPS finalized a rule in August 2026 that largely reflected provisions of EO 14399. Implementation of the rule was paused by federal district courts in August and September, and the Supreme Court denied the administration’s request for a stay of one of the lower court’s orders on September 14. USPS has reportedly confirmed that it will not enforce the rule for 2026.
Voting Systems and Post-Election Processes
The Help America Vote Act of 2002 sets some mandatory standards for the voting systems that states and localities use in federal elections, including a requirement to have at least one accessible voting system at each polling place that most jurisdictions use ballot marking devices (BMDs) to meet. It also provides for federal voting system guidelines and a program to test and certify systems for conformance to the guidelines that are voluntary under federal law but have been adopted, at least in part, by many states under their own laws or regulations. The Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG), which are developed by the EAC with assistance from its Technical Guidelines Development Committee (TGDC), address various features of voting systems, including protections against errors or interference that could affect the accuracy of the election outcomes they report.
States and localities also take other steps to ensure the accuracy of reported election outcomes. For example, election officials use a process called the canvass to account for every ballot cast in an election, including by reconciling the numbers of voters and ballots. Most jurisdictions also use one of the following types of post-election audits to check samples of paper records of votes against the election outcomes reported by their voting systems: (1) traditional audits, which review a fixed number or percentage of voting machines or districts, or (2) risk-limiting audits, which use statistical methods to provide a specified level of confidence that the outcomes reported by the voting system are the ones election officials would get with a full hand count.
The VVSG and related testing and certification are addressed in EO 14248. Some provisions of the EO say that the EAC is to (1) amend the current version of the VVSG, VVSG 2.0, to provide that voting systems should produce individual paper records voters can verify and should not use barcodes or quick-response (QR) codes to capture vote selections “except where necessary to accommodate individuals with disabilities” and, (2) if appropriate, recertify systems to the amended guidelines and rescind previous certifications. Another provision directs DHS and FEMA to “heavily prioritize compliance with [VVSG 2.0] and completion of testing through the Voting System Test Labs accreditation process” in considering funding for state and local election officials under their homeland security grant programs.
The EAC drafted an update to VVSG 2.0 that was intended to incorporate the amendments from the EO and held a meeting and three working sessions of its TGDC to discuss them. The TGDC opted against voting on the update and, as noted above, the EAC’s commission was without members as of July 2026. As with the federal mail voter registration form, the agency’s staff has indicated that it does not believe it has the authority to adopt new or modified VVSG in the absence of commissioners.
In addition to the citizenship-related conditions noted above, the NOFO for FEMA’s FY2026 homeland security grant programs includes funding conditions related to voting systems and post-election processes. To access their full allocations under the grant programs, the NOFO indicates, states and localities would have to submit a plan for transitioning from voting systems that use barcodes or QR codes to count votes to systems with hand-marked paper ballots, including a timeline for eliminating BMDs. They would also have to conduct 5% manual audits according to DHS guidelines and ensure all jurisdictions used a DHS methodology to reconcile numbers of voters and ballots.
Election Records and Information Sharing
Congress included a requirement in the Civil Rights Act of 1960 for election officials to retain specified records for federal elections for 22 months in order to “provide a more effective protection of the right of all qualified citizens to vote without discrimination on account of race.” Under the National Voter Registration Act of 1993, certain records related to voter registration have to be retained for at least two years. States may also have their own requirements that build on those timelines, such as by extending the period for retaining certain records.
The 2026 EO includes a provision that says states and localities are to preserve “all records and materials—excluding ballots cast—evidencing voter participation in any Federal election” for five years. The 2025 EO directs DOJ to enter into information-sharing agreements with states under which state officials would provide the department with information about suspected violations of state and federal election laws, with further directives to prioritize enforcement of “Federal election integrity laws” in and consider withholding funding from states that opted not to enter into such agreements or cooperate in federal investigations or prosecutions of election crimes.
In April 2025, DOJ announced the creation of a task force to implement provisions of EO 14248 in New Jersey, including provisions related to information sharing and prioritization of investigations and prosecutions of election crimes. The department has reported various enforcement activities of the task force, as well as engaging in broader efforts to request or otherwise access states’ election records. For more on federal demands for state election materials, see CRS In Focus IF13235, Federal Investigations and Seizures of Voting Records.

api_metadata.summary:
Many federal laws are subject to time limits known as statutes of limitations or statutes of repose, which generally bar enforcement of the law after a certain amount of time has passed. Congress can set or modify statutes of limitations and repose via legislation, subject to some constitutional limits. This In Focus provides a brief overview of the law related to statutes of limitations and repose with a focus on time limits that apply to civil litigation. (CRS Report RL31253 provides more information on criminal statutes of limitations.) The In Focus then discusses selected considerations for Congress regarding legislation that imposes time limits on enforcing the law.
Overview of Statutes of Limitations and Statutes of Repose
Statutes of limitations and statutes of repose both impose time limits on when a law can be enforced, but they function somewhat differently. In CTS Corp. v. Waldburger, 573 U.S. 1 (2014), the Supreme Court distinguished between the purposes and functions of the two types of laws. The Court explained that statutes of limitations “require plaintiffs to pursue diligent prosecution of known claims” and “promote justice by preventing surprises through [plaintiffs’] revival of claims that have been allowed to slumber until evidence has been lost, memories have faded, and witnesses have disappeared” (internal quotation marks and citations are omitted from all quotes in this In Focus). While statutes of repose “also encourage plaintiffs to bring actions in a timely manner, and for many of the same reasons,” the Court explained that “the rationale has a different emphasis. Statutes of repose effect a legislative judgment that a defendant should be free from liability after the legislatively determined period of time,” and “embod[y] the idea that at some point a defendant should be able to put past events behind him.”
In light of these differing rationales, the Court explained, “the time periods specified are measured from different points.” A statute of limitations “creates a time limit for suing in a civil case, based on the date when the claim accrued,” usually meaning “when the injury occurred or was discovered.” By contrast, a statute of repose “puts an outer limit on the right to bring a civil action. That limit is measured not from the date on which the claim accrues but instead from the date of the last culpable act or omission of the defendant.” A statute of repose thus bars all suits brought after the specified amount of time has elapsed, “even if this period ends before the plaintiff has suffered a resulting injury” or discovered that a legal violation or injury has occurred.
In Rotkiske v. Klemm, 589 U.S. 8 (2019), the Supreme Court explained, “When interpreting limitations provisions, as always, we begin by analyzing the statutory language.” When the statutory language is unambiguous, that ends the inquiry. If there are two plausible constructions of a limitations provision, the Court will generally
adopt the construction that starts the time limit running when the cause of action ... accrues because Congress legislates against the standard rule that the limitations period commences when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action.
The question of when a cause of action accrues can give rise to litigation. For instance, in Corner Post, Inc. v. Board of Governors of Federal Reserve System, 603 U.S. 799 (2024), the Supreme Court held that a facial claim under the Administrative Procedure Act accrues when a plaintiff is injured by final agency action, even if the injury occurs after the statute of limitations would run from the time of the challenged action.
Federal statutes set default statutes of limitations for both civil and criminal cases. For civil cases, 28 U.S.C. § 1658(a) establishes a default four-year limitations period for most federal statutes enacted after 1990 that do not contain explicit limitations provisions. 28 U.S.C. § 2401 sets a default six-year limit for civil suits against the U.S. government. As discussed in  CRS Report RL31253, the default statute of limitations for criminal cases is five years, but specific offenses may be subject to other limitations periods or no limitations period.
Considerations for Congress
Multiple questions may arise when lawmakers consider whether and how to impose time limits on enforcement of a law. Statutes and court decisions impose certain default rules with respect to such time limits, but Congress has significant authority to depart from those default rules via legislation. These considerations relate to statutes of limitations and repose in federal laws. When courts apply state law, including in federal court cases based on diversity of citizenship, they apply state statutes of limitations.
Does a limitations period apply?
The first question Members of Congress may consider in this area is whether enforcement of a law should be time-limited. As noted, federal statutes lay out default statutes of limitations for civil and criminal cases. Thus, if a piece of legislation does not expressly address time limits on enforcement, courts interpreting the law may apply a default time limit. The equitable doctrine of laches may also bar claims that are unreasonably delayed. 
If Congress does not want enforcement of a statute to be time-limited, it should expressly state that in the legislation. Some existing federal laws are not subject to a statute of limitations or statute of repose. For instance, 38 U.S.C. § 4327(b) provides that “there shall be no limit on the period for filing” a lawsuit alleging a violation of the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994.
If Congress imposes a time limit on enforcement of a statute, it may consider whether to do so via a statute of limitations or a statute of repose. A statute of limitations may allow more flexibility for plaintiffs who are delayed in discovering or addressing their injuries by circumstances beyond their control, while a statute of repose may provide greater legal certainty for potential defendants. Statutes of limitations are more commonly used in federal law than statutes of repose.
What starts the limitations period?
There are several possible events that may start the clock on a statute of limitations or repose. Statutes of repose run from when a violation of the law occurred, regardless of whether the plaintiff was injured or discovered the injury within the limitations period. Statutes of limitations often run from the time when a plaintiff is injured, regardless of whether the plaintiff is aware of the injury. As noted above, the Court in Rotskiske stated that if Congress does not specify when a statute of limitations begins running, courts will generally default to starting the clock when a plaintiff’s claim accrues, that is, when the plaintiff is injured and thus has a right to bring the claim in court. Congress may also choose to apply a rule known as the discovery rule, meaning that the clock runs from when the plaintiff discovered their injury, or when a reasonably diligent plaintiff would have discovered it. The discovery rule may increase legal uncertainty by extending the statute of limitations, potentially indefinitely, but may also protect the rights of plaintiffs who could not discover an injury promptly despite reasonable diligence. Courts sometimes read statutes to implicitly include the discovery rule and sometimes decline to do so. Congress can reduce uncertainty by expressly stating whether the discovery rule applies. 
How long is the limitations period?
Congress may also consider how long the limitations period should be. On one hand, a longer limitations period gives plaintiffs more time to discover and bring their claims, preventing potentially meritorious claims from being time-barred. This may enhance the deterrent effect of the law if defendants know they are less likely to escape liability. On the other hand, a shorter limitations period may mitigate concerns about evidence being lost or witnesses’ memories fading over time, and may provide greater legal certainty for potential defendants. Congress has applied short statutes of repose, such as 60 days, to challenges to certain agency actions to “impart[ ] finality into the administrative process, thereby conserving administrative resources and protecting the reliance interests of regulatees who conform their conduct to the regulations.”
Do exceptions apply?
Another question Congress may consider is whether exceptions should apply to the statute of limitations. The Supreme Court has recognized certain default exceptions that apply to statutes of limitations, but not statutes of repose, if Congress is silent on the matter. The first of these is equitable tolling. In CTS Corp., the Court explained that this difference between statutes of limitations and repose “underscores their differing purposes”: 
Statutes of limitations ... are subject to equitable tolling, a doctrine that pauses the running of, or “tolls,” a statute of limitations when a litigant has pursued his rights diligently but some extraordinary circumstance prevents him from bringing a timely action. Statutes of repose, on the other hand, generally may not be tolled, even in cases of extraordinary circumstances beyond a plaintiff’s control.
Second, some Supreme Court decisions have applied an equitable “fraud discovery rule,” holding that when a defendant’s fraudulent actions prevent the plaintiff from discovering an injury, the limitations period begins when the plaintiff discovers the fraud.
Congress can specify in legislation that these exceptions do not apply, or it can expressly provide for exceptions. For instance, a prior version of the Fair Credit Reporting Act’s statute of limitations provided that the plaintiff ordinarily had two years from the date liability arose to file suit, but if the defendant materially and willfully misrepresented certain information to the plaintiff, the two-year limitations period would instead run from the date the plaintiff discovered the misrepresentation. The Supreme Court has suggested that when Congress enumerates specific exceptions to a statute of limitations in statutory text, courts should not read additional, implicit exceptions into the statute. Thus, when drafting a statute of limitations, Congress may consider whether explicitly creating particular exceptions may foreclose judicial recognition of others.
Can Congress change an existing limitations period?
Members of Congress may also consider whether to add a statute of limitations or repose to an existing law or remove or modify an existing time limit. Congress’s authority in this area is subject to one firm constitutional limit, which relates to criminal law: The Supreme Court has held that the Constitution’s Ex Post Facto Clause, which forbids retroactively imposing or increasing criminal punishment, prohibits reviving a criminal statute of limitations after the limitations period has run. Congress can, however, extend a criminal statute of limitations that has not lapsed.
Changes to civil statutes of limitations are sometimes challenged on due process grounds. Review of such claims may be fact-dependent. Courts have at times invalidated changes to statutes of limitations that were found to deprive people of vested rights in property. For instance, in Stewart v. Keyes, 295 U.S. 403 (1935), the Supreme Court held that where the statute of limitations has run on an action to recover real or personal property, a later attempt “to repeal or remove the bar after it became complete” violates “constitutional provisions forbidding a deprivation of property without due process of law.”
Generally, however, due process review of statutes of limitations is deferential, and legislation will usually be upheld as long as it serves a rational purpose and does not impose undue hardships on parties. In the analogous context of due process review of state statutes of limitations, the Supreme Court has held that reviving a lapsed civil statute of limitations is not inherently unconstitutional. The Court has also stated:
It is well settled that a statute shortening the period of limitation is within the constitutional power of the legislature, provided a reasonable time, taking into consideration the nature of the case, is allowed for bringing an action after the passage of the statute, and before the bar takes effect.

api_metadata.summary:
The U.S. Geological Survey, a science agency in the Department of the Interior, assesses geothermal resources (Earth heat sources) for the development of geothermal energy in surface and subsurface geologic formations (i.e., layers of rock) in the United States as part of its mission and guided by direction in the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970, the Energy Policy Act of 1992, the Energy Policy Act of 2005, and the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007. Some older USGS assessments (such as those published in 1970, 1971, 1975, 1979, and 2008) assessed domestic geothermal resources. The Energy Act of 2020 directed the USGS to update its 2008 assessment and consider potential resources using other geothermal technologies. In 2025, the USGS published preliminary assessments for enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) and reservoir thermal energy storage systems (RTES) in some areas. According to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), geothermal resources represent a vast and largely untapped, underground resource that may provide electricity, heating, cooling, and energy storage on or off the grid. Some of this potential may require technological development, and DOE’s Office of Geothermal supports innovations in technology to reduce the risks and costs of geothermal energy development. 
Innovations in geothermal energy technologies may also lead to coproduction of geothermal, oil, gas, and minerals, especially critical minerals (such as in the Salton Sea Geothermal Field in California and the Smackover Formation project in Texas). Congress may consider whether geothermal resource assessments should be advanced and prioritized as the USGS has completed some preliminary assessments in some areas. The USGS assessments may enhance understanding of the nation’s geothermal energy and coproduction capacity to support  growing demand for electricity, heating, cooling, and energy storage for buildings, infrastructure, industrial applications, and the growing number of data centers. Assessing geothermal resources may support management of land and water resources (such as federal lands and water) for many purposes, such as agriculture, building/infrastructure, commercial, conservation, energy, industrial, mining, and recreation.
Status and Development of Geothermal Energy 
According to the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) 2025 market report, conventional geothermal energy—from a hydrothermal field of hot, wet rocks—is commercially available, accounting for about 0.4% of electricity generation in the United States in 2025. Unconventional geothermal—such as EGS using hot, dry rocks with engineered permeability and injected fluid flow—is an emerging technology that is not widely commercially available in the United States. The USGS and DOE support geologic and technological advances that may further develop geothermal energy. 
According to the NLR report, as of 2024, the United States was the world leader in installed geothermal for generating electricity, while China was the leader in installed geothermal for direct heating. Also as of 2024, conventional geothermal power plants are operating in Alaska (2 plants), California (53), Hawaii (2), Idaho (1), New Mexico (4), Nevada (32), and Oregon (4); new conventional geothermal power plants are planned in California (11), Hawaii (1), and Nevada (3); new EGS power plants are planned in California (4), New Mexico (1), Nevada (3), and Texas (1); and an additional EGS plant (which will power Meta data stations) is planned in an undisclosed location east of the Rocky Mountains. Several new EGS power plants are planned for delivery of electricity directly to data centers. Fervo Energy is advancing a commercial EGS drilling and reservoir pilot project near the Blue Mountain Geothermal Facility in Nevada.
Geothermal Energy Technology
Geothermal energy technology that specifically uses Earth’s heat involves drilling wells into hot rocks and extracting heat through production wells to generate electricity, provide heating and cooling, or store energy. For conventional hydrothermal, drilling wells target natural fluids and natural fluid flow (i.e., permeability) in hot, wet rocks and may inject additional fluids if the natural fluid source becomes depleted. For EGS, drilling wells inject fluids into hot, dry rocks to create fractures or expand natural fractures to allow fluid flow and then inject fluids that can be extracted as heat from production wells. For example, DOE’s Frontier Observatory for Research in Geothermal Energy (FORGE) near Milford, UT, has shown that an EGS engineered permeability and injected fluid geothermal reservoir can be replicated. For thermal energy storage, wells are drilled into aquifers and may store hot or cold fluids for heating, cooling, or electricity generation.
The USGS Geothermal Resource Assessments
The USGS assesses geothermal resources using data and analysis from the USGS and other sources. The USGS has developed methods and models to estimate geothermal energy efficiency (i.e., heat extraction rates) based on geologic and technological factors. Energy efficiency depends on the location, volume, and formation characteristics (including composition, structure, temperature, heat flow, permeability, and whether there is natural fluid and/or steam) and the drilling, injection, and production technology. In some cases, developed geothermal energy may provide direct electricity, heating, cooling, and/or energy storage for buildings, data centers, and other commercial/industrial processes. 
Hydrothermal Energy—Hot, Wet Rocks 
Conventional hydrothermal electricity generation relies on naturally occurring permeable, hot, wet rocks (>90°C or 194°F) with natural reservoirs of fluid and/or steam. The rocks have permeability from naturally existing fractures and pore spaces that are sufficiently connected to allow fluid flow. Conventional drilling depths range from thousands to tens of thousands of feet below the surface. 
Conventional hydrothermal resources are commonly associated with volcanic activity or tectonics (i.e., faults and fault movement, mountain building, and other crustal processes), and any constructed hydrothermal energy systems may be vulnerable to damage from natural geologic hazards. For example, The Geysers conventional hydrothermal electricity generation systems in California (the largest geothermal electrical operation in the world according to The Geysers, Calpine), are near faults and volcanoes, hazards that should be considered in system operations. The Geysers geothermal field is a vapor-dominated system (there are no natural hot fluids or geysers in the field). In 1997, electrical system operators began injecting treated Lake County wastewater into the geothermal field to offset declining steam levels. Another example, the Puna Geothermal Venture (PGV) in Puna, Hawaii Island, draws steam heated at depth by hot volcanic fluids from Kilauea volcano, among the most active volcanoes in the world, to drive turbines and supply electricity to Hawaiian Electric. PGV reinjects hot fluids to maintain its system and conserve water. PGV provided about 29% of electricity needs on the island in 2017. PGV was shut down because the 2018 Kilauea eruption led to lava flows covering the complex and eliminating access.
Induced earthquakes from fluid injection (such as fluid injection to replenish conventional hydrothermal systems or geothermal stimulation and fluid injection used in EGS) and other geothermal energy development activities are additional risks that must be considered. Induced earthquakes have been detected at The Geysers and have been attributed to drilling, injection, and production activities.
Conventional hydrothermal resources for heating, such as hot springs and steam vents, can be found at the surface to thousands of feet in depth. According to NLR, there were about 500 geothermal direct heating systems in the United States as of October 2024, including systems for the heating of resorts and pools (281 installations), space heating (77), aquaculture (47), greenhouses (37), district heating (25), and other applications (15). The oldest example of district heating in the United States is buildings in Boise, ID, directly heated by a geothermal resource, including nearby surficial hot springs. 
Enhanced Geothermal Systems—Hot, Dry Rocks 
Electricity generated in an EGS relies on engineered fluid flow systems constructed in low-permeability, hot, dry rocks. A drilled well injects fluid into the target formation of hot, impermeable rocks to create fractures or expand natural fractures to allow fluid flow. The geothermal stimulation technique is similar to hydraulic fracturing used in shale-rich formations to produce oil or gas. DOE supports research, development, and demonstration for EGS, such as FORGE and the Newberry Geothermal Project on the flank of Newberry Volcano in Oregon. Policy and industry stakeholders also suggest that the similar expertise, workforce, and infrastructure in the oil and gas industry may support the commercial development of EGS in the United States.
In 2025, the USGS completed a provisional assessment of the geothermal resources for EGS electricity generation associated with high-temperature, low-permeability, dry geologic formations of the Great Basin and noted high potential resources in California, Idaho, Nevada, and Utah. The largest uncertainty in the assessment was estimating which geologic formations can be stimulated sufficiently and economically produce geothermal energy. Establishing a functional and sustainable fracture pattern in the rock is critical for commercial EGS. The USGS plans to assess potential resources for EGS elsewhere, such as in the Williston Basin (beneath the Dakotas) and the Illinois Basin.
Underground Thermal Energy Storage Systems—Shallow to Deep Aquifers
More energy storage is needed in the United States, and there is increasing interest in developing geothermal resources for energy storage as another option besides energy storage batteries. As directed by the Energy Act of 2020, the USGS has added three types of thermal energy storage (TES) systems to its geothermal resource assessments. Aquifer thermal energy storage (ATES) stores hot or cold water in shallow aquifers. Borehole thermal energy storage (BTES) uses underground pipes to store hot or cold water. BTES can be used anywhere that groundwater flow rate is not too high, but requires more wells to store an equivalent amount of energy as other TES. Reservoir thermal energy storage (RTES) stores hot or cold water in deep aquifers, often with low-quality (i.e., saline/brackish waters) and low-flow-rate groundwater. RTES may allow more energy storage because of higher temperature differences than other TES. RTES would have less conflict with high-quality groundwater needs, because most of the deep aquifers are disconnected from other water systems. RTES may be able to repurpose idle or unproductive oil and gas wells for geothermal energy. DOE has several projects to retrofit wells or coproduce geothermal energy from producing oil and gas wells. 
The USGS 2025 Reservoir Thermal Energy Storage Pre-Assessment for the United States examined eight metropolitan areas across different climates and subsurface conditions: Albuquerque, NM; Charleston, SC; Chicago and Decatur, IL; Lansing, MI; Memphis, TN; Phoenix, AZ; and Portland, OR. All eight areas were favorable for RTES. 
Congressional Considerations
Identifying geothermal resources and developing geothermal energy systems has typically garnered bipartisan support in U.S. energy policy. The Biden Administration’s Executive Order 14141 called upon any artificial intelligence infrastructure, such as data centers, to consider using geothermal energy and established Priority Geothermal Zones. The second Trump Administration’s Executive Order 14156 identified geothermal as an essential energy that should be further developed.
Some bills in the 119th Congress would expand geothermal resource assessment to Puerto Rico (H.R. 10275, introduced), expand geothermal research and development (H.R. 8790, passed in House, and S. 4406, committee reported favorably; H.R. 7568, introduced), and expand geothermal demonstration projects (H.R. 8437, reported as substitute, and S. 4116, reported with amendment). Congress may consider whether the USGS preliminary geothermal assessments published in 2025 advance the development of geothermal energy and whether additional assessments should be prioritized.

api_metadata.summary:
The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA; 42 U.S.C. §§4321 et. seq.) sets forth a national policy with respect to environmental quality and a procedural framework for integrating environmental considerations into federal decisionmaking (i.e., through environmental review). The range of federal agencies and actions subject to NEPA is broad and includes activities such as resource management decisions, issuing permits, and funding infrastructure projects. Under NEPA, federal agencies must evaluate reasonably foreseeable adverse environmental effects, consider a reasonable range of alternatives, and prepare required documentation (i.e., environmental documents) for “major [f]ederal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.” Federal agencies may also engage other governmental entities, project applicants (i.e., project sponsors), and members of the public to identify issues, obtain relevant information, and inform environmental analyses. 
Federally recognized Tribes (Tribes) may participate in environmental reviews for various reasons. In some circumstances, federal action may arise because a Tribe proposes an activity that requires federal agency approval or involves an associated federal authorization. In other circumstances, federal action may occur on or affect tribal lands, treaty-protected rights, or resources in which the United States has responsibilities under applicable federal law. This In Focus provides an overview of the various ways in which Tribes may engage in the environmental review process under NEPA.
Tribal Roles and Participation in NEPA Reviews
A Tribe’s role in an environmental review varies depending on whether it proposes an activity requiring federal action or participates in the review of an action proposed by another entity. Potential tribal roles are outlined in this section.
Project Sponsor
A Tribe may serve as a project sponsor when it proposes an activity that requires a federal agency decision. In these circumstances, the Tribe may provide project information and other materials needed for the environmental review, while the federal agency remains responsible for the contents of the environmental document and making the federal decision. For some actions (e.g., leases or rights-of-way) on tribal lands, the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) is primarily responsible for authorization. 
Joint Lead Agency
NEPA assigns responsibilities for environmental review to the federal agency proposing a federal action or responsible for authorizing certain actions. The federal agency conducting the environmental review is typically the lead agency, but Tribes may participate in other formal roles. For many federal actions involving Tribes, the BIA is the lead agency, and in some circumstances, Tribes may participate as joint lead agencies. As a joint lead agency, a Tribe would share responsibilities related to a proposed action, including supervising the environmental review process, coordinating with other agencies, and overseeing and developing a schedule for completing the environmental review and any associated federal permits or related authorizations. Although joint lead agency arrangements involving Tribes are less common than cooperating agency participation—discussed in the next section—they may be used for proposed actions involving BIA authorizations, proposed actions affecting tribal lands, and other shared federal and tribal decisionmaking responsibilities.
Cooperating Agency
Under NEPA, the lead agency may invite any federal, state, tribal, or local agency with “jurisdiction by law or special expertise” relevant to any environmental impact to participate as a cooperating agency. A Tribe may also request cooperating agency status where appropriate. Cooperating agencies may, among other things, assist in identifying issues for analysis, developing alternatives, providing technical information, and preparing environmental documents. Acting as a cooperating agency may require a commitment of resources and time to meet the lead agency’s schedule. Although the lead agency remains responsible for the analysis, the environmental review, and any resulting decisions, cooperating agency status may provide Tribes with opportunities to engage earlier and more directly in the development of a proposed action and the environmental analysis than would otherwise occur through public participation.
Public Participation in the Environmental Review Process
Tribes may also provide input on environmental reviews through public participation opportunities. Until recently, NEPA implementation was guided by government-wide regulations, promulgated by the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ). These regulations required federal agencies to request comments from the public, as well as any state, local, or tribal government that may be affected by the proposed action during the preparation of certain environmental documents. Effective April 2025, CEQ rescinded those regulations and directed federal agencies to replace these regulations with federal-agency-specific procedures that may or may not include similar requests for public comment opportunities. Depending on agency procedures (e.g., DOI Handbook of NEPA Procedures) and level of review, these opportunities may include participation during scoping, review of draft environmental documents, submission of written comments, or public meeting input.
Federal Delegation of Authorizations and Environmental Reviews to Tribes
At times, Congress has enacted statutes that allow Tribes to authorize certain activities on tribal lands without case-by-case approval by the Secretary of the Interior (Secretary, as delegated to the BIA), provided the Tribe has an environmental review process meeting specified statutory requirements. For example, the Helping Expedite and Advance Responsible Tribal Homeownership Act of 2012 (HEARTH Act, 25 U.S.C. §415(h)) authorizes Tribes to approve tribal leases on tribal lands executed under tribal regulations approved by the Secretary. In addition, the Indian Tribal Energy Development and Self Determination Act of 2005 (25 U.S.C. §3504(e)) allows qualifying Tribes to propose tribal energy resource agreements (TERAs) with the Secretary. If the Secretary approves a TERA, that Tribe can enter into leases, business agreements, or rights-of-way to develop energy resources on tribal lands without secretarial approval. Under both statutes, Tribes must conduct environmental reviews that meet specified criteria. 
Other Opportunities for Tribal Participation 
In addition to participating in these NEPA roles, Tribes may engage with federal agencies pursuant to other statutory authorities. These other authorities differ in their legal basis, purpose, and procedural requirements, but federal agencies often coordinate compliance within the NEPA process to reduce duplication and facilitate informed decisionmaking. For example, federal agencies integrate their environmental reviews with reviews under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. Information gathered during one engagement (e.g., information regarding cultural or environmental resources) may also inform the NEPA analyses. Thus, tribal participation during an environmental review often reflects compliance with several overlapping authorities rather than NEPA alone. 
Beyond engaging with federal agencies pursuant to these statutory authorities, Tribes may request government-to-government consultations pursuant to the federal trust responsibility, treaty obligations, executive orders, or agency consultation policies. The federal trust responsibility is a legal obligation under which the United States—through treaties, acts of Congress, and court decisions—“has charged itself with moral obligations of the highest responsibility and trust” toward Tribes and tribal members. Government-to-government consultation may include correspondence, meetings, site visits, workshops, or other discussions regarding the proposed action. Tribal engagement through government-to-government consultation is different than public review of environmental documents because it typically involves meetings and communication between tribal and federal leaders, whereas during public review, Tribes engage through the same procedural opportunities available to all members of the public and other entities. 
Selected Issues for Congress
Members of Congress have considered legislation addressing tribal engagement in NEPA reviews and implementation.
Consistency of NEPA requirements. Following the rescission of the CEQ NEPA regulations, opportunities for Tribes to participate in environmental reviews and comment on draft environmental documents may vary among federal agencies and project types. While some tribal groups asserted support for the Trump Administration for “reducing unnecessary federal regulations and streamlining overly complex permitting processes that disproportionately burden” Tribes, they also urged Congress to give CEQ regulatory control over NEPA again, and to add tribal consultation requirements to NEPA. 
Application of NEPA to tribal lands and resources. NEPA is silent regarding how an agency should analyze or determine the impact of proposed actions affecting tribal lands and resources. The Standardizing Permitting and Expediting Economic Development Act (H.R. 4776) and Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (S. 5653) would amend NEPA to direct federal agencies to presume that declining to proceed (taking no action) on a tribal proposal would negatively affect the Tribe. The House Committee on Natural Resources (majority) asserted that this directive would promote tribal sovereignty. In addition, some Tribes have advocated for more power to decide whether an environmental review is necessary and how it might be conducted for projects on tribal lands. For example, the Southern Ute Indian Tribe has stated that it increased efficiencies after developing its own environmental review process under the HEARTH Act. Yet this approach may create inconsistencies in environmental review practices among Tribes and between Tribes and federal agencies.
Consideration of tribal input in federal decisions. Congress may choose to constrict, maintain, or expand statutes governing consideration of tribal input in federal decisionmaking. As discussed above, Congress has issued some direction to federal agencies on when and how to consider tribal input. While Tribes have often sought increased influence in NEPA reviews, federal agencies may find it challenging to weigh tribal input against other statutory mandates and priorities. 
Federal and Tribal Capacity. Some federal agencies and Tribes have identified limitations in agency and tribal capacity as hindering meaningful engagement, including for environmental reviews. In a GAO report on government-to-government consultation, many federal agencies cited “constraints on agency staff, financial resources, or both to support consultation.” Tribal participation in environmental reviews may also require the expenditure of tribal resources. At times, Congress has appropriated funding that has been used to help Tribes engage in environmental reviews. For example, P.L. 117-169 appropriated $350 million to the Permitting Council’s Environmental Review Improvement Fund. The Permitting Council set aside $5 million from the fund in 2023, and an additional $10 million in 2024, to support tribal engagement in the environmental review and authorization process for FAST-41-covered infrastructure projects.
