api_metadata.summary:
Introduction
The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) was enacted in 1938 with the goal of establishing minimum national labor standards, including for weekly hours of work. To that end, the FLSA requires that employers pay covered, nonexempt employees at a rate of one-and-a-half times their regular rate of pay for hours worked in excess of 40 per week in a given job. This In Focus provides an overview of the FLSA overtime pay requirements and recent legislative proposals to amend them.
General Provisions
Section 7(a)(1) of the FLSA (29 U.S.C. §207(a)(1)) provides the following:
Except as otherwise provided in this section, no employer shall employ any of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, or is employed in an enterprise engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, for a workweek longer than forty hours unless such employee receives compensation for his employment in excess of the hours above specified at a rate not less than one and one-half times the regular rate at which he is employed.
The Regular Rate of Pay
An employee’s regular rate of pay is calculated in each workweek in which the employee is entitled to overtime pay. It is an hourly rate determined using the following formula: 
/
The regular rate must include all compensation “for employment paid to, or on behalf of, the employee” in the workweek in which overtime hours occur. Total compensation includes the worker’s hourly rate of pay and other employment-related payments received during the workweek, such as nondiscretionary bonuses (e.g., productivity-based bonuses), on-call pay required by state and local laws, and the reasonable value of meals or lodging provided as compensation to employees. 
Some payments to employees are not considered to be compensation, and the act explicitly excludes them from the regular rate. These statutory exclusions include certain employer gifts, paid leave (e.g., paid sick leave, paid holidays), employer contributions to the employee’s health plan, and payments for reimbursable business expenses, among others. 
Example: Overtime Pay for an Hourly Worker
The regular rate of pay in a workweek in which an employee earned an hourly wage of $12 and worked 46 hours would be
/
The employee would be entitled to $12 per hour for 40 hours of work and $18 per hour (=1.5 x $12 per hour) for the 6 overtime hours, a total of $588 for the workweek.  
Example: Overtime Pay for an Hourly Worker Who Received a Production Bonus
If the worker received a $46 production bonus in addition to her hourly rate of $12, her regular rate of pay would be
/
In this instance, the employee would be entitled to $13 per hour for 40 hours of work and $19.50 per hour (=1.5 x $13) for the 6 overtime hours, for a total of $637 for the workweek.  
Example: Overtime Pay for a Tipped Worker
The FLSA permits employers to count up to $5.12 (per hour) in tips received by a tipped worker toward the employer’s minimum wage obligation. (The federal minimum wage is currently $7.25 per hour.) For example, an employer would meet its FLSA minimum wage obligation if it paid at least $21.30 to a tipped worker in a workweek in which the employee worked 10 hours (i.e., $2.13 per hour for 10 hours) and received tips of at least $51.20 (i.e., $5.12 per hour for 10 hours). Employers may also apply the tip credit—up to $5.12 per hour—toward their FLSA overtime pay obligations. 
Employers must use the employee’s full wage (i.e., at least the federal minimum wage) when calculating the regular rate of pay for a tipped worker and must include service charges, commissions, bonuses, and other compensation received by the tipped employee during the workweek. Any tips received by the employee in excess of the tip credit need not be included in the regular rate because such tips are not compensation paid by the employer to the employee.
For example, the regular rate for a tipped worker whose employer claimed a tip credit of $5.12 per hour, and who worked 50 hours in a workweek and received at least $256 in tips (=50 hours x $5.12 per hour), would be
/
Such an employee would be entitled to $7.25 per hour for 40 hours of work and $10.875 per hour (=1.5 x $7.25 per hour) for the 10 overtime hours, for a total of $398.75 for the workweek. Because the employee earned at least $256 (=$5.12 per hour x 50 hours) in tips during the work week, the employer could claim the maximum tip credit ($256 = $5.12 per hour x 50 hours) and pay a direct cash wage of $142.75 to the employee.
State and Local Government Employees’ Compensatory Time Option
The FLSA allows covered, nonexempt state and local government employees to receive compensatory time off (comp time)—paid time off in lieu of overtime pay—for hours worked over 40 in a workweek. Comp time is calculated at a rate that is at least one-and-a-half times the number of overtime hours worked. 
An employer and employee must agree that the employer will provide comp time in lieu of overtime pay. The agreement may be through a collective bargaining agreement or, if there is no such agreement, between the employer and individual employees. 
In general, state and local government employees may accrue up to 240 hours of comp time. Law enforcement, fire protection, emergency response personnel, and employees engaged in seasonal activities may accrue up to 480 hours of comp time. An employee must be allowed to use comp time on the date requested, unless doing so would “unduly disrupt” the operations of the agency. Employers must compensate employees for unused accrued compensatory time.
Overtime Pay Exemptions
While generally broad in coverage, the FLSA exempts several worker groups from its overtime provisions. For example, agricultural employees, certain domestic service employees, some transportation workers (including certain interstate truck drivers and taxicab drivers), movie theater employees, and some salaried executive, administrative, and professional employees, among others, are not entitled to overtime pay under the FLSA. 
The act also provides for partial exemptions from its overtime pay requirements for some groups of workers. For example, employees engaged in law enforcement and fire protection and employed by public agencies may be paid overtime on the basis of longer work periods (e.g., up to 28 consecutive days) and have higher work-hours thresholds for overtime pay (e.g., for a 14-day work period, such law enforcement personnel must receive overtime pay after 86 hours worked). 
FLSA Does Not Govern Scheduling 
The FLSA does not limit the number of hours an employee may work (e.g., there are no daily or weekly limits), and it does not govern how work hours are scheduled. For example, the act does not limit an employer’s ability to schedule 7 consecutive 24-hour workdays (but would generally require overtime pay for hours worked beyond 40 for covered, nonexempt employees). 
Enforcement
The FLSA authorizes the Department of Labor (DOL) to conduct workplace inspections and investigations to determine if FLSA violations have occurred and to enforce the FLSA provisions. 
Based on the results of an investigation, DOL may order an employer to pay back wages and liquidated damages to affected employees, may assess civil money penalties for repeat or willful violations of the FLSA overtime provisions, or both. If DOL is unable to administratively resolve a dispute, it may file a lawsuit in a U.S. district court on behalf of employees for back wages and liquidated damages, or injunctive relief (e.g., to restrain violations such as unlawful withholding of pay or retaliation against employees who cooperate with DOL). DOL may also seek an order for payment of civil money penalties from a DOL Administrative Law Judge and can recommend criminal prosecution for willful violations.
In lieu of action by DOL, employees may file a lawsuit in U.S. district court for back wages and liquidated damages, or injunctive relief. Lawsuits may be filed individually or as collective actions. A prevailing employee may recoup reasonable attorney fees and court costs from an employer who is found to violate the act.
Recent Legislative Proposals
Some bills introduced in the 119th Congress have proposed various amendments to the FLSA overtime pay provisions and related exemptions. 
Proposed amendments to the overtime pay requirement include the Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act (H.R. 10323/S. 5384) and the Double the Wage for Overtime Act of 2026 (H.R. 9216/S. 5268). 
Proposed amendments to the regular rate statutory exclusions include the Empowering Employer Child and Elder Care Solutions Act (H.R. 2270) and the Valuing Employee Stock Today Act (H.R. 8660). 
Proposals to add, modify, or remove FLSA overtime exemptions include the Outdoor Recreational Outfitting and Guiding Act (H.R. 3499), the Ensuring Access to Affordable and Quality Home Care for Seniors and People with Disabilities Act (H.R. 2304), the Restoring Overtime Pay Act of 2026 (H.R. 8868/S. 4551), the Guaranteeing Overtime for Truckers Act (H.R. 1962/S. 893), and the Fairness for Farmworkers Act (H.R. 10273/S. 5304).
The Working Families Flexibility Act of 2025 (H.R. 2870/S. 1158) would allow private sector employees to receive compensatory time in lieu of overtime pay.
The Protect Local Farms Act (H.R. 240) would preempt certain state laws entitling agricultural employees to overtime pay.

api_metadata.summary:
Introduction
Congress has historically sought to help small, “socially and economically disadvantaged” business owners overcome barriers to participating in federal contracting and compete in the national economy through the Small Business Administration’s (SBA's) 8(a) Business Development Program, (commonly known as the “8(a) program”). Congress has also established annual goals for small business participation in federal contracting, including a goal of awarding 5% of prime and subcontract awards to small, disadvantaged businesses (see CRS Insight IN12018, Federal Small Business Contracting Goals, by R. Corinne Blackford). 
For eligible businesses, 8(a) program participation offers federal contracting preferences such as federal contract set-asides and sole-source contracts. 8(a) program participants also receive dedicated business development support, including mentorship, training, and counseling designed to enhance the competitiveness of participant businesses and their long-term viability. For background on the 8(a) program, see CRS Report R44844, SBA’s 8(a) Business Development Program: Legislative and Program History, by R. Corinne Blackford. 
Although the 8(a) program was authorized in 1978 for the benefit of small businesses owned by disadvantaged individuals, Congress expanded the program in the 1980s to include entity-owned small businesses, owned by disadvantaged groups. The eligible groups or entities include
Community Development Corporations (CDCs)
Alaska Native Corporations (ANCs)
Indian tribes
Native Hawaiian Organizations (NHOs)
This In Focus highlights group- or entity-owned firm participation in the 8(a) program because these firms participate under somewhat different terms than small businesses owned by individuals.  
Legislation Expanding 8(a) Program Eligibility to Groups/Entities
CDC Eligibility 
CDCs were the first type of entity made eligible for the 8(a) program. Congress created CDCs through the Community Economic Development Act of 1981 and instructed the SBA to issue regulations ensuring that CDCs could participate in the 8(a) program (P.L. 97-35, Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981). Codified at 42 U.S.C. §9802, a CDC is defined as
a nonprofit organization responsible to residents of the area it serves which is receiving financial assistance under part A of this subchapter [42 U.S.C. §§9805 et seq.] and any organization more than 50 percent of which is owned by such an organization, or otherwise controlled by such an organization, or designated by such an organization for the purpose of this subchapter [42 U.S.C. §§9801 et seq.].
Tribal and ANC Eligibility
In 1986, two additional owner-groups, Indian tribes and ANCs, became eligible for the 8(a) program when Congress passed legislation providing that they were socially disadvantaged for 8(a) program purposes (P.L. 99-272, Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985; 15 U.S.C. §637(a)(13) and 15 U.S.C. §637(a)(4)). An ANC is
any Regional Corporation, Village Corporation, Urban Corporation, or Group Corporation organized under the laws of the State of Alaska in accordance with the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, as amended (43 U.S.C. 1601, et seq.).
For program purposes, an Indian tribe is defined at 13 C.F.R. §124.3 as
any Indian tribe, band, nation, or other organized group or community of Indians, including any ANC, which is recognized as eligible for the special programs and services provided by the United States to Indians because of their status as Indians, or is recognized as such by the State in which the tribe, band, nation, group, or community resides. 
Congress passed legislation that deemed ANCs “economically disadvantaged” in 1992 (P.L. 102-415, Alaska Land Status Technical Corrections Act of 1992). In contrast, a tribe must prove economic disadvantage the first time a tribally owned firm applies to the 8(a) Program (13 C.F.R. §124.109(b)(2)).
NHO Eligibility
Congress made NHOs eligible for the program by legislation enacted in 1988 (P.L. 100-656, Business Opportunity Development Reform Act of 1988). An NHO is defined as
any community service organization serving Native Hawaiians in the State of Hawaii which (A) is a nonprofit corporation that has filed articles of incorporation with the director (or the designee thereof) of the Hawaii Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, or any successor agency, (B) is controlled by Native Hawaiians, and (C) whose business activities will principally benefit such Native Hawaiians.
Like tribes, NHOs must prove economic disadvantage the first time an NHO-owned firm applies to the 8(a) program (13 C.F.R. §124.110(c)). 
Terms of Participation
Certain terms of participation apply to all 8(a) participants, including those owned by eligible groups. These include that the firm be “small” according to SBA size standards, be a for-profit business, be “unconditionally owned and controlled” by the disadvantaged individual or entity, demonstrate potential for success, and be of good character (applies to officers, directors, and shareholders owning more than a 20% interest in the business, or to all a firm’s “principals” in the case of CDCs). At the same time, firms owned by CDCs, tribes, ANCs, and NHOs may receive benefits not available to individually-owned firms. 
Sole-Source Contract Value
Group-owned firms may receive sole-source contracts beyond the sole-source award limits imposed on individually-owned 8(a) program participants. An 8(a) firm owned by an individual may receive a sole-source contract as long as it does not exceed $5.5 million (or $8.5 million for manufacturing contracts) (48 C.F.R. §19.805-1(b)(1)-(2)). Furthermore, an individually-owned firm may not receive additional sole-source awards once it has received a combined total of $168,500,000 in competitive contracts (via 8(a) set-asides) and sole-source contracts during its participation in the 8(a) program (13 C.F.R. §124.519). 
Per  P.L. 109-148, §8020, NHO-owned firms may only receive contracts valued over the 8(a) sole-source limits from the Department of Defense (DOD), which is using a secondary Department of War designation” under Executive Order 14347 dated September 5, 2025. 
While the 8(a) sole-source contract limits do not generally apply to group-owned firms (as mentioned, they do apply to NHO-owned firms that receive nondefense contracts), written justifications of large sole-source awards are sometimes required. A written justification for a sole-source award to a tribally- or ANC-owned firm is required for contracts in excess of $30 million, or in excess of $100 million in the case of defense contracts (P.L. 111-84;  P.L. 116-92); a written justification for a sole-source DOD award to an NHO-owned firm is also required for contracts in excess of $100 million. 
Program Participation Duration
Individuals may participate in the program for a single nine-year period (13 C.F.R. §124.108(b); 13 C.F.R. §124.2) while groups may may confer their eligibility status upon different firms on multiple occasions. This allows groups to indefinitely participate in the 8(a) program by owning multiple firms, with limitations; groups may also own more than one 8(a) program participant at a time, with limitations. Groups may not own 51% or more of another firm that “either at the time of [8(a) program] application or within the previous two years,” obtains the majority of its revenue from the same “primary” industry as another one of its firms (13 C.F.R. §124.109(c)(3)(ii); 13 C.F.R. §124.110(f); and 13 C.F.R. §124.111(d)). Groups may own multiple firms that “conduct secondary business” in the same industry, and that earn less than 50% of their revenue in the same primary industry. 
Socially Disadvantaged Status
The SBA has recently proposed to revise the criteria by which individuals establish their social disadvantage in 8(a) program applications. The proposal would not affect firms owned by CDCs, tribes, ANCs, or NHOs. For more information, see CRS Insight IN12698, Proposed SBA Rule Would Establish New Test for Social Disadvantage Under 8(a) Program, by April J. Anderson and R. Corinne Blackford.  
Community Benefits Reporting Requirements
Group-owned firms must report the community benefits of program participation for tribes, ANCs, NHOs, and CDCs. SBA regulations (13 C.F.R. §124.604) state
As part of its annual financial statement submission (see § 124.602), each Participant owned by a Tribe, ANC, NHO or CDC must submit to SBA information showing how the Tribe, ANC, NHO or CDC has provided benefits to the Tribal or native members and/or the Tribal, native or other community due to the Tribe’s/ANC's/NHO's/CDC’s participation in the 8(a) BD program through one or more firms. This data includes information relating to funding cultural programs, employment assistance, jobs, scholarships, internships, subsistence activities, and other services provided by the Tribe, ANC, NHO or CDC to the affected community.
Federal Contracts Awarded
According to data published in the SBA Procurement Scorecard for FY2025, group-owned firms make up about 16% of firms in the program and received 67% of the contract award dollars made to 8(a) firms in FY2025. GSA’s Small Business Goaling Reports show that 8(a) contract dollars (to any type of participant) have risen in the past five fiscal years. Introduction
A federal student loan made under Title IV of the Higher Education Act of 1965 (P.L. 89-329), as amended, is considered delinquent the first day after a borrower fails to make a scheduled payment. The Department of Education (ED), through its contracted loan servicers, reports delinquencies to the nationwide, private consumer reporting agencies (CRAs; i.e., Equifax, Experian, TransUnion, Innovis) after 90 days or more of delinquency. Generally, a loan is in default after 270 days of a missed scheduled payment, which is reported to CRAs. 
Since 2020, the portfolio of ED-held federal student loans (ED-held loans) has experienced unusual fluctuations in delinquency and default trends. This In Focus highlights these trends and how various loan-servicing-related issues may have affected these patterns and borrower credit scores. For purposes of this In Focus, loan servicing refers to daily management of a loan. The tasks associated with loan servicing are typically performed by ED-contracted servicers. Their duties include issuing billing statements, collecting regular payments, administering forbearances and alternative repayment plans for past-due borrowers, and reporting loan status to CRAs.
Delinquency and Default Trends
Borrowers of ED-held loans were afforded up to two periods of loan repayment relief in response to and following the COVID-19 pandemic. First, a series of congressional- and Administration-authorized forbearances suspended borrowers’ monthly payment obligations between March 2020 and August 2023 (the payment pause). Second, after P.L. 118-5 ended the payment pause, ED instituted an on-ramp policy, from September 2023 through September 2024. Under this policy, monthly student loan payments were due, but ED placed borrowers more than 90 days delinquent in a retroactive administrative forbearance. This placed a loan’s status to “current repayment” (i.e., not delinquent) and delayed certain consequences of loan delinquency, such as negative credit reporting, until January 2025. 
In light of these policies, notable shifts in delinquency rate patterns of ED-held loans began in March 2020. Similar shifts in default rates occurred several months later at a more gradual pace, as both policies effectively prevented loans from entering delinquency or default. (Loans in default prior to the policies’ implementation remained in default during the policies’ effective dates unless a borrower took steps to resolve the default). In the pre-pandemic period from FY2017 Q1 to FY2020 Q1, between 6% and 8% of loans were 31-270 days delinquent. This rate declined to 0% in FY2020 Q3, the first full quarter in which the payment pause was in effect. The delinquency rate remained at 0% through FY2023 Q4, reflecting the impact of the pandemic-era forbearance policies.
Figure 1 shows that the share of borrowers with better credit scores (teal & purple) generally grew relative to those with weaker credit scores (red & blue) a bit more beginning in 2020. However, these data may not fully reflect a borrower’s actual creditworthiness, as they overlap with the COVID-19 student loan forbearance and on-ramp policies.
Figure 1. Student Loan Borrowers by Credit Score
2004-2024
/
Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 2025 Student Loan Update (direct download). 
Note: Includes borrowers of non-ED-held student loans.
Additionally, the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston found that for borrowers with ED-held loans affected by the payment pause, their credit scores increased to a greater extent than did scores of individuals without student loans. Their analysis suggests that a loan servicing practice—forbearance—rather than a borrower’s ability to repay their debt influenced the rise in credit scores.
Following the static student loan delinquency and default rates of the pandemic era, loan portfolio volatility rose along with the adoption of new federal policies. Figure 2 shows rising delinquencies that are transitioning into defaults over the FY2023 Q4 to FY2026 Q3 period. The rate of recipients with ED-held loans who were 31-270 days delinquent increased from 0% in FY2023 Q4 to 16% the following quarter. Borrowers who exited retroactive administrative forbearance in FY2025 Q1 without curing their delinquency or newly became 31-90 days delinquent transitioned to being 91-270 days delinquent in FY2025 Q2. The default rate remained relatively steady until increasing from 12% (5.3 million recipients) in FY2025 Q3 to 19% (8.8 million recipients) by the next quarter. Over the same period, the share of recipients with loans that were 91-270 days delinquent decreased from 12% (5.5 million) to 4% (1.9 million), likely representing a substantial portion of delinquent borrowers transitioning into default status.
Figure 2. ED-Held Loans: Delinquency, Default Rates 
FY2023 Q4 to FY2026 Q3
/
Source: CRS analysis; U.S. Department of Education, Federal Student Aid Data Center, “Federal Student Loan Portfolio.”
Loan Servicing and Repayment Topics
Various factors contributed to the rising delinquency and defaults on ED-held loans beginning in FY2024 Q1. This discussion focuses on factors related to loan servicing, an issue raised by some current news and research. Economic factors (e.g., college costs, general affordability issues) or borrower educational experiences are not discussed.
Extended Forbearance Policies
The FY2025 Q4 increase in defaults (sometimes referred to as a “default cliff”) has been linked to congressional and Administration forbearance policies established in response to and following the COVID-19 pandemic. After the payment pause and on-ramp policies ended, many borrowers may have become disconnected from their loan servicers and fallen out of the practice of making monthly loan payments. ED has also noted the higher risk of delinquency or default following prolonged periods of forbearance. 
Observers hypothesize that other forbearance policies may generate more loan defaults. Since July 2024, ED placed millions of borrowers enrolled in the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) repayment plan in forbearance in response to litigation challenging ED’s authority to establish the plan. After a federal court vacated the SAVE plan, borrowers must enroll in a different repayment plan or be placed in a standard repayment plan. As with previous forbearances, observers argue that prolonged periods without borrowers making payments may increase the likelihood that they become delinquent or default. Furthermore, research indicates that borrowers in income-driven repayment (IDR) plans, which base monthly payments on income (e.g., the SAVE plan), have lower default rates relative to those in standard repayment plans. Thus, placing SAVE plan enrollees who fail to select an IDR plan into a standard repayment plan raises concerns about potential future defaults.
Loan Servicing Issues
Historical and seemingly ongoing issues encountered in the loan administration environment may impact a borrower’s ability to successfully repay their loans, which may lead to negative impacts on their credit history. For example, in 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau reported that “loan servicers routinely made basic payment processing errors,” including misreporting payment amounts. Findings show that borrowers have received conflicting, confusing, or inaccurate information from their loan servicers, contributing to some inadvertent or mistaken delinquencies appearing on borrower credit reports.
ED directed the transfer of servicing rights among student loan servicers in 2023, which may have contributed to nearly 2 million credit reporting errors. CRAs allegedly were not informed of the transfer, which could have affected credit profiles. For example, a single debt might appear as two duplicate loans, portraying borrowers as carrying higher debt amounts. If a loan appears closed and a “new loan” opened, then borrowers’ credit histories may be incorrectly shortened. Some borrowers’ on-time credit histories may not properly carry forward during transfer. 
Finally, implementation of 2025 statutory changes made to the federal student loan programs (e.g., the repeal of some existing and the authorization of new loan repayment plans) may further complicate loan administration. 
Negative Credit Reporting Issues
ED servicers may report both favorable and negative (late) payment history to the private CRAs. Student loan delinquencies can reduce credit scores by more than 150 points, limiting borrowers’ future credit access. Similarly, negative payment information reported to the Credit Alert Verification Reporting System (CAIVRS), a federal database managed by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, can also limit credit access for some borrowers. CAIVRS is used to screen applicants and track delinquencies and defaults for loans that were made or insured by federal agencies such as the Federal Housing Administration, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Small Business Administration, and ED. Unlike private CRAs, CAIVRS includes only information about federally made or insured loans that are 90 days or more past due—or have defaulted. Only authorized loan originators and federal agencies, and not private CRAs, can access CAIVRS. A federal agency, for example, may report negative information to CAIVRS without notifying private CRAs, causing an individual to appear creditworthy based solely on a private credit inquiry. (Conversely, someone with past-due loans that have no federal guarantee will not appear in CAIVRS.) Notably, individuals must rely on approved lenders to view their CAIVRS status. Thus, if a borrower’s loan status is reported to CAIVRS by ED servicers without the borrower’s knowledge, they may discover the reporting to CAIVRS while applying for a federally guaranteed mortgage or small business loan. Consequently, after resolving issues with ED, some borrowers may still need to dispute inaccurate information.

On October 20, 2026, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a Notice of Order Regarding Exclusion and Removal of DeepSeek Products from Federal Civilian Executive Branch Information Technology Systems and Procurements in the Federal Register. This notice requires federal civilian executive branch (FCEB) departments and agencies to bar products made by the People’s Republic of China (PRC)-headquartered firm DeepSeek from their networks, and to remove any DeepSeek products that may have already been deployed. The DHS order follows a similar action made by the Department of Defense (DOD, which is “using a secondary Department of War designation,” under Executive Order 14347) on September 8, 2026. The Director of National Intelligence (DNI) issued a similar order concurrently with DHS. This In Focus discusses these actions and their implications related to supply chain security.
Overview of DeepSeek 
Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd. (DeepSeek) is an artificial intelligence (AI) company located in the PRC. DeepSeek develops open-weight large language models (LLM), such as (the eponymously named) DeepSeek and DeepSeek-R1. 
DeepSeek’s AI products have been noted for their general and cost efficiency. While their models are not as powerful as U.S. models, DeepSeek’s models have cheaper token costs, can perform tasks quickly, and can be downloaded, hosted, and customized. Because of their price-to-performance advantage, DeepSeek’s (and other PRC AI) models have been adopted by some U.S. companies. 
The U.S. government issued warnings about the risks of PRC AI models and their adoption. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the National Security Agency (NSA) have said that DeepSeek and its peer companies have carried out large-scale distillation campaigns (e.g., the systemic querying of an AI model and using its responses without authorization to train another model) on U.S. models to develop their products. Further, the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) found that DeepSeek’s AI models are more prone to jailbreaking, more likely to follow malicious commands than U.S. models, and more often provided users with narratives consistent with messaging from the Communist Party of China (CPC). 
DeepSeek models are available to U.S. users through several pathways. They can be accessed directly from DeepSeek (e.g., from their mobile application), through domestic cloud service providers and AI platforms, or downloaded and run on a user’s hardware.
Select Legislative Actions on DeepSeek
The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (enacted December 18, 2025) requires that DOD issue an exclusion and removal order for DeepSeek technologies. That order was issued on September 8, 2026. The Department of the Air Force issued an exclusion and removal order on July 10, 2025. 
The U.S. House of Representative’s (House) Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party (Select Committee on China) issued a report on risks from DeepSeek and the company’s actions to subvert U.S. policy on April 16, 2025. The House Committee on Science Space and Technology held a hearing on DeepSeek on April 8, 2025. 
Exclusion and Removal Order
The Federal Register notice for the DHS order on DeepSeek products includes a copy of Exclusion and Removal Order #2026-01 from July 24, 2026. It states that DeepSeek poses risks to the United States because:
The company is subject to PRC laws, including the 2017 cybersecurity law (which could allow the government to compel disclosure of sensitive information from DeepSeek);
Signing up for a DeepSeek account would require the collection of personally identifiable information (PII);
DeepSeek collects inputs and outputs, which could result in sensitive information being transmitted to U.S. adversaries; and
Any information leaked through DeepSeek could be used, or combined and used, with other information for actionable intelligence against the United States.
DHS also raises concerns that DeepSeek’s applications (such as the aforementioned mobile application) are configured in ways that are insecure.
Because of these risks, federal departments and agencies are required to bar DeepSeek, its affiliated entities, and their products from procurements. Further, any previously acquired products must be immediately removed. This order extends to federal contractors and firms doing business with the prime contractor.
Agencies may petition CISA for an exception to this order. Further, CISA will assist agencies in implementing the order. The order suggests that it should be reviewed within a year and annually thereafter.
This is the first time that DHS has exercised its authority to issue exclusion and removal orders—a tool to mitigate supply chain risks at federal agencies.
Authority to Combat Technology Risks
The U.S. government has taken several actions since 2017 to address potential foreign cyber technology risks. In September 2017, DHS issued a Binding Operational Directive ordering the removal of Kaspersky-branded software products from federal agency use. In December 2017, Congress passed a statute codifying that directive. 
Recognizing that foreign adversaries may seek to use information and communications technology (ICT) supply chains to compromise organizations, Congress sought to create a repeatable process for restricting potentially dangerous ICT from federal agencies. A precursor bill was debated and passed in the Senate before being enacted as the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 (Title II of the SECURE Technology Act of 2018). This act, among other actions, created the Federal Acquisition Security Council (FASC).
Federal Acquisition Security Council 
The FASC is an interagency body that serves as a government-wide forum to identify, assess, and manage ICT supply chain risks to the federal government. It can recommend that federal agencies exclude particular entities and products from federal procurement because they pose an unacceptable risk to national security.
Per FASC’s implementing rule, a senior official from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) chairs the FASC. Other members include the General Services Administration (GSA), DHS, CISA, the DNI, the National Counterintelligence and Security Center (NCSC), the Department of Justice (DOJ), the FBI, DOD, NSA, the Department of Commerce, and NIST. These agencies provide the council with procurement, cybersecurity, intelligence, law enforcement, national security, and technical expertise.
U.S. government agencies may refer cases to FASC. The FASC may investigate such cases and coordinate across federal departments and agencies (not just FASC members) on the risk posed by the product or company, develop and recommend potential remedies to address those risks, and (if necessary) issue requirements for agencies to exclude certain vendors or products from federal networks and remove such vendors or products. 
Exclusion and removal orders are issued by DHS for the FCEB, DOD for the military, and the DNI for the intelligence community (IC). All three agencies need not coordinate combined orders. The first exclusion and removal orders issued under this authority were by DNI and DOD (almost a year apart) for Acronis—a cybersecurity firm. DHS has not issued a similar order.  
The recent orders against DeepSeek are the first time that all three agencies have acted to address the risks from a single vendor. This is the first time DHS has exercised this authority. This is also the first time that DHS, DOD, and DNI have issued similar orders in close succession.
Considerations for Congress
The exclusion and removal orders issued by DOD, DNI, and CISA may spark interest among policymakers on what further actions Congress may take to combat the threat from DeepSeek, other PRC firms, and cyber supply chain risk management in both the public and private sectors.
Congress may seek to conduct oversight. The DeepSeek orders provide Congress a case study on the efficacy and utility of the FASC. Congress may choose to ask the Comptroller General (GAO), or the inspector generals for DHS, DOD, and the IC to evaluate the FASC’s implementation of the DeepSeek order as well its broader operations, including processes for referrals, coordinating and evaluating risk across the interagency, and barriers to issuing orders. GAO has previously assessed the FASC’s establishment and DOD’s support. 
The FASC limits federal procurement but does not restrict non-governmental access to and use of DeepSeek. Congress may choose to consider the extent to which the Federal Acquisition Regulation’s extension of prohibitions to contractors creates a broader disincentive for the private sector to adopt the barred companies. (For example, when Congress barred Huawei Technologies Company and ZTE Corporation telecommunications equipment from servicing the government, it served as a disincentive for wider adoption in the private sector.) Congress may also choose to consider whether a federal prohibition for a cloud service provider (CSP) that contracts with federal government extends to the nonfederal instances of the services that a CSP provides. 
Relatedly, Congress might evaluate the risks that DHS, DOD, and the DNI determined regarding DeepSeek products and consider whether broader U.S. use restrictions are needed. Congress might also assess whether other PRC firms or technologies also merit scrutiny. While the FASC can create vendor prohibitions for the federal government, other departments and agencies can act broadly across the economy. For example, the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019 authorizes the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to prevent communications equipment that poses national security risks from being deployed on U.S. networks. The FCC implements this through their Covered List. Congress may choose to examine the extent to which the FASC and other federal agencies have sufficient authority to combat transnational security risks from technology (e.g., AI). 
While the FASC process seeks to protect the federal government against ICT supply chain threats through procurement policy, those same threats extend to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments; the private sector; academia; and other non-governmental organizations. Congress also could assess whether new authorities are needed to ensure adequate identification, analysis, and mitigation of ICT supply chain risks across the nation, and whether agencies can efficiently work on whole-of-government approaches to ICT supply chain security and threat mitigation.

State Proposals to Change Daylight Saving Time Observance
Daylight saving time (DST) is a period of the year between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time (ST). The United States first adopted DST in 1918. DST begins on the second Sunday in March and ends on the first Sunday in November. The beginning and end dates are set in statute (15 U.S.C. §260a). 
Congressional interest in the potential benefits and costs of DST has resulted in changes to DST observance (including changes to its start and end dates, periods of temporary year-round DST, and periods of no federal DST observance). Though the authority to change DST observance rests solely with Congress, since 2015, a majority of states have had legislation introduced to change the observance of DST—seeking to establish either DST or ST year round. State-enacted permanent DST would go into effect if and when such action is allowed by Congress.

Forty-seven states and DC have had legislation introduced proposing some variation of permanent year-round DST. 
* Introduced permanent DST
* Enacted permanent DST (19 states)
* Adopted nonbinding resolution in support of permanent DST
* No DST legislation introduced
Forty-two states have had legislation introduced to establish permanent year-round ST. The Uniform Time Act of 1966 as amended (15 U.S.C. §§260-267) allows states to exempt themselves from observing DST.
* Introduced permanent ST 
* No ST legislation introduced
* Observes permanent ST 

Sources: State legislation information from Lexis Advance “Statutes and Legislation” database; state legislature websites/databases; National Council of State Legislature’s Daylight Saving Time | State Legislation resource; CQ.com’s Policy Note database. 
Notes: American Samoa, most of Arizona, Guam, Hawaii, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands do not observe DST. CRS identified introduced legislation from January 2015 to August 2026 that would amend time observance; in this search, CRS did not identify any introduced legislation for the U.S. territories that would amend time observance. 
For more information, see CRS Report R45208, Daylight Saving Time (DST).
Information as of October 19, 2026. Prepared by Corrie E. Clark, Specialist in Energy Policy; Lynn J. Cunningham, Senior Research Librarian; Cassandra E. Higgins, Geospatial Information Systems Analyst; and Amber Wilhelm, Visual Information Specialist.

On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched military operations against Iran. The same day, President Donald Trump listed among the operation’s objectives preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, destroying Iran’s missiles, and “[razing] their missile industry to the ground.” Some Members of Congress have questioned the U.S. military operations in Iran given President Trump’s previous assertion that, as a result of the June 2025 U.S.-Israeli strikes, “Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated.” Other Members have supported the President’s action, citing Iran’s post-2025 efforts to reconstitute its nuclear program and its ballistic missile capabilities. Reports on the status of Iran’s missile and drone programs vary as of October 2026 amid continued, albeit reduced, military confrontation between the United States and Iran.
Iran’s Ballistic Missile and Drone Programs 
Iran has developed short- and medium-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and space-launch vehicles. Iran has also mass-produced various long-range one-way attack drones, such as the Shahed-136, and has provided drones to Russia for use in its war in Ukraine. After Israeli strikes on Iranian missile sites in 2024 and 2025, Iran “focused on rebuilding damaged infrastructure and pursuing Russia- and China-origin systems and materials to replace equipment,” according to an April 2026 U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) assessment.
Beginning on February 28, 2026, U.S. and Israeli aircraft targeted bases and equipment associated with Iran’s ballistic missile program, including missiles Iran may have stored in underground facilities. The White House stated on April 8, after the United States and Iran agreed to a temporary ceasefire, that the operation involved strikes on “more than 450 ballistic missile targets” and “approximately 800 attack drone targets,” and that “Iran’s ballistic missile arsenal and production capacity has been razed.” Since April, the United States has continued to target Iranian missile and drone facilities, and Iranian ballistic missiles and drones have struck U.S. and partner military and civil sites, as well as vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
DIA assessed in April 2026 that Iran “retains thousands of missiles and one-way attack UAVs that can threaten U.S. and partner forces throughout the region, despite degradations to its capabilities from both attrition and expenditure.” News articles in July, August, and September, citing satellite imagery and U.S. and Israeli military and intelligence officials, stated that Iran may have begun rebuilding military infrastructure, restoring access to missile bases, and resuming missile production using stockpiled components. An Iranian official reportedly asserted in August that Iran has sufficient “stockpiles in our underground missile and drone cities” to enable continued production. Some reports have highlighted the damage to Iranian production facilities and the difficulties Iran may face in reconstituting its missile development and production capability.
Iran’s Nuclear Program
Iran for decades has maintained a uranium enrichment program. Uranium enrichment can produce both low-enriched uranium, which can be used in nuclear power reactors, and highly enriched uranium, which is one of the two types of fissile material used in nuclear weapons. Tehran asserts its enrichment program is only meant to produce fuel for peaceful nuclear applications.
Whether the U.S.-Israeli strikes since February 28 have affected Iran’s nuclear facilities is unclear. On March 4, based on analysis of satellite imagery, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported “no damage to facilities containing nuclear material in Iran,” but some damage “at entrances” to the Natanz enrichment facility. The agency subsequently reported that analysis of such imagery revealed “damage to additional non-nuclear-related buildings” near this facility. The IAEA, which implements safeguards on Iran’s nuclear facilities because the government is a state party to the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, withdrew inspectors from Iran in June 2025 after U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. In November 2025, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran was not enriching uranium.
The IAEA has not been able to inspect the attacked Iranian nuclear facilities since the June 2025 strikes. U.S. government reports have provided differing assessments of the June 2025 strikes’ impacts. According to the 2025 U.S. National Security Strategy, the strikes “significantly degraded” Iran’s nuclear program, while the 2026 National Defense Strategy stated the strikes “obliterated” the program. 
The U.S. intelligence community has for years assessed that Iran could have the capability to produce nuclear weapons at some point, but also that Tehran halted its nuclear weapons program in late 2003 and had not mastered all of the necessary technologies for building such weapons. U.S. intelligence also assessed, through 2025, that Tehran had not reauthorized the development of nuclear weapons. Prior to the 2026 airstrikes, Iran “was intending to try to recover from the devastation of its nuclear infrastructure,” the 2026 Annual Threat Assessment (ATA) of the U.S. Intelligence Community states. On March 2, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi stated the agency had no evidence of “a structured [Iranian] program to manufacture nuclear weapons.” 
Legislative Activity
The House Armed Services Committee (HASC), in a report accompanying the HASC-reported version of a National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H.R. 8800; H.Rept. 119-698), directed the Secretary of Defense (who is using “Secretary of War” as a “secondary title” under Executive Order 14347, dated September 5, 2025) to submit to the committee a report by February 1, 2027, on the “impact of United States military operations ... on Iran’s nuclear and missile capabilities.”
Considerations for Congress
Congress may consider assessing the status and scope of existing reporting requirements on Iran, including of Section 1245 of P.L. 111-84 (10 U.S.C. §113 note), which directed the Secretary of Defense to submit to Congress an “annual report on military power of Iran” by January 30 of each year. Congress has modified this requirement, including by directing the Secretary to provide additional information about Iran’s nuclear and drone programs (P.L. 119-60, §1222). Congress may consult that report to determine whether or not it should include additional information. Congress may consider directing the Pentagon to publish a public version of the report. Members could ask questions concerning the above topics during threat assessment hearings.

Since the United States and Israel launched military operations against Iran on February 28, 2026, some Members of Congress have raised concerns about and sought information from the Department of Defense on the stockpiles and availability of munitions (e.g., ammunition, bombs, missiles, torpedoes, anti-aircraft weapons, and missile interceptors). (DOD is “using a secondary Department of War designation,” under Executive Order 14347 dated September 5, 2025.) Following the Trump Administration’s request for FY2026 supplemental funding, including $67.1 billion for military operations against Iran and other DOD activities, the House adopted a concurrent resolution (H.Con.Res. 113) that would allow for accelerated consideration of reconciliation legislation to provide $60 billion in mandatory defense funding beginning FY2027, potentially to include funding for munitions. 
In September 2026, President Donald Trump said, “we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using,” and DOD officials have said sufficient munitions are available. The DOD Office of Inspector General, citing the DOD Office of the Under Secretary for Acquisition and Sustainment, stated that “the munitions expenditure in [Operation Epic Fury] has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply” and that the “defense industrial base requires significant lead time’ to expand production capacities.” 
U.S. Capabilities Expended in Operations Against Iran
DOD has not made public the precise numbers of specific types of munitions expended in the conflict. The House and Senate Committees on Armed Services have reportedly received classified briefings with Administration officials on the conduct of operations. In congressional testimony on May 14, Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), stated that the U.S. military conducted more than “13,500 strikes” in the initial 38 days of “major combat operations.” The United States and regional partners “intercepted over 6,000 one-way attack drones and more than 1,500 ballistic missiles,” according to Admiral Cooper. 
An April 2026 assessment by a U.S. think tank estimated that the United States had expended substantial quantities of selected, high-cost munitions in the conflict, including Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) and Patriot interceptors, Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles, and Tomahawk missiles. An August 2026 news article, citing U.S. officials, reported the U.S. military had expended approximately 1,700 Patriot, 200 THAAD, and 150 Standard Missile interceptors. In September 2026, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), comparing public reporting on U.S. missile defense interceptor munition purchases with reported conflict usage, estimated that the United States had “probably used between one-half and two-thirds” of its inventory of certain missile interceptors.
Cost of Expended Munitions
On June 24, 2026, the Office of Management and Budget submitted to Congress a supplemental funding request for defense and other Administration priorities that included a $21 billion request for “munitions.” Subsequently, DOD presented varying estimates of the cost of replacing munitions expended since February 2026. For example, DOD has also estimated the cost of replacing expended munitions at $27.7 billion, according to CBO. In September, CBO, citing reporting from publicly available sources on the quantities of munitions expended, estimated the cost to replace munitions expended through August 1, 2026, was $21.7 billion, including “$7.3 billion for the land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for the missile defense interceptors, and $1.2 billion for other munitions.” CBO estimated that it “would probably take at least five years” to replace certain interceptors even at an increased rate of production. 
Congressional Action on FY2026 Supplemental Request
On July 22, the House adopted a concurrent budget resolution (H.Con.Res. 113) that included reconciliation instructions to the House Armed Services Committee to “submit changes in laws within its jurisdiction that increase the deficit” by no more than $60 billion for the period FY2027-FY2036. The resolution did not specify the amount to be allocated to munitions. In a statement, Representative Jodey Arrington, chair of the House Budget Committee, stated that the resolution would provide the “bombs, bullets, and battlefield readiness ... to finish the fight.” On July 23, the resolution was received in the Senate. As of this product’s publication date, the Senate has not considered the measure. 
Potential Considerations for Congress
Appropriations for Munitions. In FY2025 and FY2026, Congress took steps to increase munitions stockpiles and production by authorizing and appropriating funds, among other actions. Congress may consider whether or not to provide additional funds for munitions used in the Middle East. Congress may also consider whether or not to increase funding for munitions in FY2027 appropriations and subsequent years. 
Munitions Inventories. Congress is considering legislation that would require reporting on the financial cost of operations against Iran (H.R. 8800, §1089E), as well as on the status of U.S. munitions stockpiles and inventory requirements (H.R. 8800, §321; S. 4784, §872). Congress may also consider conducting oversight of related issues, such as the amount of time required to replenish munitions stocks, as well as options for low-cost alternatives to existing missile interceptors and weapons for countering drone threats.
Missile Defense Integration and Foreign Military Sales (FMS). The United States has sought to integrate missile defense efforts with allies and partners in part through sales of U.S. equipment. Finite U.S. industrial base capacity introduces trade-offs between filling FMS orders and replenishing U.S. stockpiles. FMS delivery delays may result in cancellations, potentially affecting U.S. and partner interoperability and integration. Congress is considering legislation that would require the integration of FMS demand into industrial base planning (H.R. 8800, §1817). Congress may also consider how the executive branch develops and updates prioritization criteria for FMS and whether coproduction efforts could augment U.S. capacity.
Tactical and Strategic Vulnerabilities. Congress may consider the potential vulnerabilities associated with shortages of certain munitions and reported damage to associated defense systems. In the near term, potential vulnerabilities may include a narrowing of options for sustaining operations in Iran and sustaining U.S. allies. In the medium term, Congress may assess how depleted stockpiles may affect the U.S. ability to “erect a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain” in the Indo-Pacific, as described in the 2026 National Defense Strategy.

The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to hire temporary foreign workers for specialty occupation positions (i.e., positions that require specialized knowledge and a college degree). To date in 2026 the Trump Administration has announced several policy changes aimed at addressing perceived abuses of the program, such as replacing U.S. workers with lower-paid foreign workers. These executive actions come on the heels of policy changes announced in 2025.
Increased Costs for Employers
In February 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) implemented a weighted (instead of random) selection process for the H-1B lottery to “favor the allocation of H-1B visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid” workers. The first affected lottery was for H-1B employment starting in October 2026.
In March 2026, the Department of Labor (DOL) published a proposed rule to increase H-1B prevailing wage requirements. DOL asserted that under the current regulation, “employers were permitted to hire alien workers at wage levels below those that similarly employed U.S. workers were paid, resulting in adverse effects to the wages and working conditions of U.S. workers.” H-1B prevailing wage requirements differ by skill level (See Table 1), specialty occupation, and Metropolitan Statistical Area.

Source: CRS Presentation of 91 Federal Register 15454.
DOL estimated these proposed wage requirements would increase H-1B employer costs by approximately $1.46 billion in the first year.
In August 2026, DHS issued a proposed rule to establish a new $103,265 fee to “generate dedicated revenue to support the costs of administering the lawful immigration system.” The new fee would apply to each cap-subject petition submitted by employers for H-1B workers. This is separate from the $100,000 fee the Administration imposed in September 2025 on U.S. employers petitioning for new H-1B workers from abroad (which was in effect for most of the past year but is currently temporarily blocked due to ongoing litigation).
In August 2026, DHS issued a final rule that applies an existing $4,000 “9-11 Biometric Fee” to petitions filed by certain employers on behalf of H-1B or L-1 workers (within-company transfers to the United States) who are extending their status. Before this rule, DHS had interpreted the 9-11 Biometric Fee passed by Congress in 2015 to apply only to petitions for new workers or those changing employers. Employers subject to this fee—before and after the change—are those with more than 50 employees in the United States, of whom more than 50 percent are in H-1B or L-1 status. The 9-11 Biometric Fee is scheduled to sunset on September 30, 2027. 
Increased Scrutiny of Employers
In July 2026, the DOL Office of the Inspector General announced an investigation and intensified enforcement efforts “to combat fraud and human trafficking” in the H-1B program, focusing on fraudulent applications and coercive wage-kickbacks. This initiative includes a nationwide awareness program encouraging workers to report concerns to DOL. It builds on the 2025 launch of “Project Firewall,” an initiative to strengthen labor enforcement of the H-1B program by “prioritizing investigations where there are signs of displacements, inadequate recruitment of U.S. workers, or other abuses.” Data on DOL H-1B compliance enforcement actions in FY2026 are not yet available.
In September 2026, President Trump issued an executive order, requiring more coordination between agencies to “ensure the compliance ... with statutory requirements” and requires them to “take into account in any labor condition application, petition, visa, and entry of aliens entering or attempting to enter the United States as H-1B nonimmigrants ... whether the employer sponsor directly or indirectly engaged in layoffs within the previous year or plans future layoffs.” Current law does not bar employers with recent layoffs of U.S. workers from employing H-1B workers. DHS is also considering “revising eligibility for cap exemptions, providing greater scrutiny for employers that have violated program requirements, and increasing oversight over third party placements.” 
In October 2026, DHS proposed removing a policy of deferring to prior approvals when employers petition to extend H-1B workers’ employment. Removing “prior deference” would increase scrutiny of extension requests when the circumstances of H-1B employment are unchanged.
Restrictions for Workers
In September 2026, DHS proposed eliminating a grace period (implemented in 2017), which allows H-1B and certain other temporary workers to remain in the United States for up to 60 days after their employment ends. In October, DHS eliminated automatic extensions of work authorization for spouses of H-1B workers and is considering removing their eligibility for work authorization altogether. 
Some employers sponsor their H-1B workers for permanent labor certification (known as PERM). If approved, these workers may become LPRs, which allows them to more easily change employers (and to eventually become U.S. citizens). The administration has initiated rulemaking “improving the minimum standards for recruiting qualified U.S. workers, strengthening safeguards for U.S. workers impacted by layoffs, and enhancing employer compliance with program requirements related to non-discriminatory recruitment and hiring practices.” Such changes could result in fewer H-1B workers being approved for PERM. 
Impacts Thus Far
There are indications that employers are filing fewer petitions for H-1B workers coming from abroad. DHS data show reduced petition filings from both cap-subject and cap-exempt employers following the implementation of the $100,000 fee in 2025. For example, during the first eight months that the fee was in effect, the number of initial H-1B petitions that DHS received for consular processing from cap-exempt employers dropped 91% from the same period the year before. Similarly, cap-subject companies that typically had high numbers of H-1B employees coming from abroad submitted significantly fewer entries to the FY2027 H-1B lottery. Among the highest lottery entrants in FY2026 were Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata, which submitted 100%, 91%, and 95% fewer registrations in FY2027, respectively.

On October 1, 2026, the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) published for comment revised policy guidance for the Capital Investment Grants Program (CIG). In the Federal Register notice, FTA stated “the proposed revisions are intended to streamline the CIG process, improve accountability of CIG project sponsors, and improve overall readability of the policy guidance.” Among other things, FTA proposes a new formal methodology for calculating the federal share of a proposed project’s cost from a CIG grant. This proposed methodology includes greater CIG funding shares for projects in places with higher than average birth rates and marriage rates, in line with the Department of Transportation’s (DOT’s) “family friendly” policy.
CIG provides funding to support the construction of fixed-guideway transit systems (e.g., light rail), including new systems and additions to existing systems. A CIG project is categorized as a “New Starts” project, unless as a “Small Starts” project it costs less than $400 million and CIG program funding is less than $150 million. “Core Capacity” projects are investments in existing fixed-guideway systems that increase capacity of a corridor by 10% that is at or will be at capacity in 10 years (49 U.S.C. §5309(a)).
To evaluate proposed CIG projects, FTA computes ratings of statutory project justification and local financial commitment criteria on a 5-point scale (high, medium-high, medium, medium-low, low). The project justification criteria are mobility improvements, environmental benefits, congestion relief, economic development effects, land use (or capacity needs of the corridor for Core Capacity projects), and cost effectiveness. Cost effectiveness, for example, is measured by estimated capital and operating and maintenance costs per trip.
Federal law limits the maximum federal share of a project’s cost from the CIG program funds to 60% for New Starts projects and 80% for Small Starts and Core Capacity projects (49 U.S.C. §5309(l)). Many projects have received a commitment from FTA for a CIG share below the maximum. 
FTA’s October 2026 proposal is for a “formal methodology [that] would provide a uniform and consistent approach for FTA to consider project merits, such as cost-effectiveness and transit ridership, when determining the CIG percentage share and corresponding CIG funding amount for a New Starts or Core Capacity project.” Accordingly, projects with an overall medium or higher rating would start with a 40% CIG share of project costs. This share would then be adjusted on the basis of the ratings of the project justification criteria up to the maximum allowed by law (Table 1). FTA states that it “believes these adjustment factors are appropriate because they clearly put the emphasis on cost-effectiveness and ridership, which will allow FTA to provide a higher CIG percentage share to projects that are cost-effective and projected to have high transit ridership, and will ensure Federal taxpayer funds are supporting worthy investments.”

Note: *New Starts only; **Core Capacity only.
FTA’s proposed CIG policy would also increase the CIG funding share for relatively high birth rates and marriage rates within the project corridor, defined as a one-mile buffer around the project corridor using census tract data from the Census Bureau. The increase would be an additional five percentage points each if the average birth or marriage rate in the project corridor is more than 1% above the national average, three points if the birth or marriage rate is equal to the national average or up to 1% percent higher than the national average, and one point if the average birth or marriage rate is within 1% below the national average. 
According to FTA, these proposed adjustments are consistent with DOT Order 2100.7, “Ensuring Reliance Upon Sound Economic Analysis in Department of Transportation Policies, Programs, and Activities,” issued on March 10, 2025, by the Secretary of Transportation. The order states DOT should “give preference to communities with marriage and birth rates higher than the national average (including in administering the Federal Transit Administration’s Capital Investment Grant program).”
Some question whether this proposed addition to the funding share calculation, as FTA states in the Federal Register notice, would “ensure Federal taxpayer funds are supporting worthy investments.” The birth rate and marriage rate adjustments may offset poorer scores on other metrics, possibly leading to less effective projects. For example, together high birth rate and marriage rate adjustments can be worth as much as a medium-low cost effectiveness score.
In terms of ridership, fixed-guideway transit modes are most effective in high density urban corridors. Critics of the FTA proposal point to research on the geography of birth rates and marriage rates indicating that places with relatively high rates tend to be located farther away from urban centers than places with relatively low rates. Households in high birth and high marriage rate areas tend to be higher income, more likely to own a car and drive alone to work, and less likely to walk, bike, or take public transit to work. Residents of places with high marriage and high birth rates are more likely to be White and less likely to be Black or Hispanic. 
Adjusting the federal CIG funding share on the basis of marriage and birth rates may incentivize more commuter rail projects, which are designed to provide longer distance trips to outlying places with lower density uses. In a study of commuter rail agencies, the Government Accountability Office found that commuter rail can provide economic and mobility benefits for less urbanized communities but that there are “considerable infrastructure and operational costs making commuter rail more expensive to provide compared to some other transit modes.”
