Various searches by federal agents of sitting Members of Congress can raise questions about the intersection of Fourth Amendment principles and the privilege held by Members under the Speech or Debate Clause of the Constitution. In one of these examples, reporting indicates that agents from Homeland Security Investigations seized documents and the Member’s cellphone and laptop as part of an immigration-related investigation. It has also been reported that the search in the previous example was executed pursuant to a warrant and that the issuing judge imposed special procedural requirements on law enforcement in light of the Member’s constitutional protections under the Speech or Debate Clause. The Member has reportedly alleged that some of those protocols were not followed, including a requirement that the Member and the House General Counsel be notified prior to execution of the warrant. Similar questions regarding the Fourth Amendment and the Speech or Debate Clause were raised in September 2026 in an interim staff report detailing the Department of Justice’s (DOJ’s) access to Member phone records during Special Counsel Jack Smtih’s investigation of the events of January 6, 2021. 
This Legal Sidebar discusses the intersection of the Fourth Amendment’s prohibition on unreasonable searches and seizures, the search warrant requirement under that Amendment, and the sometimes-countervailing protections afforded by the Speech or Debate Clause.
Fourth Amendment Background
The Fourth Amendment prohibits unreasonable searches and seizures. As a result, law enforcement generally must obtain a search warrant from a “neutral and detached magistrate” before entering a private space to look for evidence. The Amendment states that “no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.” The Supreme Court has characterized the probable-cause standard as “the kind of fair probability’ on which reasonable and prudent’” people act. 
To obtain a search warrant, law enforcement must establish probable cause that the materials sought are contraband or evidence that will “aid in a particular apprehension or conviction,” or otherwise “seizable by virtue of being connected with criminal activity.” Law enforcement must also demonstrate “a fair probability” that these materials “will be found in a particular place.” (This requirement may include a place occupied by a person not “implicated in the crime.”) The Supreme Court has held that the privacy interest protected by the Fourth Amendment is strongest in people’s homes.
Where a proposed search may implicate certain constitutional, statutory, or common-law privileges, such as the attorney-client privilege, courts sometimes impose search protocols that law enforcement must follow to preempt potential law enforcement access to privileged material. These processes can involve preliminary review by a “filter team”—meaning a group of law enforcement agents and prosecutors who are separate from the prosecution team and agree not to disclose any privileged information to the prosecution team. In other situations, where materials might be especially sensitive or otherwise subject to heightened concern, a judge or a special master can review the government’s privilege determinations or conduct a filter review in the first instance.
DOJ policy requires certain procedural steps to be taken before law enforcement may execute a search warrant in which a Member of Congress is involved. These steps include consultation with the Department’s Public Integrity Section and the filing of an “Urgent Report” to Department leadership. 
Speech or Debate Background
The Speech or Debate Clause ensures that, “for any Speech or Debate in either House,” Members of Congress “shall not be questioned in any other Place.” The Clause is a key pillar in the separation of powers and serves chiefly to protect the independence, integrity, and effectiveness of the legislative branch by barring executive or judicial intrusions into the protected legislative sphere. Despite its text, courts have found the protections afforded by the Clause extend well beyond “speeches” or “debates,” instead providing Members with a series of privileges and immunities in both civil and criminal contexts that are meant to shield Members from a “hostile judiciary” or “intimidation by the executive.” The Clause does not, however, turn Members into “super-citizens” by providing them with a blanket exemption from legal liability for all illegal acts. Rather, the Clause shelters only a certain class of actions, known as “legislative acts,” which the Court has defined as conduct that is an “integral part of the deliberative and communicative processes” through which Congress implements “matters which the Constitution places within the jurisdiction of either House.” 
The Clause’s protections are implemented in a variety of ways. First and foremost, the Clause provides Members with absolute immunity from civil or criminal liability for all “legislative acts” taken in the course of their official responsibilities. Second, even where absolute immunity is not applicable, the Clause provides Members with complementary evidentiary and testimonial privileges. The evidentiary component prohibits evidence of legislative acts from being introduced in court for use against a Member, while the testimonial component of the Clause generally may be invoked when a Member is questioned about his legislative acts, either in a trial, before a grand jury, or in a deposition. As a result of the breadth of these protections, criminal prosecution of a Member can be complicated, but this impact on executive enforcement of the law was fully understood at the time the Clause was adopted and was considered a necessary consequence of protecting legislators from undue influence or intimidation.
Most relevant for this Sidebar, courts have divided over whether to extend the Clause further to prohibit not only the use of legislative act material at trial, but also the mere disclosure of that material to the executive branch—for example, during an administrative or criminal investigation. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia (D.C. Circuit), the federal circuit court with jurisdiction over the District of Columbia, has held that the Clause includes a “non-disclosure privilege,” which can prohibit the disclosure of protected legislative act documents pursuant to a subpoena or during a search executed as part of a criminal investigation. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit have rejected this “non-disclosure privilege,” considering it an undue expansion of the Clause. Instead, these courts have held, at least in criminal cases, that the Clause prohibits only the evidentiary use of privileged documents, not disclosure to the government for review as part of an investigation. The disagreement has not been addressed by the Supreme Court.
Intersection of the Fourth Amendment and the Speech or Debate Clause 
Various courts have addressed how the Fourth Amendment and the Speech or Debate Clause interact. These cases suggest that whether a search violates the Speech or Debate clause may depend on (1) whether the circuit at issue recognizes a non-disclosure privilege; (2) a fact-specific inquiry as to whether the location of the search is realistically likely to contain legislative materials; and (3) whether a reviewing court views filter team procedures as adequately protective of the privilege.
In United States v. Rayburn House Office Building, the D.C. Circuit held that a Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) search of Rep. William Jefferson’s office pursuant to a warrant obtained from a federal judge violated the Clause because the manner in which the search was carried out “denied the Congressman any opportunity to identify and assert the privilege with respect to legislative materials before their compelled disclosure to Executive agents” (emphasis added). The FBI had adopted special procedures for the search (approved by the judge who had issued the warrant), which required that the agents who searched the office have no other role in the investigation. All hard drives in the office were copied, and these copies along with any collected documents were then turned over to a separate filter team, which was required to assess the material as follows: 
Materials determined to be privileged or not responsive would be returned without dissemination to the prosecution team. Materials determined by the filter team not to be privileged would be turned over to the prosecution team, with copies to the Congressman’s attorney within ten business days of the search. Materials determined by the filter team to be potentially privileged would, absent the Congressman’s consent to Executive use of a potentially privileged document, be submitted to the district court for review, with a log and copy of such documents provided to the Congressman’s attorney within 20 business days of the search.
These precautions, the court held, were inadequate under the Clause because they “called for review by FBI agents and the several members of the Justice Department filter team before the Congressman would be afforded an opportunity to identify potentially privileged materials.” Any physical act of searching the office, the court reasoned, would inevitably expose the agents to protected legislative materials in violation of the non-disclosure privilege. For that same reason, however, the court held that the copying of hard drives did not violate the Clause, since no executive branch agents had yet viewed the electronic material. The opinion did not articulate a permissible procedure to be applied when the executive branch obtains a warrant to search a Member’s office, but the court did suggest that an accommodation could be reached whereby the office is “seal[ed]” and the Member is “afforded an opportunity to identify potentially privileged legislative materials prior to any review by Executive agents.” Regardless, the D.C. Circuit held that the Member must have the opportunity to assert the protections of the Speech or Debate Clause prior to executive agents conducting any search of the office.
The majority opinion in Rayburn did not directly address whether its holding would extend beyond Members’ offices to cover searches of other areas or devices. There was, however, language in the opinion that could suggest that the principles established in Rayburn may appropriately be applied when searches “occur[] in a location where legislative materials [are] inevitably to be found.” Moreover, a circuit judge who concurred in the judgment but not in majority’s reasoning was critical of the breadth of the majority’s non-disclosure privilege, expressing concern that criminal investigations would be hampered by the need to provide a Member with advance notice “of any search of his property, including property outside of his congressional office, such as his home or car, and further that he be allowed to remove any material he deemed to be covered by the legislative privilege prior to a search.”
In 2023, the D.C. Circuit considered the application of the Speech or Debate Clause to an FBI search of Representative Scott Perry’s cell phone pursuant to a search warrant. In that case, the FBI obtained a warrant to seize and create a forensic digital image of the phone, and then another warrant to review the contents of that copy. Pursuant to Rayburn, the second warrant provided that Representative Perry “would have an opportunity to assert any claims of privilege under the Speech or Debate Clause before the government could review the phone’s content.” In considering Representative Perry’s claims of privilege, the court rejected the government’s threshold argument that Rayburn should be limited to Members’ physical offices and consequently that the cell phone was not privileged at all. The court wrote that “Rayburn, however, explained that the privilege applies whenever the Executive Branch searches a location where legislative materials [a]re inevitably to be found,’” and that a Member’s cell phone “is realistically such a location.” 
By contrast, in a criminal case against Representative Christopher Collins, a judge in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York (which is located within the jurisdiction of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit) found that certain device and account data obtained by the government pursuant to search warrants was not subject to the Speech or Debate privilege because, as a threshold matter, the Clause did not include a non-disclosure privilege. Further, “in stark contrast” to the Rayburn case, the court found that “the searches did not involve congressional offices or official accounts but were of the personal electronic devices and accounts of certain current and/or former staff members of Defendant Collins.” Finally, the court wrote that “even if the protections provided by the Speech or Debate Clause includes a non-disclosure privilege, the procedures undertaken by the Government to identify and segregate any protected materials without involving the prosecution team were sufficient under the facts and circumstances presented here.” The government had used a filter team to ensure that “any materials that were arguably legislative materials potentially protected by the Speech or Debate Clause were not reviewed by or made available to the prosecution team.”
A recently reported search of a Member’s home occurred in the District of Columbia. As such, under the controlling precedent of Rayburn, a court might look to whether the search is of a place “where legislative materials [a]re inevitably to be found.” If so, a court might find that the non-disclosure privilege applies and might require the Member to be given the opportunity to assert the protections of the Clause prior to the disclosure of any privileged materials to executive branch agents. Whether a Member’s home—or a personal office within a home—would be subject to the same protections as a Member’s office appears to be an open question. In appealing Rayburn to the Supreme Court (an appeal that was denied), the Solicitor General warned that the Rayburn rule “threaten[ed] to impede searches of Members’ homes, vehicles, or briefcases.” “Within the District of Columbia,” the Solicitor General stated, “the United States will no longer search for documents in an office of a Member located in his home because of concerns that such a search could (under the court of appeals’ decision) taint an investigation.” 
One reason why the Rayburn court seemed willing to create procedural guardrails for the executive branch was that the “historical record” was “utterly devoid” of searches of a Member’s office—the search at issue in Rayburn was the “first time a sitting Member’s congressional office [had] been searched by the Executive.” Executive searches of a Member’s home, though also rare, have reportedly occurred on several occasions. For example, the FBI had searched Representative Jefferson’s home and found $90,000 in cash in his freezer before executing a search of his office. While Representative Jefferson filed a motion to suppress evidence from the search of his home, the motion does not appear to have raised the Speech or Debate privilege.
With respect to the seizure of electronic devices, under the D.C. Circuit’s opinion regarding Representative Perry’s cell phone, any search or seizure of a Representative’s electronic devices in the District of Columbia—at least if the device is used for official purposes—would likely require the Representative to be given an opportunity to shield legislative materials from disclosure. The D.C. Circuit’s non-disclosure rule may be applicable not only to the search of a Member’s phone, but also to law enforcement acquisition of remotely held toll records indicating calls made and received by Member phones. At least one other court has reasoned that toll records can “fall within the protection of the Speech or Debate Clause,” and the House Judiciary Committee majority interim staff report on the Jack Smith investigation concluded that non-disclosure orders that barred notification to Members that their records were being disclosed “violated controlling D.C. Circuit precedent stating that a Member must be allowed the opportunity to assert the [Speech or Debate] privilege before the Executive scour[s] his records.’”
Considerations for Congress
Congress has options for protecting potentially privileged material from executive branch search and seizure and has on multiple instances legislated with respect to executive search and seizure authority. Among Congress’s options, should it seek to enhance protections for potentially privileged materials, is to impose procedural requirements on the execution of search warrants. Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41 governs processes for federal search warrants. Congress could choose to impose requirements in that rule to govern the execution of warrants in special circumstances, like requiring filter teams or other safeguards in cases where the search might expose privileged legislative materials. For example, Congress could codify the procedure endorsed in Rayburn, requiring that a Member of Congress have an opportunity to review materials being searched prior to law enforcement access to that material. 
In another example, following revelations of law enforcement access to Senate toll records during the Jack Smith special counsel investigation, Congress amended 2 U.S.C. § 6628 in 2025 to require that the Senate Sergeant at Arms (SAA) or any third-party provider of an “electronic communication service” or “remote computing service” for a Senate office notify the “Senate office,” whenever the SSA or provider receives a subpoena or other “legal process” for covered Senate data, with certain exceptions when the Senator is a target of the criminal investigation. The law does not define “legal process,” but that phrase generally can refer to a variety of processes, including search warrants.
Alternatively, Congress may opt to leave the matter to the courts, including waiting to see whether the Supreme Court takes up the non-disclosure privilege in light of the current circuit split.

The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) has implemented a number of measures during the second Trump Administration to promote economic deregulation of the airline industry. For example, in November 2025, DOT withdrew an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on airline passenger rights initiated during the Biden Administration, which would have required airlines to provide cash compensation, meals, lodging, and other amenities to airline consumers experiencing significant flight disruptions. In July 2026, DOT issued a notice of proposed rulemaking to amend the agency’s existing rule on air fare advertising to provide “greater flexibility for regulated entities in how air fare is displayed.” 
DOT’s recent deregulatory actions have drawn attention to the respective roles of the federal government and state governments in policing airline business practices. When Congress enacted the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 (ADA), it included an express preemption provision “[t]o ensure that the States would not undo federal deregulation with regulation of their own.” That provision, as amended, preempts state laws “related to” an airline’s “price, route, or service.” Under Supreme Court precedent, the ADA’s preemption provision applies broadly and can preempt even generally applicable state laws that indirectly affect airline prices, routes, or services. This Legal Sidebar provides background on the ADA and its preemption provision, examines the provision’s scope, and discusses considerations for Congress.   
Background 
Prior to Congress enacting the ADA in 1978, federal law subjected the airline industry to a “system of detailed economic regulation” in which airlines “operate[d] like a public utility.” Under the Federal Aviation Act of 1958, the now-abolished Civil Aeronautics Board “closely regulated” air carrier prices, routes, and services. In enacting the ADA, Congress sought to “plac[e] maximum reliance on competitive market forces” and encourage “an air transportation system relying on actual and potential competition ... to provide efficiency, innovation, and low prices.” While the ADA scaled back federal control over airlines’ business practices, DOT still enforces economic regulations governing the airline industry, and DOT has statutory authority to prohibit airlines from engaging in unfair or deceptive practices and unfair methods of competition. 
Scope of the ADA’s Preemption Provision
The Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution (Article VI, clause 2) provides the basis for the doctrine of federal preemption, under which “state laws that interfere with, or are contrary to,’ federal law” are superseded. Federal law can preempt state law in multiple ways. Federal law may impliedly preempt state law, but Congress also may enact legislation with language expressly preempting state law, as it did in the ADA. The ADA’s preemption provision is codified as amended at 49 U.S.C. § 41713(b)(1) and provides as follows:
[A] State, political subdivision of a State, or political authority of at least 2 States may not enact or enforce a law, regulation, or other provision having the force and effect of law related to a price, route, or service of an air carrier that may provide air transportation under this subpart.
The Supreme Court has emphasized that, regardless of the type of preemption at issue, Congress’s intent is the “ultimate touchstone” of a statute’s preemptive effect. In evaluating Congress’s preemptive intent, courts look primarily to the statutory text itself. 
The Court has interpreted the ADA’s “related to” language as having an “expansive” scope. The Court has held that state laws are “related to” airline prices, routes, or services where the laws have either a “reference to” or “connection with” the prices, routes, or services. The ADA’s preemption provision thus not only preempts state laws directly regulating airline prices, routes, or services, but also can preempt generally applicable state laws that have only an indirect effect on airlines, including common-law rules that states have not enacted in a statute. 
While the Supreme Court has recognized that the phrase “related to” in the ADA “express[es] a broad pre-emptive purpose,” the Court has also emphasized limits on the phrase’s preemptive scope when used in the ADA and other federal statutes. The Court has cautioned against strictly literal interpretations of “related to” preemption provisions. Rather than reading “related to” language “to the furthest stretch of its indeterminacy,” the Court has looked to Congress’s statutory objectives as a guide to the scope of preemption under such provisions. The Court has thus explained that preemption under the ADA “occurs at least where state laws have a significant impact’ related to Congress’ deregulatory and pre-emption-related objectives,” and that some state laws may affect airline prices, routes, or services “in too tenuous, remote, or peripheral a manner” to give rise to preemption.
Determining whether the ADA preempts a particular state law can involve difficult interpretive questions and require fact-intensive, case-by-case analysis. In addition to questions over the scope of the ADA’s “related to” language, the preemption provision’s use of the term “services” has posed interpretive challenges for courts, and federal courts of appeals have split over the meaning of the term. Most federal courts of appeals that have interpreted the meaning of “service” in the ADA have concluded that the term encompasses not only the provision of transportation, but also other features or amenities that passengers bargain for or anticipate as part of their transaction with the airline, such as boarding procedures, provision of food and drink, and baggage handling. In contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (Ninth Circuit) has adopted a narrower definition of “service.” According to the Ninth Circuit, “the word service’ in ... the ADA’s preemption clause ... refer[s] to the prices, schedules, origins and destinations of the point-to-point transportation of passengers, cargo, or mail ... [and] was not intended to include an airline’s provision of in-flight beverages, personal assistance to passengers, the handling of luggage, and similar amenities.” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit (Third Circuit) has favorably described the Ninth Circuit’s narrower interpretation, but lower courts debate whether the Third Circuit has adopted the Ninth Circuit’s interpretation. 
Application of the ADA’s Preemption Provision to Different Categories of State Laws 
Below are selected examples of how courts have applied the ADA’s preemption provision in certain state law contexts. The examples include each of the Supreme Court’s decisions to date applying the ADA’s preemption provision (Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc.; American Airlines, Inc. v. Wolens; and Northwest, Inc. v. Ginsberg), as well as selected decisions of federal courts of appeals. Additionally, the Supreme Court has provided relevant guidance on the ADA’s preemption provision in cases interpreting a similarly worded provision governing motor carriers in the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA). The examples include one of the Court’s FAAAA preemption decisions. 
Consumer Protection Law
The Supreme Court has recognized that the ADA can broadly preempt the enforcement of state consumer protection laws against airlines. In Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc., the Court held that the ADA preempted states from “prohibiting allegedly deceptive airline fare advertisements through enforcement of their general consumer protection statutes.” A group of airlines had sued state attorneys general to block them from enforcing guidelines that purported to “explain in detail how existing state laws apply to air fare advertising and frequent flyer programs.” In the majority opinion authored by Justice Scalia, the Court rejected the argument that the ADA only preempts states from “actually prescribing” airline prices, routes, or services, and imposes “no constraints on laws of general applicability” that do not target the airline industry. In the Court’s view, the state restrictions on airline fare advertisements had a “forbidden significant effect upon fares” because the restrictions would significantly limit the airlines’ “ability to market their product,” and thus, as a matter of economics, would have a “significant impact upon the fares they charge.” 
Three dissenting Justices in Morales objected to the Court’s broad interpretation of the ADA’s preemption provision. Focusing on the ADA’s legislative history, the dissent concluded that Congress intended to preempt state laws that relate “directly” to airline prices, routes, or services, but not generally applicable advertising laws that only “indirectly” relate to airline prices.
The Supreme Court also addressed the ADA’s preemption of a consumer protection law in American Airlines, Inc. v. Wolens. In Wolens, members of an American Airlines’ frequent-flyer program had sued American because its retroactive changes to the program’s terms allegedly violated an Illinois consumer fraud statute and constituted a breach of contract. In a majority opinion authored by Justice Ginsberg, the Court held that the ADA preempted the consumer fraud claims, but not (as discussed below) the contract claims. The Court explained that the consumer fraud law did not “simply give effect to bargains offered by the airlines and accepted by airline customers,” but instead “serve[d] as a means to guide and police the marketing practices of the airlines.” In the Court’s view, the state consumer fraud law demonstrated the “potential for intrusive regulation of airline business practices inherent in state consumer protection legislation.” Justice Stevens dissented with respect to preemption of the consumer fraud claim and argued that the ADA does not preempt generally applicable laws.
Contract Law
In the Wolens case described above, the Supreme Court also held that the ADA did not preempt the plaintiffs’ state-law breach of contract claims alleging that the airline violated the terms of its agreement with passengers. The Court reasoned that the terms and conditions the airline offered to passengers were “privately ordered obligations and thus d[id] not amount to a State’s “enact[ment] or enforce[ment] [of] any law, ... regulation, ... or other provision having the force and effect of law” within the meaning of [the preemption provision].’” The Court explained that, although “the ADA’s preemption prescription bars state-imposed regulation of air carriers,” it does not protect airlines from lawsuits “seeking recovery solely for the airline’s alleged breach of its own, self-imposed undertakings.” In a dissenting opinion joined by Justice Thomas, Justice O’Connor argued that the ADA preempts state contract law “where the terms of a private contract relate to airline rates and services, and those terms can only be enforced through state law.”
The Supreme Court addressed preemption of state contract laws again in Northwest, Inc. v. Ginsberg, where the Court unanimously held that the ADA preempts state common-law contract claims that seek to “enlarge the contractual obligations that the parties voluntarily adopt[ed].” The plaintiff’s lawsuit against Northwest had alleged, among other things, that the airline breached an implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing under Minnesota contract law by revoking his frequent flyer membership “in a way that contravened his reasonable expectations.” In support of its conclusion that the implied-covenant claim sought to enforce a state-imposed obligation, the Court noted that Minnesota law did not permit contracting parties to agree not to be bound by the implied covenant, and that Minnesota law excluded certain types of contract claims from the implied covenant for policy reasons. 
Employment Law
A number of federal appellate courts have concluded that generally applicable state employment laws are often too tenuously connected to airline prices, routes, and services to fall within the ADA’s preemption provision. Examples of state employment laws that some courts have held not preempted under the ADA include racial discrimination laws, wage laws, meal and rest break laws, and whistleblower laws. 
Courts have, however, held in some circumstances that the ADA preempted a generally applicable employment law. For instance, in DiFiore v. American Airlines, Inc., the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit held that the ADA preempted a Massachusetts law regulating tips for service employees. The tips law prohibited employers from taking fees “that a patron or other consumer would reasonably expect to be given to a ... service employee ... in lieu of, or in addition to, a tip.” American Airlines charged passengers a $2 fee for each bag checked with the skycaps at Boston’s Logan Airport, and the skycaps brought a lawsuit alleging that the fee violated the tips law. 
In concluding that the ADA preempted the tips law, the court reasoned that preemption under the ADA distinguishes between laws that regulate “merely how the airline behaves as an employer or proprietor,” and laws that regulate “how an airline service is performed and how its price is displayed to customers.” In the court’s view, because complying with the tips law would require the airline to change the way it provided curbside check-in service or how it advertised the price for that service, the law did not “simply regulate the employment relationship between the skycaps and the airline.” 
Public Health Law
The FAAAA’s preemption provision for motor carriers of property provides that no state may enact or enforce laws “related to a price, route, or service of any motor carrier ... with respect to the transportation of property.” In Rowe v. New Hampshire Motor Transport Association, the Supreme Court applied its ADA preemption precedents in holding that a Maine law regulating the delivery of tobacco products to customers impermissibly “related to” a motor carrier’s “service” and was therefore preempted under the FAAAA. The challenged law required, among other things, that tobacco retailers use only delivery services that provided a specified age-verification service. 
In concluding that the FAAAA preempted the state law, the Court rejected Maine’s primary argument that state public health laws are categorically outside the scope of the preemption provision. The Court concluded that Maine’s law would have a “significant’ and adverse impact’” on the FAAAA’s “pre-emption-related objectives” because the law would substitute the state’s “own governmental commands for competitive market forces’ in determining (to a significant degree) the services that motor carriers will provide.” The Court also emphasized that if each state were permitted to require carriers to provide a special recipient-verification service, the “state regulatory patchwork” that could ensue would be “inconsistent with Congress’ major legislative effort to leave such decisions, where federally unregulated, to the competitive marketplace.”
Considerations for Congress
In recent years, some advocacy groups and state officials have proposed amending the ADA’s preemption provision to give states a larger role in policing airlines, particularly with respect to consumer protection issues. In 2022, for instance, the National Association of Attorneys General sent a letter to Congress arguing that DOT does not adequately protect airline consumers and that Congress should enact legislation authorizing states to enforce state and federal consumer protection laws against airlines. 
In contrast, Congress has also considered proposals to amend the ADA’s preemption provision to explicitly preempt state laws related to additional subjects beyond airline prices, routes, and services. For instance, a withdrawn amendment to the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 would have amended the preemption provision to explicitly preempt state laws related to “the pay or scheduling of the flight crew of an air carrier.” An airline industry group advocating for broad preemption under the ADA has argued that “[p]reemption of patchwork state regulation has helped create a cost-effective and efficient transportation network throughout the United States.” 
Congress may choose to monitor how courts apply the ADA’s preemption provision and evaluate whether the scope of state laws preempted under the ADA aligns with Congress’s determination of the appropriate balance of federal and state authority over regulating airline business practices. Congress could amend the ADA’s preemption provision to narrow, expand, or otherwise clarify its scope.

api_metadata.summary:
The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) is a statute that authorizes grant programs that support special education and early intervention services for children with disabilities. Under IDEA, a series of conditions are attached to the receipt of grant funds. These conditions aim to provide certain educational and procedural guarantees for children with disabilities and their families. 
Part B of IDEA contains two sections—Part B, Section 611 contains provisions relating to special education for school-aged children with disabilities (ages 3-21) and Part B, Section 619 addresses the supplemental state grants program for preschool children with disabilities (ages 3-5). The grant programs authorized under Part B of IDEA provide federal funding to states and local educational agencies (LEAs) for the provision of special education and related services to children with disabilities. IDEA requires, as a condition for the receipt of such funds, the provision of a free appropriate public education (FAPE; i.e., specially designed instruction, provided at no cost to parents, that meets the needs of a child with a disability). IDEA, Part B also outlines and requires the use of procedural safeguards pertaining to the identification, evaluation, and placement of students in special education services that are intended to protect the rights of parents and children with disabilities. These procedures include parental rights to resolve disputes through a mediation process, and to present and resolve complaints through a due process complaint procedure and through state complaint procedures.
More than 8 million children with disabilities ages 3-21 receive educational services under Part B of IDEA according to U.S. Department of Education (ED) estimates. To be covered under IDEA, a child with a disability must meet the categorical definition of disability in the act, and the child must require special education and related services as a result of the disability in order to benefit from public education. Once a child meets IDEA’s eligibility criteria, FAPE is implemented through the Individualized Education Program (IEP), which is the plan for providing special education and related services by the LEA. The IEP is developed by an IEP team composed of school personnel and the child’s parents or guardian. IDEA requires that children with disabilities be educated in the least restrictive environment. That is, to the maximum extent appropriate they are to be educated with children who are not disabled. According to the most recent data from ED, approximately 68% of all school-aged children with disabilities who were served by IDEA, Part B spent 80% or more of their time in a regular classroom.
To implement IDEA, states and other entities (i.e., the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Bureau of Indian Education, the outlying areas, and the freely associated states) receive grants based on a statutory formula. In FY2026, appropriations for IDEA (including supplemental funding) were $15.6 billion, with approximately 95% of the funding going to Part B. Most of the federal funds received by states are passed on to LEAs based on a statutory formula. IDEA also contains fiscal requirements aimed at increasing overall special education spending of states and LEAs, rather than substituting federal funds for special education spending at the state and local levels.
Originally enacted in 1975, IDEA has been the subject of numerous reauthorizations to extend services and rights to children with disabilities. The most recent reauthorization of IDEA was P.L. 108-446, enacted in 2004. Funding for Part B, Assistance for Education of all Children with Disabilities, the largest and most often discussed part of the act, is permanently authorized. Funding for Part C, Infants and Toddlers with Disabilities, and Part D, National Activities, was authorized through FY2011. Funding for these programs continues to be provided through annual appropriations acts.

api_metadata.summary:
Policy debate over the role of nuclear power in the nation’s energy mix is rooted in the technology’s fundamental characteristics. Nuclear reactors can produce potentially vast amounts of useful energy with relatively low consumption of natural resources and low emissions of greenhouse gases and other pollutants. However, facilities that produce nuclear fuel for civilian power reactors can also produce materials for nuclear weapons. In addition, the process of nuclear fission (splitting of atomic nuclei) to generate power produces radioactive material that can remain hazardous for thousands of years and must be contained. How to manage the weapons proliferation and safety risks of nuclear power, or whether the benefits of nuclear power are worth those risks, are issues that have long been debated in Congress. Numerous bills in recent Congresses have focused on nuclear energy as a low-carbon source of electricity and on the potential for advanced reactor designs to reduce costs and increase safety margins.
The 94 licensed nuclear power reactors at 54 sites in the United States generate about 20% of the nation’s electricity. About a dozen new reactors of various designs are planned or proposed. Whether they eventually move forward will likely depend largely on their economic competitiveness with natural gas and renewable energy sources, as well as overall growth in electricity demand. Similar economic forces affect existing reactors. Thirteen U.S. reactors were permanently closed during the period from February 2013 through April 2022. However, several states have taken action to prevent reactor shutdowns, and Congress has enacted federal tax credits and other support for existing reactors. Owners of three of the recently closed reactors are planning to restart them within the next four years. President Trump issued Executive Order 14302 on May 23, 2025, to have 10 new large conventional reactors under construction in the United States by 2030.
The Department of Energy (DOE) and its predecessor agencies for decades have conducted research on “advanced” reactor technologies, such as fast neutron reactors, that would differ significantly from existing commercial nuclear plants and potentially be far smaller. Proponents of advanced reactors contend that they would be safer, more efficient, and less expensive to build and operate than today’s U.S. conventional light water reactors (cooled by ordinary water). Skeptics raise concerns regarding weapons-proliferation risks and cast doubt on advanced reactors’ affordability and sustainability. DOE is providing support for several proposed advanced reactor demonstrations, which could indicate whether the anticipated benefits can be realized. Legislation supporting U.S. production of nuclear fuel was enacted by Congress on December 14, 2023, in the National Defense Authorization Act for FY2024 (P.L. 118-31, §3131). The Accelerating Deployment of Versatile, Advanced Nuclear for Clean Energy (ADVANCE) Act of 2024, signed into law July 9, 2024, as Division B of P.L. 118-67, called for greater efficiency in nuclear plant licensing and regulation by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). In response to the ADVANCE Act and four executive orders signed by President Donald Trump on May 23, 2025, including Executive Order 14302, NRC issued new regulations and proposed rules for licensing advanced reactors. Advanced reactor bills in the 119th Congress include proposals for providing cost-overrun support (S. 3814), building demonstration reactors (H.R. 6805), and encouraging spent fuel reprocessing (S. 3016). 
Highly radioactive spent nuclear fuel that is regularly removed from nuclear reactors is currently stored primarily at power plant sites. Development of a permanent underground repository at Yucca Mountain in Nevada was suspended by the Obama Administration, and no funds for the project have been appropriated since. The Obama Administration appointed the Blue Ribbon Commission on America’s Nuclear Future to recommend an alternative approach to the Nuclear Waste Policy Act’s focus on Yucca Mountain for permanent high-level waste disposal. The Commission’s recommendations included selecting nuclear waste storage and disposal facilities through a consent-based process. On January 28, 2026, DOE invited states to host Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses, which could include spent fuel storage and disposal sites. In the meantime, Yucca Mountain remains the sole authorized candidate site for permanent disposal, despite its lack of funding. Nuclear waste bills in the 119th Congress include proposals to require state and local government consent for siting a nuclear waste repository (H.R. 466, S. 101).
Encouraging exports of U.S. civilian nuclear products, services, and technology while making sure they are not used for foreign nuclear weapons programs has long been a fundamental goal of U.S. nuclear energy policy. Recent proposals to build reactors in several countries without nuclear power, including the Middle East, have prompted concerns about the effectiveness of international nonproliferation controls. The ADVANCE Act includes provisions to encourage nuclear-energy-related exports. In the 119th Congress, H.R. 1474 would require U.S. officials at multilateral development banks to advocate for removal of restrictions on nuclear energy assistance.

Administered by the U.S. Department of Education (ED), the Impact Aid program is one of the oldest federal education programs, dating from 1950. Impact Aid, authorized under Title VII of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA, P.L. 89-10, as amended), compensates local educational agencies (LEAs) for the financial burden resulting from certain federal activities carried out in their areas. These activities include federal ownership of certain lands, as well as the enrollments in LEAs of children of parents who work or live on federal land (e.g., children of parents in the uniformed services and children living on Indian lands). The federal government provides compensation because these activities deprive LEAs of the ability to collect property or other taxes from these individuals (e.g., members of the uniformed services living on military bases) or their employers, even though the LEAs are obligated to provide free public education to their children. Impact Aid also provides support for certain students with disabilities and for school construction. 
The largest Impact Aid component, Section 7003(b) payments (also known as Basic Support Payments), compensates LEAs for enrolling “federally connected” children. For FY2026, Section 7003(b) accounted for $1.477 billion, 90.6% of all funds appropriated for the Impact Aid program. As Section 7003(b) payments account for the majority of all Impact Aid funding, this report primarily focuses on these payments. 
All Impact Aid payments are funded through the Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies (L-HHS-ED) annual appropriations act. Funds are provided through “budget year appropriations,” meaning the funds would be available for the budget year beginning on the first day of the fiscal year (e.g., October 1, 2025, for the FY2026 L-HHS-ED appropriations act), unless otherwise specified. This availability generally is retroactive to October 1 if annual appropriations are enacted after the fiscal year has begun. The Impact Aid program is also authorized to receive appropriations through advance appropriations and forward funding. In current practice, advance appropriations become available one fiscal year after the budget year covered by a given appropriations act (e.g., appropriations provided for FY2027 in an FY2026 appropriations act). Forward funding becomes available during the last quarter of the budget year (e.g., starting July 1, 2026, for the FY2026 appropriations act) but remains available through at least the following fiscal year (e.g., available from July 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027). 
Without advance appropriations or forward funding, when full-year appropriations are not provided prior to the beginning of the budget year, LEAs are generally unable to receive their full Section 7003(b) payments until sometime after October 1. This can create financial difficulties for LEAs, particularly those that are heavily dependent on Impact Aid funding. Providing funds for Section 7003(b) payments through advance appropriations or forward funding has the potential to ease some of these difficulties, but either change has budget enforcement implications that may complicate any attempt to transition to an alternative funding schedule.
This report considers three different appropriations scenarios for Impact Aid Section 7003(b) payments that are an alternative to budget year appropriations: (1) providing forward funding for Section 7003(b) payments, (2) providing advance appropriations for Section 7003(b) payments, or (3) using both forward funding and advance appropriations to provide Section 7003(b) payments, as is done for other federal education programs such as Title I-A Grants to Local Educational Agencies authorized by the ESEA or Grants to States authorized under Part B of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). Each of these scenarios has budget implications that may require at least a one-time increase in discretionary appropriations, a change in the limit set on advance appropriations (if applicable), or some combination of both.

States, territories, and the District of Columbia (DC) administer federal elections. Each of these jurisdictions has its own process for counting votes and declaring election winners, though all follow similar steps. These processes have drawn renewed congressional and public attention during recent election cycles.
The results that voters see reported on election night are the culmination of several steps in the election administration process, but are not the end of that process. Finalizing federal election results typically occurs days or weeks after election day. Among other steps, state, territorial, and local election officials canvass votes to ensure that ballots are valid and counted correctly. Election observers, audits, and other measures are designed to help ensure transparency and accuracy.
This updated report addresses frequently asked questions on these and related subjects. The discussion emphasizes the period between the time a voter casts a ballot and when states, territories, and DC finalize or certify the results.

api_metadata.summary:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is authorized by statute to perform various duties and functions that are related to human resources management and personnel policies for the federal government. The antecedent of OPM may be traced to the enactment of the Civil Service Act of 1883, known as the Pendleton Act, which statutorily established some underlying aspects of today’s federal personnel system. The act also established the Civil Service Commission (CSC), which was originally intended to insulate the hiring and management of federal employees from partisan political influence. 
The CSC continued with much the same role until 1978, when Congress passed the Civil Service Reform Act and replaced the CSC with OPM. OPM currently identifies several areas central to its work that are referred to as “key functions,” including human capital management, administration of federal employee benefit programs, and the vetting of job candidates.
OPM’s funding is included in the annual Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Act. For FY2026, OPM’s operating budget—including discretionary appropriations, mandatory administrative authorities, revolving fund activities, advance and reimbursements, and Office of the Inspector General (OIG) discretionary appropriations—was $920,950,825, and the agency had 2,171.2 full-time-equivalent employees.
This report discusses OPM’s establishment, statutory authority, mission, key functions, organization, budget, and performance. In practice, OPM’s role in federal workforce management spans a spectrum, from functions in which it exercises substantial government-wide authority and oversight to those in which it establishes broad requirements and delegates more discretion to individual executive branch agencies. This report discusses three examples of workforce activities—hiring, performance, and reductions in force—where this balance between centralization within OPM and delegation to agencies can be analyzed. Finally, this report raises several issues for congressional consideration regarding OPM’s role in implementing federal workforce reforms, OPM’s capacity to deliver on its mission, and potential trade-offs associated with the varying degrees to which workforce management is centralized within OPM.

This report explains the current law concerning copyright protection for technical standards developed by private organizations and subsequently incorporated by reference into federal, state, or local law. It reviews the outcomes and reasoning of prominent case law on the issue from the federal courts and the potential effect of legislative proposals introduced in recent Congresses.
Technical standards—such as fire prevention and building codes—play an important role in protecting public health and safety, as well as ensuring compatibility and interoperability in particular industries. Federal policy generally encourages federal agencies to use privately developed, voluntary consensus standards, instead of “government-unique” standards. Private standards-developing organizations (SDOs) often create these standards by bringing together experts and stakeholders in particular areas and reaching consensus on effective technical solutions. SDOs may fund their activities by publishing and selling copies of their standards (e.g., an electrical code handbook) to people who use those standards (e.g., a property developer).
Privately developed standards are used by federal, state, and local governments in various ways. In particular, governments may incorporate such standards into law or regulation by reference. For example, a state or locality may adopt a privately developed electrical code, making that standard a legal requirement for the electrical design of a building in that jurisdiction. Other incorporated-by-reference (IBR) standards may serve as references or as guidance but do not formally impose legal obligations. 
SDOs may rely on copyright protection to fund their standards-development activities. Copyright grants authors of creative works (e.g., books) the exclusive right to copy and sell their work, among other things. As an original work of authorship, standards are generally entitled to copyright protection if they are created by a private entity. Copyright protection, when applicable, may allow SDOs to prevent third parties from making and distributing unauthorized copies of their standards. 
When technical standards are incorporated into law, maintaining copyright protection on them can raise constitutional and policy concerns about public access to the law. Under federal law, standards incorporated by reference into federal regulations must be made reasonably available to interested parties. State and local governments also often use IBR standards and may have differing policies for public access. Many SDOs choose to make their standards available in some form online, even if they assert copyright ownership over the IBR standards, while charging for printed copies or online versions with greater functionality than the free online versions. 
Some public-access organizations, as well as commercial entities, have disregarded SDOs’ copyright assertions and posted technical standards online, including making them available for download. These groups argue that IBR standards lose copyright protection once they are incorporated into law or that their activities are a permitted fair use of SDOs’ copyrighted material. Several copyright disputes brought by SDOs have led to protracted litigation in multiple forums. 
Despite decades of decisions, courts have not reached consensus on whether technical standards remain protected by copyright after they are incorporated into law. U.S. Courts of Appeals for different regional circuits reached seemingly conflicting conclusions on that question in the 1980s–2000s. Following the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit’s decision in American Society for Testing and Materials v. Public.Resource.Org (ASTM v. PRO I), 896 F.3d 437 (D.C. Cir. 2018), courts have increasingly focused on whether copyright’s fair use doctrine permits public-access groups or commercial entities to make IBR standards available online. After ASTM v. PRO I and the Supreme Court’s decision on a related issue in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020), recent cases have generally ruled against SDOs’ copyright infringement claims, mainly on fair use grounds, although the results have not been uniform.
The Pro Codes Act (H.R. 4072 in the 119th Congress) seeks to address this issue legislatively. The Pro Codes Act would explicitly provide that otherwise copyrightable IBR standards retain their copyright protection even after a government incorporates them into law. At the same time, the bill would require that SDOs make IBR standards publicly available online in a readable, accessible format at no monetary cost to users. The Pro Codes Act would not require SDOs to make IBR standards available for printing or download, and SDOs could require users to agree to terms and conditions before accessing the standards.

Tourism—both international and domestic—contributes millions of jobs and billions of dollars of spending to the national economy. In the past decade, the tourism industry has experienced a period with some disruptions. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic caused a sudden, dramatic decrease in tourism worldwide, including in and among the United States. By many measures, U.S. tourism spent the ensuing years rebounding from those losses. For example, international arrivals to the United States rose every year from 2020 through 2024. 
In 2025, international arrivals to the United States fell 5.5% from 2024. This made the United States one of two countries among those with the 10 most international arrivals to see a decline in international tourists from 2024 to 2025. In addition, U.S. domestic airline passengers declined 1.0% from 2024 to 2025. Possible developments factoring into these trends include increased immigration enforcement, travel restrictions, new fees on nonimmigrant visas, and reduced funding for tourism promotion entities.
In Congress, various committees and subcommittees, including those of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, and the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, have held hearings touching on different aspects of U.S. tourism in recent years, including rural tourism, the impact of daylight saving time on tourism, and pandemic recovery efforts relative to tourism. P.L. 119-21, the FY2025 reconciliation act, reduced the annual cap on federal funds provided to Brand USA—a public-private entity promoting international tourism to the United States—from $100 million to $20 million. Subsequent bills, including H.R. 6128 and S. 3220, would restore or increase Brand USA funding. Previous Congresses have also passed legislation related to U.S. tourism. For example, the 117th Congress passed the Visit America Act (Subtitle A, Title VI, Division BB of P.L. 117-103, the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022) which, among other things, authorized the creation of a new Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism within the Department of Commerce. 
Several considerations concerning tourism may be of interest to Congress. They include
The U.S. tourism outlook. As noted, both international arrivals to the United States and U.S. domestic airline passengers decreased in 2025 from 2024, making the United States an outlier among major tourism destinations. These developments come as the United States prepares to host the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles and 2034 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City. 
Tourism-related leadership positions. Although the Visit America Act established the position of the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism, to date, the position has not yet been filled. In addition, the U.S. Travel and Tourism Advisory Board (a Federal Advisory Committee Act body that provides recommendations related to tourism to the Secretary of Commerce) appears to not have met since October 2024—despite its charter calling for meetings twice annually.
Brand USA funding. As mentioned, legislation in the 119th Congress reduced the annual cap on Brand USA’s federal funds. In addition, Brand USA’s statutory funding structure—that allows it to access federal funding—is set to expire at the end of FY2027 unless Congress acts.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regulates wells used for underground injection of carbon dioxide, known as Class VI wells. The Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), administered by EPA, prohibits underground injection of fluids without a permit, including underground injection of carbon dioxide for geologic sequestration. Under SDWA, EPA is authorized to delegate primary enforcement authority, or primacy, for underground injection control (UIC) programs to individual states that meet minimum UIC program requirements. As the number of carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) projects using deep well injection has increased in the United States in recent years, Class VI permitting and state program primacy have been topics of interest to Congress.
EPA has established minimum permitting requirements for Class VI injection wells and for state UIC programs. Requirements are specified for well siting and construction, operation and maintenance, monitoring and testing, reporting and recordkeeping, site closure, financial responsibility, and post-injection site care. The minimum contents of a permit are established in regulation, but each Class VI permit is developed and approved based on the site-specific characteristics of the injection well project and is designed to address potential leakage or endangerment of underground sources of drinking water. 
Currently, there are at least 8 federal EPA-permitted Class VI projects with at least 13 permitted wells operating in 5 U.S. states. According to EPA, 142 Class VI permit applications are currently pending review by the agency. Additional permits are under review by states with delegated authority for state Class VI UIC programs.
Class VI permits are required to include information about the project and underground formations, demonstrate site suitability, and provide financial assurances. Permits must also include six required plans that provide detail on how the owner or operator will conduct injection well activities throughout the project lifecycle of the project. When reviewing permit applications, the permitting authority (either EPA or a state) typically conducts five stages of review: completion review, technical review, draft permit, public comment, and final permit. The technical review, which involves evaluation of information and plans in the application package, is the longest and most complex step in the permitting process. Once the permit is in place, the permitting authority is responsible for ensuring the permit requirements continue to be met.
EPA has approved UIC Class VI program primacy for six states: Arizona, Louisiana, North Dakota, Texas, West Virginia, and Wyoming. When granted primacy for a class of UIC wells, a state administers that UIC program through enforcement of state laws and regulations in lieu of EPA regulations. EPA retains oversight authority over all state UIC programs under federal law. EPA UIC regulations set out the specific requirements for state programs in permitting, compliance evaluation, enforcement, and information sharing. A state must demonstrate that it has the legal authorities and processes in place to administer the Class VI program. A memorandum of agreement between a state and EPA, which is submitted along with other required documents, typically serves as the foundation of a state’s specific responsibilities and commitments in administering the Class VI program.
Congress has appropriated funding in recent years to EPA for implementation of federal and state Class VI programs. On top of regular annual appropriations in several fiscal years for Class VI activities, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA; P.L. 117-58) provided $50 million in supplemental appropriations to EPA for grants to states that have or are working toward Class VI primacy and $25 million to EPA for Class VI program administration. As Congress continues to debate policy on Class VI well permitting and state primacy, several issues may arise regarding Class VI wells, including EPA appropriations, legislation, and EPA oversight. These issues may include 
the levels of EPA resources needed to process and oversee Class VI permits and state primacy applications;
state resources and capacity to administer UIC Class VI programs; 
whether EPA’s Class VI regulations should be amended; and 
whether Congress should address stakeholder concerns about public participation in the permit and primacy process, and concerns about the potential environmental and community impacts of carbon sequestration through Class VI wells.

api_metadata.summary:
The National Park Service (NPS) has a multibillion-dollar backlog of deferred maintenance—maintenance that was not performed as scheduled or as needed and was put off to a future time. NPS’s deferred maintenance, also known as deferred maintenance and repairs or the maintenance backlog, was estimated for FY2025 at $24.237 billion. Other federal land management agencies also have deferred maintenance, but NPS’s backlog is the largest and has drawn the most congressional attention. 
During the past decade (FY2016-FY2025), NPS deferred maintenance grew by $12.906 billion (+114%) in nominal dollars and $7.263 billion (+43%) in inflation-adjusted dollars. Many factors might contribute to the growth or reduction of deferred maintenance, including the aging of NPS assets, availability of funding for maintenance activities, acquisition of new assets, agency management of the backlog, completion of individual projects, changes in construction and related costs, and alterations in the methods used to estimate deferred maintenance. NPS reported that a 60% nominal-dollar increase in the backlog between FY2020 and FY2021 was due in part to changes in how the agency estimates deferred maintenance. NPS’s deferred maintenance is distributed unevenly among states and territories, with California, the District of Columbia, Arizona, and Wyoming having the largest amounts. The amounts also vary among individual park units. Among the various types of assets that NPS maintains, deferred maintenance is highest for the agency’s paved roads and buildings.
Sources of funding to address NPS deferred maintenance have included discretionary and mandatory appropriations, allocations from the Department of Transportation, park entrance and concessions fees, and donations, among others. Often it is not possible to determine the total amount of funding from these sources that NPS has allocated each year to address deferred maintenance, because NPS does not aggregate these amounts in its budget reporting. In 2020, the Great American Outdoors Act (GAOA; P.L. 116-152) provided a major new source of mandatory funding to address deferred maintenance of NPS and other federal land management agencies. The GAOA’s National Parks and Public Land Legacy Restoration Fund (LRF) received $1.9 billion annually for five years (FY2021-FY2025), with 70% of the funds—approximately $1.3 billion annually—going to NPS. In the 119th Congress, H.R. 9250 and S. 1547 would reauthorize deposits to the fund for FY2027-FY2031. For more information, see CRS Insight IN12729, Legacy Restoration Fund for Deferred Maintenance: 119th Congress Reauthorization Bills.
Congressional attention in the 118th and 119th Congresses has focused on NPS’s use of the LRF funding provided under the GAOA, including the agency’s project selection priorities, the funds’ impact in addressing the backlog, the reasons for changes in NPS’s deferred maintenance estimates, and proposals to reauthorize deposits to the LRF. Separately from the LRF, Congress also has debated the sufficiency of ongoing annual appropriations for NPS deferred maintenance, as well as appropriations for preventive maintenance that could keep assets from deteriorating to the point that deferred maintenance is accrued. Some in Congress also have expressed interest in potential actions to reduce the backlog without additional funding, such as through public-private partnerships or disposal of unneeded assets.

The demand for energy storage batteries has increased considerably from 2000 through 2024 because of increases in demand for electric vehicles (EVs), renewable energies, and a wide range of consumer goods. Energy storage batteries are manufactured devices that accept, store, and discharge electrical energy using chemical reactions within the device and that can be recharged to full capacity multiple times throughout their usable life. Although a wide range of chemistry types for such batteries are available, the lithium-ion battery became the most widely adopted across a wide range of end uses (e.g., EVs, power grid storage, computers, electric bicycles) during the 2010s and 2020s.
Congress has created a broad array of policy frameworks supportive of the domestic battery manufacturing industry. Such policies initially tended to be more focused on supporting downstream consumers of batteries, which in turn generated demand for batteries and indirectly supported the battery manufacturing industry. Over time, this policy framework shifted focus toward the battery manufacturing industry itself with legislation such as the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 (ARRA; P.L. 111-5). More recently, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021 (IIJA; P.L. 117-58) and P.L. 117-169 (the FY2022 reconciliation act) further expanded and specified this policy framework. P.L. 119-21 (the FY2025 reconciliation act) reduces the duration and scope of certain industrial policies affecting the battery industry.
Manufacturers in the People’s Republic of China (China) dominate the U.S. and global supply of lithium-ion batteries. China’s share of the global battery manufacturing supply chain is approximately 70%-90%. Imports of lithium-ion batteries and battery parts from China to the United States grew at accelerated rates into the 2020s. Manufacturers in China captured market share partly because of historically lower prices compared with global and U.S. competitors. Manufacturers located in China are able to maintain lower prices because of certain industrial practices or policies, which commonly occur there, such as vertical integration, economies of scale, trade protections, subsidies, and currency devaluation. Although lower-priced batteries may benefit battery consumers (e.g., EV manufacturers) in the short term, reliance on imports for these critical components may present supply chain diversification risks and long-term market vulnerabilities.
Investments in some aspects of the domestic battery manufacturing supply chain have occurred, and imbalances within the domestic supply chain may continue. The U.S. manufacturing industry for lithium-ion energy storage batteries has largely matured in some downstream processes, such as battery pack assembly. Domestic investment in further upstream activities, such as battery cell component manufacturing and active material manufacturing, has not kept pace with investment in further downstream processes. If domestic pack and cell assemblers, for example, continue to be reliant on imports for certain components and materials, then the energy independence and supply chain resilience issues may continue to be areas of concern for some Members of Congress.
Congress might consider a range of policy options that may impact the battery manufacturing industry, including (1) overseeing existing programs; (2) further adjusting the EV tax credit; (3) adjusting or eliminating the battery and critical mineral production subsidies; (4) introducing job training programs for advanced battery manufacturing; (5) assessing trade barriers; and (6) augmenting supply chain visibility tools. Some of these options were considered by the 119th Congress when it enacted P.L. 119-21.
If Congress were to consider taking further action related to the battery manufacturing industry, certain potential trade-offs or themes might emerge, including (1) tension between battery consumers (e.g., EVs, grid power, computers) and battery manufacturers; (2) conflict with trade agreements and trading partners; (3) market distortions when the government takes action in a market economy; (4) integration or disintegration between domestic supply chain participants; (5) impacts on federal expenditures; and (6) creation of market uncertainty.

api_metadata.summary:
The motion to recommit in the House of Representatives proposes to send legislation under consideration on the floor back to committee. A Member may move to recommit a measure prior to a vote on final passage of a bill, providing a late-stage opportunity for a vote in relation to the legislation. Priority in recognition to offer the motion is given to an opponent of the measure, and the motion is considered to be a minority party right.
The motion to recommit is one of the most common roll call votes taken on the House floor, as House rules guarantee the opportunity to offer the motion during initial consideration of a bill or joint resolution under the terms of a special rule. Specifically, the Committee on Rules cannot report a special rule that precludes the minority leader or a designee from moving to recommit the underlying legislation. 
Historically, a motion to recommit could include “instructions” that proposed to immediately amend a measure on the House floor. Oftentimes, the minority party would use such a motion to obtain a vote in connection to a favored policy. Since the 117th Congress, however, Members may no longer use a recommittal motion to directly propose changes to a legislative text. Nevertheless, minority Members often connect the vote on the motion to recommit to a policy proposal during general debate on the bill. They sometimes present an amendment they would like to have offered, if allowed, or that they would like the committee to consider if the motion to recommit is successful.

api_metadata.summary:
The first two provisions of the U.S. Constitution’s First Amendment, known as the Religion Clauses, state that “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.” Together, the Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses require the government to be neutral toward religion, neither providing impermissible support nor demonstrating impermissible hostility. 
The Supreme Court acknowledged in Walz v. Tax Commission, 397 U.S. 664, 668 (1970), that the Religion Clauses “are not the most precisely drawn portions of the Constitution.” Over the years, the Supreme Court has employed a variety of tests to analyze whether government support for religion violates the Establishment Clause. Among these methods of analysis, the Court employed the three-part Lemon test for several decades. The Lemon test asked courts to ensure that the challenged government action has a secular purpose, that its primary effect neither advances nor inhibits religion, and that it does not foster excessive government entanglement with religion. Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U.S. 602, 612–13 (1971), abrogation recognized by Groff v. DeJoy, 600 U.S. 447 (2023).
In 2022, however, the Supreme Court announced that it had “abandoned Lemon.” Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507, 534 (2022). Instead, the Court instructed lower courts to interpret the Establishment Clause by “reference to historical practices and understandings.” Id. at 535. While Kennedy announced this new “historical practices and understandings test,” it did not overrule prior decisions that applied the Lemon test or other types of analyses. 
The Kennedy decision did not instruct courts on how to conduct an analysis by reference to historical practices and understandings, but older Supreme Court precedent contains some guidance. For example, the Court looked to Founding-era understandings and practices to invalidate state laws requiring public officials to declare a belief in the existence of God, as well as a state law requiring a specified prayer to be recited at the beginning of a school day. Torcaso v. Watkins, 367 U.S. 488, 496 (1961); Engel v. Vitale, 370 U.S. 421, 424 (1962). The Court also looked to evidence of long-standing historical practices to uphold prayers at the beginning of legislative sessions. Town of Greece v. Galloway, 572 U.S. 565, 569–70 (2014). In Kennedy itself, however, the Court did not look to specific historical practices similar to the challenged government action. Instead, it referenced its own prior precedent evaluating whether similar practices were coercive. Kennedy thus suggests some prior Supreme Court precedent that did not look to historical practices or understandings may remain good law.
After Kennedy, lower courts have taken different approaches to evaluating Establishment Clause claims. Many courts have attempted to apply Kennedy’s instruction to look to historical practices and understandings. Some have sought evidence of practices from the Founding era or later that are in line with the challenged government action; others have looked for evidence of certain historical hallmarks of a religious establishment. At the same time, some lower courts have continued to apply controlling Supreme Court precedent that did not employ a historical analysis. As a general principle, lower courts are still bound to follow the outcomes of any Supreme Court precedent that has direct application. E.g., Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/Am. Express, Inc., 490 U.S. 477, 484 (1989). Lower courts have reached different conclusions, however, about whether specific Supreme Court cases remain controlling after Kennedy. For instance, courts have disagreed about the continuing validity of Supreme Court precedent evaluating laws requiring public display of the Ten Commandments, with ongoing appeals making their way to the Supreme Court. Compare Nathan v. Alamo Heights Indep. Sch. Dist., 173 F.4th 576, 590–91 (5th Cir. 2026), petition for cert. filed, No. 26-257 (U.S. Aug. 27, 2026), with Stinson v. Fayetteville Sch. Dist. No. 1, 824 F. Supp. 3d 792, 807 (W.D. Ark. 2026), appeal docketed, No. 26-1722 (8th Cir. Apr. 17, 2026).
This unsettled state of jurisprudence can make it difficult to assess how courts might review existing federal laws or any new laws that arguably support religion. Courts might look to historical practices and understandings, but there are open questions regarding how to conduct this inquiry. Further, courts may still have to assess whether existing Supreme Court precedent has direct application to the facts before them, requiring them to rule a certain way regardless of historical practices or understandings.
